## SECTION XVI.

### ABOUT ARABIA IN GENERAL.

---

## Chapter I.

->*Concerning the Description of Arabia.*<-

Man, even in a society where civilization has perhaps been carried to excess—where artifice stifles or disguises the sentiments of nature—never forgets his original destination. He is still fond of even the mere shadow of that liberty, independence, and simplicity which he has lost through refinement, although they are so congenial <note>original: "congenial" – meaning naturally suited or essential to one's character.</note> to his existence. He is charmed to encounter these again, even in the illusions of pastoral poetry <term>Pastoral poetry: A genre of literature that portrays the life of shepherds and rural people in an idealized, simple manner.</term>.

<vocab>Arabia, civilization, nature, liberty, independence, simplicity, refinement, pastoral poetry</vocab>

<summary>Carsten Niebuhr introduces his general description of Arabia by reflecting on the universal human longing for the liberty and simplicity of nature, which he suggests is preserved in Arabian society but lost in over-civilized European cultures.</summary>
<keywords>Arabia, civilization, human nature, liberty, independence, simplicity, pastoral poetry, Carsten Niebuhr</keywords>

--- Page 20 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the description of Arabia, following the author's reflection on the human desire for simplicity and liberty.</meta>

<page-num>2</page-num>
<header>NIEBUHR’S TRAVELS</header>

We are no less fond of tracing these native features of the human mind where they are to be discovered in the records of remote ages, in which the natural manners of mankind appear undisguised by affectation <term>Affectation: Artificial behavior or speech designed to impress; pretension.</term> and are not yet altered by the progress of arts or government <note>original: "policy" – here referring to the systems of civil administration and organized society.</note>. Even without considering <note>original: "adverting to"</note> the causes of the pleasure we feel, we are always pleased to find even some faint traces of our natural and primary rights, and of the happiness for which we were originally intended.

If any people in the world offer in their history an instance of high antiquity and of great simplicity of manners, the Arabs surely do. Coming among them, one can hardly help imagining themselves <note>original: "fancying one’s ſelf"</note> suddenly carried backward to the ages that immediately followed the Great Flood <term>The Great Flood: A reference to the biblical narrative of Noah's Ark, used here as a chronological marker for early human history.</term>. Here, we are tempted to imagine ourselves among the ancient patriarchs <term>Patriarchs: The biblical fathers of the human race, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, often depicted as nomadic leaders.</term>, with whose adventures we were so entertained <note>original: "amused"</note> during our childhood. The language, which has been spoken since time immemorial and which so closely resembles that which we are accustomed to regard as being of the most distant antiquity <note>original: "distant antiquity" – likely referring to Hebrew, which scholars of Niebuhr's time closely linked with Arabic.</note>, completes the illusion that the similarity of their manners began.

The country inhabited by this nation offers many objects of curiosity that are no less unique <note>original: "singular"</note> and interesting. Intersected by sandy deserts,

<summary>Niebuhr describes the Arabs as a people who preserve the ancient simplicity and manners of the biblical patriarchs, noting that their language and lifestyle offer a glimpse into the earliest ages of human history.</summary>
<keywords>Arabs, antiquity, patriarchs, human nature, Arabic language, biblical history, simplicity, Carsten Niebuhr</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the geography and historical isolation of Arabia. The previous page established the Arabs as a people of high antiquity and simple manners, similar to biblical patriarchs.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>
<header>IN ARABIA, &c.</header>

and vast ranges of mountains, it presents on one side nothing but desolation in its most frightful form, while the other is adorned with all the beauties of the most fertile regions. Such is its position that it enjoys, at once, all the advantages of both hot and temperate climates. The unique products <note>original: "peculiar productions"</note> of regions far distant from one another are produced here in equal perfection. Having never been conquered, Arabia has scarcely known any changes except those produced by the hand of nature; it bears none of the marks of human violence <note>original: "fury" — referring here to the destruction and scars left by war and conquest.</note>, which appear in so many other places.

With all these circumstances, so naturally calculated to engage curiosity, Arabia has been until now very little known. The ancients, who made their discoveries of countries by conquering them, remained ignorant of the state and history of a region where their armies could never penetrate. What Greek and Latin authors mention concerning Arabia proves, by its obscurity, their ignorance of almost everything respecting the Arabs. Prejudices regarding the inconveniences and dangers of traveling in Arabia have until now kept modern writers in equal ignorance. I shall have occasion to remark that our best books of geography abound with major <note>original: "capital"</note> errors on this subject; as, for instance, <meta>catchword: stance,</meta>

<summary>Niebuhr describes Arabia as a land of geographical contrasts that has remained largely unknown to the West because it was never conquered by the Greeks or Romans. He argues that existing European geographical accounts are filled with major errors due to these historical prejudices and the perceived dangers of travel.</summary>
<keywords>Arabia, geography, exploration, isolation, Greek authors, Latin authors, conquest, geographical errors</keywords>

<page-num>4</page-num>

<meta>catchword: of</meta>

stance, concerning the subjection of the Arabs to the Turks and Persians.

For these reasons, I have decided to give a more detailed and thorough <note>original: "minute and circumstantial"</note> description of a country and a people who deserve to be better known than they currently are. In the first part of my travels, I mentioned some of what I saw myself. However, because my stay in Arabia was so short, I only had time to travel through a few provinces of that vast country. Therefore, I sought information about the rest from various honest and intelligent Arabs. I was most successful in obtaining this information from scholars <note>original: "men of letters"</note> and merchants; those in public office were more preoccupied with their own affairs and generally had a more reserved character.

This method of gathering my information seemed to offer several distinct advantages. It will be equally useful for me to distinguish between what I witnessed firsthand and what I was told by others. In this way, the reader will be able to tell the difference between what I report based solely on my own observations and what I recount based on the collective evidence of many of the nation’s most enlightened people. I will find many more favorable opportunities
of

<summary>Niebuhr explains his methodology for documenting Arabia, noting that he supplemented his personal observations with information gathered from reliable Arab scholars and merchants. He aims to provide a distinction between firsthand accounts and reported information to ensure the accuracy of his geographical and social descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>methodology, travel writing, Carsten Niebuhr, Arabic scholars, merchants, primary sources, geographical accuracy</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page concludes Niebuhr's introductory remarks on his methodology and the challenges of researching Arabic history before beginning the geographical description of the region.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>IN ARABIA, etc.</header>

...of introducing certain details <note>original: "particulars"</note> which I could not have otherwise included in the account of my travels without interrupting the progress of the narrative too frequently. The reader will also be better entertained when presented with a sketch illustrating the features of the country as well as the people who inhabit it.

I would have liked to add a brief summary <note>original: "compend"</note> of the history of this unique <note>original: "singular"</note> nation. However, I found this impossible. In the East, there are no libraries and no men of deep learning <note>original: "erudition"</note>—resources that a traveler could find with great ease in Europe. Yet, there are ancient Arabic historians; but copies of their works are very rare, as I learned in Cairo <note>original: "Kahira"</note> and Mocha <note>original: "Mokha"</note>. It would be of great importance, however, to examine those authors who are still unknown in Europe. I am convinced the search would hardly be pointless. Those works would shed new light on several eras <note>original: "epochs"</note> in the history of ancient nations (A).

### CHAPTER II.

->*The Extent and the Divisions of Arabia.*<-

**A**rabia, strictly speaking <note>original: "properly so called"</note>, is that great peninsula formed by the Red Sea <note>original: "Arabic Gulph"</note>, the Indian Ocean, and the Persian Gulf. The ancients seem 

<meta>catchword: appear</meta>

<summary>Niebuhr explains the lack of accessible libraries and scholars in the East as an obstacle to writing a complete history of Arabia, though he notes the existence of rare Arabic manuscripts. He then begins Chapter II by defining the geographical boundaries of the Arabian Peninsula.</summary>
<keywords>Arabic history, Cairo, Mocha, Arabic historians, geography, Red Sea, Persian Gulf, Indian Ocean</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the geographic boundaries of Arabia, following the definition of the peninsula begun on the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>NIEBUHR'S TRAVELS</header>

appear to have included <note>original: "comprehended"</note> under the name of Arabia the whole region <note>original: "tract"</note> lying between those seas and a line drawn from the tip of the Persian Gulf to that of the Red Sea <note>original: "Arabic Gulph"</note>. This line, however, was not the real boundary of the country, but was merely imagined to be so out of ignorance.

Whatever one might think of the limits assigned to this country by the ancients, a much larger area must, in any case, be recognized as modern Arabia. Due to the conquests and settlements of the Arabs in Syria and Palestine, the deserts of these countries are now considered part of Arabia. Thus, it can be viewed as bounded on one side by the River Euphrates and on the other by the Isthmus of Suez.

Yet, we should not consider all those countries where these people have made conquests or established colonies as forming a part of Arabia. Of all nations, the Arabs have spread the farthest across the world; and throughout all their migrations <note>original: "wanderings"</note>, they have preserved their language, manners, and unique customs better than any other nation. From east to west, from the banks of the Senegal River to the Indus River, one encounters Arab colonies. From north to south, they are scattered from the Euphrates to the island of Madagascar. Even the Tartar hordes have not occupied such a vast portion of the globe.

### CHAP. III.

#### *Of the Revolutions of Arabia* <note>In this context, "revolutions" refers to the major political changes, turnovers in power, and historical shifts in the region.</note>

All that is known concerning the earliest period of the history of this country is that it was governed in those days by powerful monarchs called ***Tobba***. This is thought to have been a title common to all those princes, just as the name of ***Pharaoh*** was to the ancient sovereigns of Egypt.

There exists, however, a fairly distinct tradition among learned Arabs regarding those ancient kings which deserves to be noted. They claim to know, from ancient monuments, that ***Tobba*** was the family name of those sovereigns; that they came from the neighborhood of **Samarkand** <note>original: "Samarcand"; a major city in modern-day Uzbekistan, then part of Tartary</note>, were fire-worshipers <note>This likely refers to Zoroastrianism</note>, and conquered and civilized Arabia. This tradition aligns with the plausible hypothesis of a clever writer who derives the knowledge and civilization of the southern people from a nation that once flourished in that part of **Tartary** in which **Samarkand** is situated (D) <note>The letter (D) likely refers to a citation or footnote in the original text, possibly referencing Enlightenment theories about the Central Asian origins of civilization</note>.

One thing I had the opportunity to observe myself seems to support the same hypothesis. A Dutch renegade <note>original: "renegado"; a person who has deserted their religion or country, often used in this period for Europeans who converted to Islam</note> who had traveled through Arabia several times showed me, at Mocha <note>original: "Mokha"; a major port city on the Red Sea in Yemen, famous for its coffee trade</note>, a copy of an inscription in strange and unknown characters that he had found in a province far from the sea coast. I was in poor health at the time and neglected to copy it. However, the unusual form of the characters—which consisted entirely of straight lines—made such an impression on my memory that, upon my return, I recognized that the inscriptions at Persepolis <note>An ancient ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire, known for its extensive cuneiform inscriptions</note> were written in the same alphabet (E) <note>Likely a reference to cuneiform, which Niebuhr was one of the first Westerners to accurately copy and help decipher</note>. Thus, it appears that both the Arabs and the Persians had sovereigns from the same nation who spoke the same language, or at least used the same characters for writing.

Whatever the origin of those conquerors may have been, many circumstances combine to prove that, in ancient times, the Arabs played an important role on the stage of human affairs, even though the memory of the political shifts <note>original: "revolutions"</note> that occurred among them has not been passed down to future generations. There can be no doubt that they conquered Egypt at a time before the beginning of Greek history.

As those families multiplied, the younger branches still retained some respect for the eldest branch. Of all the descendants <note>original: "progeny"</note>, the eldest was considered the closest to the parent stem. And, although the subdivisions became more and more numerous, they still regarded themselves as composing but one body in remembrance of their common origin. Such a collection of families, all descended from the same stock, forms what we call a tribe. In this manner, it was easy for the representative of the eldest branch to retain some of the original paternal authority over the entire tribe to which he belonged.

Sometimes, when a family became too numerous, it split off from the rest with which it was connected and formed a new tribe. This primitive <note>original: "primitive"; here meaning original or ancient</note> form of government, which has always existed without alteration among the Arabs, proves the antiquity of this people and makes their present state more interesting than it would otherwise be. Among the Bedouins <note>original: "Bedouins"; nomadic Arab people of the desert</note>, it is preserved in all its purity. For now, I shall content myself with making some general reflections upon the spirit of the Arabian government.

The Bedouins, or pastoral Arabs who live in tents, have many Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; leaders or elders of a tribe</note>, each of whom governs his family with power that is almost absolute. All the Sheikhs, however, who belong to the same tribe, acknowledge a common chief who is called *Sheikh al-Shuyukh* <note>original: "Schech es Scheuch"; Sheikh of Sheikhs</note>, or *Sheikh al-Kabir* <note>original: "Schech el Kbir"; the Great Sheikh or Grand Sheikh</note>, and whose authority is limited by custom. The dignity of Grand Sheikh is hereditary within a certain family; but the inferior Sheikhs, upon the death of a Grand Sheikh, choose the successor out of his family without regard to age, direct lineage, or any other consideration except for superior abilities.

Despotism <term>The exercise of absolute power, especially in a cruel and oppressive way.</term> would never have been known in Arabia, even in the slightest degree, had it not been for theocracy <term>A system of government in which religious leaders rule in the name of God or a higher power.</term>, which is its usual source. The Imams, being regarded as the successors and descendants of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, are acknowledged as both the temporal <note>Secular or political, as opposed to spiritual.</note> and spiritual heads within their dominions. They have thus found ways to take advantage of the simple faith <note>original: "simplicity"</note> of their subjects to increase their own authority. Nevertheless, the spirit <note>original: "genius"</note> of the people, their customs, and even their religion are all hostile to the progress of despotism, and they work together to check the Imams in the exercise of their power.

The idea of forming republican governments seems never to have occurred to the Arabians. This form of government is not a necessary consequence of the original condition of mankind. It must have originated among people whose patience was exhausted by the outrages of arbitrary power; or perhaps, sometimes, from the accidental gathering <note>original: "fortuitous concourse"</note> of persons not connected by family ties. <keywords>Sheikhs, despotism, theocracy, Imams, Muhammad, political structure, Hashid, Bekil, Yemen, tribal independence</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on different forms of Arabian governance, moving from the semi-independent Sheikhs under larger empires to confederations of princes and unique independent communities.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>IN ARABIA, etc.</header>

The Bekil <note>A major tribal confederation in Yemen, often paired with the Hashid.</note> are not so much a federated republic as an association of several minor princes joined together for mutual defense against their common enemies. Their government resembles the Holy Roman Empire <note>original: "German empire"</note> rather than the republics of Switzerland or the United Provinces <note>The Dutch Republic.</note>. Regarding the so-called Republic of Barawa <note>original: "Brava," a port city in modern-day Somalia.</note> on the eastern coast of Africa, little is known for certain. There is reason to believe that it is also merely a confederation of Arab Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> in that country.

The colony of Jews who occupy a district in the province of Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas," a region in western Saudi Arabia.</note> is governed by an independent, hereditary Sheikh. Having been separated from their fellow countrymen for centuries, they have adopted the form of government they saw practiced by their immediate neighbors.

This large number of minor sovereigns causes several inconveniences for the general population. Wars inevitably arise frequently among states whose territories are so closely intertwined and whose rulers must manage such a variety of conflicting interests. Fortunately, however, these quarrels almost never result in very fatal consequences. An army of a thousand Arabs will retreat and consider themselves defeated if they lose even seven or eight of their men.

These conflicts are ended as easily as they are started.

There is no doubt that such a large number of nobles and minor princes—whose numbers are constantly growing due to polygamy <note>Since rulers had many wives, they produced many sons who all claimed noble status, leading to a crowded and expensive ruling class.</note>—has a negative impact on the general well-being of the people. It is surprising to see the Arabs, living in such a rich and fertile land, so poorly housed, poorly fed, badly clothed, and lacking almost all the basic comforts of life. However, the reasons for this situation fully explain the results.

The poverty of the wandering Arabs <note>The Bedouin tribes.</note> is clearly a choice. They prefer freedom to wealth, and the simple life of a herder to a life of restriction and hard labor, even though such labor might provide them with a wider variety of pleasures. On the other hand, those who live in cities or work the land are kept in poverty by the excessive taxes demanded from them. The entire wealth of the people is consumed to support their many princes and priests. The example of the territory of Zebid <note>A city and surrounding fertile region in western Yemen.</note>, which I mentioned in my description of that city, shows that a farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> cannot survive such extreme taxes <note>original: "imposts"</note> without being reduced to misery.

One general cause for the economic decline of Arabia is undoubtedly that it is no longer the primary route for trade with India, following the discovery of the sea route around the Cape of Good Hope <note>The Portuguese discovery of this route in 1498 bypassed the traditional Arab-controlled land and Red Sea routes, leading to a major loss of revenue for the region.</note>.

## SECTION XVII.

### OF THE PROVINCE OF HEJAZ <note>original: "Hedjas"</note>.

---

#### CHAPTER I.

->*On the General Appearance of this Province, and Some of its Towns.*<-

Hejaz <note>The region of western Saudi Arabia that contains the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.</note> is bordered on the east by Najd <note>original: "Nejed"; the central highland region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>; on the north by the Sinai Desert; on the south by Yemen; and on the west by the Arabian Gulf <note>original: "Arabic Gulph." In the 18th century, this term was commonly used to refer to what we now call the Red Sea.</note>. I cannot claim to know its inland borders precisely, as I have only seen the coastline. Anything I mention regarding the other parts of the region is based entirely on hearsay.

From what I have heard, this district looks very much like Yemen. Starting from the seashore, a plain of varying width stretches inland to the base of a mountain range, which runs in

This plain, like the Tihamah <note>original: "Tehama"; the coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula along the Red Sea.</note>, is entirely sandy and barren, with the only exceptions being the openings of the valleys, which may be watered by torrents from the mountains.

The highlands of Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas"</note> produce an abundance of fruits and other various commodities; yet, I have not heard coffee mentioned among their products. The Balm of Mecca <note>A fragrant resin, also known as Balsam of Gilead, harvested from the *Commiphora gileadensis* tree and highly valued in antiquity for medicine and perfume.</note> comes from those lofty regions, and chiefly from the extensive mountain of Safra, which is a three-day journey away from the Arabian Gulf <note>The Red Sea.</note>.

This barren plain cannot support a large population. I have mentioned already that I could see no towns or villages during my passage from Suez to Al-Luhayyah <note>original: "Loheya"</note>. I have described Yanbu <note>original: "Jambo"</note>, Jeddah <note>original: "Jidda"</note>, and Al Qunfudhah <note>original: "Ghunfude"</note>, which are the only towns or harbors on all this extensive coast. The other villages that may be thinly scattered here and there are too few and too paltry to merit notice.

In the interior parts of this country, I could discover no considerable city except Ta’if <note>original: "Taaif"</note>, situated upon a lofty mountain in so agreeable a country that the Arabs compare its environs to those of Damascus and Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note>. This city supplies Jeddah and Mecca with excellent fruits, particularly raisins, and carries on a considerable trade in almonds, which grow in great plenty in its territories.

## CHAP. II.

->*Concerning the Power of the Turks in the Hejaz.*<-

THE Grand Signior <note>A historical title for the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.</note> styles himself Sovereign of the Hejaz; and our geographers, trusting in that empty title, represent this part of Arabia as a province of the Turkish empire. However, the authority of the Sultan here is nothing but a mere shadow, which the Arabs would have abolished long ago if they had not found it in their interest to preserve it.

Notwithstanding the lofty pretensions of the Grand Signior, his power in Arabia consists solely of a few slender privileges. He sends

Yet, the income generated this way is not even enough to cover the expenses of the Pasha’s household. Consequently, a Turk considers himself disgraced when appointed to this "fine" government and remains miserable until he is recalled.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Concerning the Sharif of Mecca.*<-

**SHARIF** <note>original: "Sherriffe"; a title for the descendants of the Prophet Muhammad</note>, as I have already mentioned, is the title given to the descendants of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> through *Hasan ibn Ali* <note>the grandson of Muhammad</note>. Although this branch of Muhammad’s descendants has never attained the rank of Caliph <note>the supreme religious and political leader of the Muslim community</note> or Imam, they nevertheless seem to have always held sovereignty over most of the cities in the Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas"; the western region of the Arabian Peninsula containing Mecca and Medina</note>.

The descendants of *Hasan ibn Ali* are now divided into several branches. Of these, the family of *Ali Bunemi*—which consists of at least three hundred people—enjoys the exclusive right to the throne of Mecca. The *Ali Bunemi* are, in turn, subdivided into two smaller branches: the *Dhawi Zayd* <note>original: "Darii Sajid"</note> and the *Dhawi Barakat* <note>original: "Darii Barkad"</note>. Sometimes one branch and sometimes the other has provided the rulers of Mecca and Medina when those cities were separate states.

The Turkish Sultan is not only indifferent to the order of succession within this family,

The Grand Sharif is seldom able to maintain himself on the throne, and it is even rarer for his reign not to be disturbed by the revolt of his nearest relations. There have been instances of a nephew succeeding his uncle, an uncle succeeding his nephew, and sometimes of a person from a remote branch taking the place of the reigning prince of the ancient house.

When I was in Arabia in 1763, the reigning Sharif *Mesad* had sat for fourteen years on the throne. ## CHAPTER IV.

### *Of the City of Mecca.*

This city is situated in a dry and barren region, a full day’s journey from Jeddah <note>original: "Jidda"</note>. However, a few leagues <term>league: a traditional unit of distance, usually measuring about three miles</term> beyond it, toward the highlands, an abundance of excellent fruit can be found. In the summer months, the heat is excessive in Mecca; to avoid and moderate it as much as possible, the inhabitants carefully shut their windows and water the streets. There have been instances of people suffocating in the middle of the streets due to the burning wind called the *Simoom* or *Samiel* <note>original: "Samoum or Samiel"; a hot, dry, dust-laden desert wind</note>.

As many of the highest nobility in the Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas"</note> live in Mecca, the buildings here are better than in any other city in Arabia. Among its elegant buildings, the most remarkable is the famous *Kaaba* <note>original: "Kaba"</note>, or House of God, which was held in high veneration by the Arabs even before the days of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>.

My curiosity would have led me to see this sacred and unique structure, but no Christian dares enter Mecca. This is not because there is any express prohibition in the laws of Muhammad, or because liberal-minded Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> would be offended, but rather because of the prejudices of the people in general,

Neither the stone of Abraham nor that of Ishmael <note>original: "Ismael"</note> receives the same honors; pilgrims are not obliged to either visit or kiss them.

The Arabs venerate the Kaaba as having been built by Abraham and having been his house of prayer. Within the same enclosure is the well of Zamzam <note>original: "Zemzem"</note>, valued for the excellence of its water and no less for its miraculous origin. Hagar, when banished by her master, set young Ishmael down here while she went to find some water to quench his thirst. Returning after an unsuccessful search, she was surprised to see a spring bursting up from the ground between the child’s legs. That spring is the present Well of Zamzam.

Another ornament of the Kaaba is a row of metal pillars surrounding it. These pillars are joined by chains, on which hang a vast number of silver lamps. The porticos or arcades mentioned above are designed to protect the pilgrims from the intense <note>original: "torrid"</note> heat of the day. They also serve another purpose; for the merchants, of

### CHAPTER V.

#### *Concerning the Pilgrimage of Muslims.* <note>original: "of the Mussulmans"</note>

It is well known that every Muslim is obliged, once in his life, to visit Mecca and perform acts of devotion in the sacred places. If this law were strictly observed, the gathering <note>original: "concourse"</note> of pilgrims would be immense; the city could not contain such crowds from every country in which the Islamic religion <note>original: "Mahometan religion"</note> has been introduced. It may be presumed, therefore, that none but those who are exceptionally devout fulfill this duty.

Indeed, those whose financial circumstances do not allow them to undertake such a distant journey are permitted to hire a person to perform it on their behalf.

<summary>Niebuhr describes the sacred boundaries of Mecca where pilgrims must change into ritual attire and explains that while the Hajj is a universal obligation for Muslims, many fulfill it through proxies due to the immense scale of the journey.</summary>

them. But a pilgrim acting in this capacity <note>original: "character"</note> can represent only one person at a time. To prevent fraud <note>original: "imposture"</note>, he must bring back a formal certificate <note>original: "attestation"</note> from an Imam <note>a religious leader or scholar</note> in Mecca. This document states that he has actually performed the required religious rituals <note>original: "appointed devotional exercises"</note> in the holy places in the name of that person, whether they are living or dead. For even after the death of a man who neglected to fulfill this religious law during his lifetime, the duty may still be performed in his name and for his benefit. I have sometimes met professional pilgrims who had been poorly paid by their employers and were forced to beg for charity <note>original: "ask alms"</note>.

Although the caravans are few compared to the total number of Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note>, even those few consist largely of people traveling for reasons other than religious devotion. These include merchants who view the caravan as the safest way to transport <note>original: "conveyance"</note> their goods and the best opportunity to sell them; suppliers <note>original: "purveyors"</note> of all kinds who provide the pilgrims with necessities; and soldiers paid by the caravan to escort them. Consequently, many people have seen Mecca several times without ever visiting it for any reason other than personal gain <note>original: "views of interest"</note>.

The most significant of these caravans is the Syrian one, commanded by the Pasha <note>original: "Pacha"; a high-ranking official or governor in the Ottoman Empire</note> of Damascus. At a certain distance from Mecca, it joins the caravan from Egypt, which is the second largest in numbers.

## CHAPTER VI.
### *Of the City of Medina.*

About a day's journey away from the port of Yanbu <note>original: "Jambo"</note> stands Medina, a city of medium size, surrounded by mediocre <note>original: "indifferent"</note> walls and situated in a sandy plain. It belongs to the Sharif <note>original: "Sherriffe"</note> of Mecca, but has recently been governed by a sovereign of its own from the family of *Dahri Barakat* <note>original: "Darii Barkad"</note>. At this present time, the Sharif rules it through a Vizier <note>original: "Vizir"</note>, who must be a member of the royal family.

Before the days of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, this city was called *Yathrib* <note>original: "Jathreb"</note>. But it was called *Madinat al-Nabi* <note>original: "Medinet en Nebbi"</note>, the City of the Prophet, from the time when Muhammad, following his expulsion from Mecca by the Quraysh <note>original: "Koreischites"</note> tribe, took refuge here and continued to make it his place of residence for the rest of his life.

The tomb of Muhammad at Medina is held in great respect by Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note>, but they are not required to visit it to perform any devotional exercises. However, as the caravans from Syria necessarily pass near Medina on their return from Mecca, they turn aside to see the Prophet’s tomb.

I also obtained from a Turk a drawing of the mosque in which the tomb stands. It is situated in a corner of the great square, whereas the Kaaba <note>original: "Ka-ba"</note> is in the middle of the square at Mecca. For fear that the people might superstitiously offer worship to the remains <note>original: "ashes"</note> of the Prophet, the tomb is enclosed within iron rails and can only be seen by looking through these. It is made of plain masonry in the form of a chest, and this is the entire monument. I could never learn the origin of the ridiculous story, which has been circulated in Europe, concerning vast magnets said to support the coffin of Muhammad in the air.

This tomb is placed between two other tombs, in which rest the remains of the first two Caliphs <note>Abu Bakr and Umar, the first leaders of the Muslim community after Muhammad</note>.

Although it is no more magnificent than the tombs of the founders of most other mosques, the building that covers the tomb is draped with a piece of silk fabric embroidered with gold. This fabric is replaced every seven years by the Pasha <note>original: "Pacha"</note> of Damascus.

Forty eunuchs guard this building, mainly to protect the treasure said to be kept within it. This treasure consists primarily of precious stones, which are the offerings of wealthy Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note>. However, there was such an obvious mixture of legend in the accounts I received that I did not know what to believe. Several respected Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> seriously assured me that the philosopher’s stone—or a large quantity of powder used for turning other metals into fine gold—was one of the most valuable items in that treasure. A prominent Arabian merchant informed me that the guards were stationed there for no other purpose than to keep away the common people, who had begun throwing dirt onto the tomb, which they would later scrape off and keep as a kind of religious relic.

Some Muslims whom I could trust assured me that the Jews did indeed provide auxiliary troops to the Arab army that had lately pillaged the caravan from Damascus; but the actual leaders of that enterprise were the Sheikh of the **Harb** tribe in the Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas"</note> and the Sheikh of the **Anaesse** tribe in Najd <note>original: "Nejed"</note>.

Yet the country they inhabit is surrounded by such vast and sandy deserts that, without a caravan, such a secluded region cannot be safely entered or left.

## SECTION XVIII.

### OF YEMEN IN GENERAL.

---

#### CHAP. I.

->*Of the Boundaries and Subdivisions of Yemen.*<-

This large province, which includes the finest and most fertile part of Arabia, is surrounded by the Arabian Gulf <note>original: "Arabic Gulph"; here referring to the Red Sea</note> and by the provinces of Hadramawt, Najd, and Hejaz <note>original: "Hadramaut, Nejed, and Hedjas"</note>.

Yemen is naturally divided into two parts, which differ greatly in soil and climate. The region bordering on the Arabian Gulf is a dry and sandy plain, nearly a two days' journey in breadth, and is scorched by the most intense heat. The other region, extending immediately beyond this, is a highland country full of steep yet fertile hills, and enjoying a much more temperate climate. However, these circumstances will be more appropriately covered within the natural history of Arabia; here, I am speaking only of its political divisions.

Yemen is, like the rest of Arabia, divided <note>original: "parcelled out"</note> among a number of different sovereigns in unequal portions. Some of them are princes of

A traveler who only stops for a short time on his journey could no more learn the names of every minor state here than they could identify all the tiny baronies in Germany. What I know for certain, however—having seen many striking examples of it—is that these endless subdivisions of territory among such a multitude of petty sovereigns are largely the cause of the state of decline in which Arabia currently appears. Such a collection of conflicting interests is naturally fatal to trade and industry.

## CHAPTER II.

### *Of the Principality of Aden.*

This small state is bounded on the south by the Indian Ocean, on the west and north by the territories of the Imam <note>The Imam of Sana'a, the ruler of Yemen</note>, and on the east by the country of Yafa <note>original: "Jafa"</note>. It formerly belonged to the Imam; but, in 1730, the inhabitants expelled the Imam's governor and elected a Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note>, who is completely independent.

Aden, an ancient and celebrated city, gives its name to this principality. It still has a good harbor, although it has declined significantly from what it once was. Its trade is now insignificant, for the sovereign is never at peace with his neighbors. Coffee from Yafa is the only article for export that this city provides.

Among a number of cities and several castles of no great strength belonging to this small state, the only place that is still in any degree significant is Lahij <note>original: "Lahadsje"</note>, the seat of the current Sheikh Abd al-Karim al-Fadhli <note>original: "Abd ul Kerim el Foddeli"</note>. This town was besieged by the famous Abd Rabbuh <note>original: "Abd Urrab"</note>, from whom it suffered considerably. Al-Fadhli <note>original: "Foddeli"</note> is a narrow district containing a city and several villages, known for having been the original seat of the reigning family.

## CHAP. III.

### *Of the Principality of Kawkaban.*

The country bearing this name is surrounded on almost every side by the territories of the Imam of Sana'a <note>The capital city of Yemen</note>; it only meets the territory of the confederated Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> of Hashid wa Bakil <note>original: "Haschid-u-Bekil"; these are two major tribal confederations in Yemen</note> on one side. The reigning family are descendants of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> through Al-Hadi, the Imam of Sa'dah <note>original: "Saade"</note>. For several centuries <note>original: "ages"</note>, they possessed considerable territories in Yemen and retained the title of Imam even during the Turkish occupation <note>original: "usurpation of the Turks"</note>. 

However, when the Turks were driven out of Yemen by Qasim al-Kabir <note>original: "Khassem el Kebir"; Qasim the Great, founder of the Qasimid dynasty</note>, that illustrious family was forced to yield the title of Imam to the new Arabian conqueror and to content themselves with the title of Sayyid <note>original: "Sidi or Sejid"; a title denoting a descendant of Muhammad</note>. Nevertheless, they still retain sovereign authority over a significant territory.

A list of these sovereigns was shared with me, but I could not find any way to verify its authenticity. The reigning prince in 1763 was Sayyid Ahmad <note>original: "Sejid Achmet"</note>. He had several sons and brothers, and a great many nephews.

He resides at Kawkaban <note>original: "Kaukeban"</note>, a small, unfortified town, but situated on the summit of an almost inaccessible mountain...

### CHAP. IV.

->*Of the Allied Princes of Hashid wa Bakil.*<-
<note>original: "Haschid-u-Bekil"; these are the two most powerful tribal confederations in the Yemeni highlands, still significant in modern Yemeni politics</note>

The extensive country of Hashid wa Bakil, held by a number of confederated Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note>, is properly named *Bilad al-Qabayil* <note>original: "Bellad el Kobail"</note>, the "Country of the Highlanders." However, the name expressing the confederacy is the one by which it is more commonly known. It extends northward as far as the Desert of Amasia; on the south and the east, it is bounded by the dominions of the Imam and the Principality of Kawkaban <note>original: "Kaukeban"</note>; westward, it meets the sovereign state of Abu Arish <note>original: "Abu Arisch"</note>.

Arish. A republican spirit is so rare throughout Asia that these states should be seen as a unique political phenomenon in the East.

This highland country contains many Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; tribal leaders or lords</note> descended from very ancient noble families, each of whom rules within his own domains as a sovereign prince. These Sheikhs, finding themselves unable to individually offer any successful resistance to a powerful neighbor, have joined together to defend themselves through their combined strength.

Even in Europe, it is not easy to obtain a thorough knowledge of the principles of any political constitution; but among the distrustful and suspicious inhabitants of the East, such a task is almost impossible. I was unable to learn the specific laws and conditions upon which the Hashid wa Bakil <note>original: "Hascid-u-Bekil"; a powerful tribal alliance in Yemen that remains influential today</note> confederation is maintained. All I know is that they choose a certain number of chiefs and, during wartime, several generals to command their united forces.

These allied princes and their subjects are much better soldiers, and more inclined toward war, than other Arabs. The Imam of Sana’a and the Sharif <note>original: "Sherriffe"; the ruler and religious protector of the holy city</note> of Mecca each maintain several regiments of these highlanders and pay them better than their other troops. They require officers from their own nation, and the Sheikhs usually both recruit the regiments and nominate <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "nominate."</note>

nominate the officers. For this reason, the Imam <note>The religious and political ruler of Sana’a</note> fears to quarrel with the confederates. When they go to war with the Sovereign of Sana’a, their countrymen who are in his service desert him and join their own people.

A tradition concerning their common origin may have been the cause that first gave rise to the confederation among those Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; tribal leaders</note>, and which has inclined them to maintain it until now. *Hashid* and *Bakil*, whose names the confederates have adopted, were, according to this tradition, brothers—the sons of a man named *Babroscham* and a princess called *Nedsjema*. *Babroscham*, who was born to honorable parents in *Anatolia* <note>original: "Natolia"; modern-day Turkey</note>, after some romantic adventures, carried off that princess, who was the daughter of the King of *Bithynia* <note>An ancient region in northwest Asia Minor</note>, and sought refuge in these mountains of *Yemen*. There, through his sons *Hashid* and *Bakil*, he became the ancestor of all the Sheikhs of *Bilad al-Qabayil* <note>original: "Bellad el Kobail"; Arabic for "Country of the Tribes"</note>; accordingly, they all look up to him as their common father.

It is certain, however, that there are Sheikhs in this country whose families can be traced further back than the date of this tale. In the district of *Khiwan* <note>original: "Kheivan"</note>, and in the city of *Beit at-Toba*, resides the chief of the family of *Toba*, a descendant of the ancient Arabian monarchs of this name <note>Referring to the "Tubba" kings of the ancient Himyarite Kingdom</note>.

I was told of fifty of these independent Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; tribal leaders</note>, some of whom possess lands in the middle of the Imam’s <note>The religious and political ruler of Sana’a</note> territories. It is unnecessary to list all their names here.

The country inhabited by these confederates has varying levels of fertility. Some valleys, which produce fruit in great abundance, are scattered among the hills; even the higher grounds are cultivated and fertile.

A number of castles are scattered across the heights, but few large villages are visible. The town of Khiwan <note>original: "Kheivan"</note>, in the district of the same name, is notable for having been the seat of power, first for the Himyarite <note>original: "Hamjare"; the ancient South Arabian kingdom that preceded the Islamic era</note> monarchs and later for the Imams. Ruins of a very ancient palace can still be seen there.

In some other small villages, there are several monuments which suggest that before the Turkish conquest, a large part of *Bilad al-Qabayil* <note>original: "Bellad el Kobail"; Arabic for "the Country of the Tribes"</note> was under the rule of the ancient Imams.

His son Muhammad, the reigning Sharif of Abu Arish, has so far withstood all the efforts of the Imam to force him back into obedience. It appears, indeed, that they deviate significantly in several points from pure Islam <note>original: "Mahometism"</note>; their practice of circumcision, at least, is totally different. It might be thought that these wandering Arabs, having never been conquered by either Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> or his successors, have retained some parts of their ancient religion. Muslims generally consider the Bedouins to be barely orthodox and reproach them for not being true believers.

These Arabs of the Bani Hilal <note>original: "Beni Halal"</note> tribe inhabit a barren territory. They are poor and survive on the meager produce of their flocks.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Of the Territories of Sahan and Khaulan.*

The Arabs call the mountainous tract between Hashid and Bakil <note>original: "Haschid-u-Bekil"; these are two of the most powerful tribal confederations in Yemen</note> and Hejaz <note>original: "Hedjas"</note>, Sahan <note>original: "Saham" in the chapter heading</note>. This region of the country is of considerable extent and produces an abundance of excellent fruits of all kinds, but especially grapes. Iron mines have also been discovered there, but for want of wood for fuel, they have not been worked. Because of this, iron in Yemen is both expensive and of poor quality.

The inhabitants of this country—especially the highlanders, who have little interaction with strangers—are said to speak the best Arabic. Their speech corresponds more closely to the language of the Quran <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> than that spoken anywhere else; yet, at the same time, they are almost complete strangers to the book itself.

These people differ essentially in their manners from the Arabs in the cities of Yemen. They seldom take more than one wife each. Their women are not permitted to marry until they have completed their fifteenth year, whereas in the dominions of the Imam <note>the Zaydi spiritual and political leader of Yemen</note>, girls are married at the age of nine or ten. They live upon meat, honey, milk, and some vegetables. Their country provides plenty of these items.

There are many independent lordships in this country. The most important of these is *Sa'dah* <note>original: "Saade"</note>, which is held by Prince *Qasim* <note>original: "Khaſſem"</note>, a descendant of Imam *al-Hadi* <note>original: "Hadi"</note>. He comes from the same lineage as the current royal families of Kawkaban <note>original: "Kaukeban"</note> and Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note>. This Prince also takes the title of Imam, but his territory is so small that he can barely defend himself against the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> of the neighboring mountains.

At Sa'dah, his capital and place of residence, there is a custom-house that brings him a significant income. All goods coming from the territories of the Imam <note>the ruler of Sana'a</note> must pass through here on the way to Najran <note>original: "Nedſjeran"</note>, Qahtan <note>original: "Kachtan"</note>, or Mecca, and high taxes <note>original: "duties"</note> are collected. Near this city is a high hill, famous for being the position where a prince of this state endured a seven-year siege by the Turks <note>referring to the Ottoman Empire's historical attempts to control Yemen</note>.

A part of the great desert of *Amasia* lies between Sa'dah and Hashid-u-Bakil <note>original: "Haſchid-u-Bekil"</note>. In the middle of that desert is *Birket Soidan*, which is the only place where travelers can stop for rest and food.

## CHAPTER VII.

### *Concerning the Principalities of Najran and Qahtan.*

Najran <note>original: "Nedsjeran"</note> is situated in a pleasant and well-watered country, a three-day journey northeast of Sa'dah. This narrow territory is fertile in grain <note>original: "corn"; in the 18th century, "corn" referred to any cereal crop, likely wheat or barley in this context</note> and fruits, especially dates. It provides excellent pasture, and its horses and camels are highly sought after throughout all of Arabia.

Its current Sheikh, whose name is Makrami <note>original: "Mecrami"</note>, has earned a very high reputation. It is said that he does not come from the lineage of the ancient nobility. In his youth, he traveled through all of Arabia, Persia, and India. After his return, the Imam of Sa'dah entrusted him with the government of the province of Najran. However, scarcely had Makrami been appointed to this office before he renounced his allegiance <note>The Makrami family became the religious and political leaders of the Ismaili community in Najran</note>.

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*Regarding the Principalities of Nihm and Khawlan.*<-

NIHM <note>original: "NEHHM"</note> is a small district located between Al-Jawf <note>original: "Dsjof"</note> and the territories of the Hashid and Bakil tribes <note>original: "Haſchid-u-Bekil"; these are two major tribal confederations in Yemen that remain politically significant today</note>. The current Sheikh, who possesses a warlike character and is often troublesome to the Imam, is an independent prince. He owns a few small, minor towns, along with a fertile mountain upon which many villages are situated. The inhabitants of *Deiban* are free, but they always join the Sheikh of *Nihm* in his wars against the Imam.

The wandering Arabs in this country have a martial character. In their military expeditions, they ride upon horses or camels. They are quite troublesome to their neighbors who are settled in villages, plundering them and often carrying off their young women. These Bedouins of Al-Jawf are said to have uncommon talents for poetry, and to excel all the other Arabs in this elegant art.

### CHAPTER 10.

->*Regarding the Country of Yafa <note>original: "Jafa"</note>.*<-

**This** territory is surrounded by Aden, some part of the Imam's dominions, and the extensive province of Hadramaut. It is fertile and abounds particularly in coffee and cattle.

## Chapter II.

### *Origin and History of the Imams.*

In my summary of the revolutions of Arabia, I briefly mentioned the one by which the expulsion of the Turks was accomplished. This event took place in 1630; and from this period, we date the rise of the current royal family of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note>. Their great ancestor is Al-Qasim Abu Muhammad <note>original: "Khassem Abu Mahomed"</note>, who was the primary architect of that revolution.

Al-Qasim was a descendant of Muhammad <note>the Prophet</note> through Imam Al-Hadi <note>original: "Hadi"</note>, who is buried at Sa'dah <note>original: "Saade"</note>, where his descendants still rule. From him are descended both the Imams of Sa'dah and the princes of Kawkaban <note>original: "Kaukeban"</note>, whom the Turks were never able to conquer. Al-Qasim lived as a private citizen, supported by the income from an estate left to him by his ancestors on the mountain of Shaharah <note>original: "Schaehara"</note>, northeast of Al-Luhayyah <note>original: "Loheya"</note>. Although he was only a private individual, he enjoyed the friendship of the independent Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> in the Highlands; and, seeing that the Turks were hated by his countrymen, he attacked the Pashas <note>original: "Pachas"; Turkish provincial governors</note> with the help of those Sheikhs,

The Imam is properly the religious leader <note>original: "clergyman"</note> who leads public prayers in the mosques. The royal successors of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> have continued the practice of performing these religious services to prove that they possess spiritual as well as temporal power. Various Arabian princes, who do not dare to assume the title of Caliph, content themselves with that of Imam or *Amir al-Mu'minin* <note>original: "Emir el Mumenim"</note>, which means "Prince of the Faithful." All these sovereigns who are invested with spiritual authority, whether they are Caliphs or Imams, follow the ancient custom of changing their name—much like the Popes in Christendom—upon ascending the throne. Imam Al-Mutawakkil chose Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note> as his place of residence, and there he reigned in peace for ten years.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Of Al-Mahdi, the reigning Imam.*<-

Imam Al-Mansur left several sons, the eldest of whom, *Ali*, naturally had the strongest right to succeed him. His mother was the first wife his father had married and the daughter of the prince of Kawkaban. Consequently, he was a direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> through both his father and his mother. However, the princess, who was still living in Sana'a in 1763, did not have enough influence or political skill <note>original: "address"</note> to secure the succession for her son, even though it was the general wish of the country that he should be the sovereign.

A son named *Abbas* had been born to Al-Mansur by an enslaved Black African woman <note>original: "negress slave"</note>. This woman cleverly concealed her master’s death until the *Kadi* <note>original: "Ka-", with catchword "di"; a Kadi is a Muslim judge or magistrate.</note>

However, in the following year, 1758, the Imam’s general surprised and defeated the allies.

Imam Al-Mahdi Abbas was forty-five years old and had reigned for seventeen years as of 1763. He had a dark complexion, like his ancestors on his mother’s side, and did not at all resemble the other descendants of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>. ## Chapter IV.

->*History of Sheikh Abd Urrab.*<-

Of the enemies with whom Imam Al-Mahdi <note>original: "El Mahadi"</note> had to contend, the most formidable—due to both his intelligence <note>original: "genius"</note> and his courage—was Sheikh Abd Urrab of Al-Hujariyah <note>original: "Hodsjerie"</note>. When speaking of the siege of Taiz <note>original: "Taaes"</note>, I mentioned in passing something of the adventures of this Sheikh, who is regarded as a hero among his countrymen. I found his history interesting, and I shall now describe it at greater length, because it involves several details that illustrate the principles of the Imam’s government and the general customs of the Arabs.

Abd Urrab, the son of a *Naqib* <note>original: "Nakib"; a high military rank or local leader</note> or General who was governor of a small province, succeeded his father in that government. The Imam, pleased with his services, granted him the governorship of Qataba <note>original: "Kataba"</note>, which was a more significant position; at the same time, he entrusted him with a commission to demolish the castles of some neighboring lords. ### CHAPTER V

->*Concerning the Constitution and Government of the Dominions of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note>.*<-

The throne of Yemen is hereditary. If he is generally approved by the subjects, the eldest legitimate son of an Imam is considered the rightful successor.

But the revolutions I have briefly narrated show that this order of succession is often violated. In the despotic governments of the East, indeed, no order can be closely observed because there are no fundamental laws. The practice of polygamy also has a tendency to confuse the order of succession in Asia, as it often happens that brothers by different mothers base their claims to succeed their father upon grounds that are equally false or equally plausible <note>original: "specious"</note>. In such cases, the blind preference of a father who has fallen into senility <note>original: "dotage"</note>, or the intrigues of a favorite, determines the outcome.

The Imam is an absolute prince, and all the more so for uniting in his own person supreme authority—both spiritual and temporal <note>original: "temporal"; meaning secular or worldly power</note>—over his subjects. However, his jurisdiction in religious <note>original: "ecclesiastical"</note> matters does not extend over the dominions of other sovereigns of the same sect. These states each have a Mufti <note>a Muslim legal expert empowered to give rulings on religious law</note> or Cadi <note>a judge</note> for their own spiritual needs.

Although the Imam is absolute, he is checked in the exercise of his authority by the supreme tribunal of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note>, of which he is only the president. This tribunal, consisting of a certain number of Kadis <note>original: "Kadis"; Muslim judges who interpret and administer Islamic law</note>, possesses the sole power of life and death. The Imam may not order any of his subjects to be executed except for those who have been condemned as a result of a criminal prosecution before this court. The Kadis are generally esteemed

Acts of tyranny have commonly ended in the deposition of the prince who risked them. This fate seems to await the current Imam, whose cruelty and extortion have nearly exhausted the patience of his subjects.

At the Imam's court, public offices are numerous, but titles of honor are few. The first minister has no title other than *Faqih* <note>original: "Fakih"; an Arabic term for a person trained in Islamic jurisprudence or a legal scholar</note>; an appellation so vague that his secretaries and men of learning, who think themselves in any degree above the common people <note>original: "vulgar"</note>, adopt it as well as the minister. Every small district in the territories of the Imam has its own governor. I have already noted that the Sovereigns of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note> generally find it to be the best policy to grant these governorships to men who have risen purely by personal merit, rather than to their nobles.

A *Dola* in Yemen is much like a *Pasha* <note>original: "Pacha"</note> in Turkey, though he operates on a smaller scale. He commands the forces stationed in his province, regulates the civil administration <note>original: "police"</note>, and collects the taxes. From lucrative governments, the *Dolas* are recalled every two or three years to prevent them from accumulating too much wealth. When the Imam keeps a *Dola* in his office, he sends him a horse, a saber, and robes. All are required to provide an account, from time to time, of their administration; and when they are guilty of high misdemeanors or convicted of corruption <note>original: "malversations"</note> in office, they are punished by imprisonment or by the seizure of their property, but they are seldom executed <note>original: "punished... capitally"</note>. Sometimes a *Dola* who has been thus disgraced is raised from prison to a new office.

This spy often succeeds the Governor who has been removed based on his reports; however, another *Baskateb* is sent at the same time to do to him what he did to his predecessor.

Every city in which a *Dola* resides also has a Qadi <note>original: "Kadi"; a judge ruling according to Islamic law</note>, who is dependent on the Chief Qadi of Sana'a. The Qadi is the sole judge in civil and religious <note>original: "ecclesiastical"</note> affairs; the *Dola* may not interfere to contradict his sentences or make them ineffective. The Qadis in the provinces, no less than those in the capital, have a high reputation for wisdom and integrity.

In the sea-port towns, the *Amir al-Bahr* <note>original: "Emir Bahrr"; literally 'commander of the sea', acting as a port inspector or harbor master</note>, who is the inspector of the port, holds the chief authority under the *Dola*. ### CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the Revenues of the Imam*<-

It is undoubtedly difficult for a traveler to gain a reasonably accurate understanding of the public revenue of a state where he stays for only a short time. In Arabia, this is particularly difficult; a traveler must be very cautious when asking questions so as not to make himself look suspicious among a nation where so few people have any knowledge of public affairs.

However, I had the advantage of consulting someone on this subject who had held positions in which he could not help but become familiar with the state of the Imam’s finances. This person was Oraki the Jew, the surveyor-general of buildings, who had been a favorite of two successive Imams. I have already provided some account of his adventures in the narrative of our journey to Sana'a.

I was told that in the provinces, every *Dola* <term>a governor of a province or city</term> pays the troops under his command and covers the costs of the police. After deducting all necessary public expenses, he sends the remaining surplus to the Imam.

This revenue comes from long-standing land and poll taxes, as well as duties on commercial goods. The tax on coffee provides a very large portion of this income. ## CHAPTER VII.

### *Regarding the Military Force of Sana'a*

The Imam maintains a body of regular troops, though I could not learn their exact number. According to common opinion, the force normally consists of four thousand infantry—recruited mainly from the *Hashid* and *Bakil* <note>original: "Haschid-u-Bekil," the two most powerful tribal confederations in Yemen</note>—and one thousand cavalry.

The principal commanding officers of this army were the four Sheikhs of *Hamdan*, *Wada’a* <note>original: "Wada"</note>, *Sufyan* <note>original: "Sefian"</note>, and *Khawlan* <note>original: "Khaulan"</note>. Besides these four general officers of noble birth, many *Naqibs* <term>an officer rank below a Sheikh</term> or officers of lower social descent (some of whom had even been slaves in their youth) were also in the army. *Naqib* is the highest title that the Imam himself can bestow. "Sheikh" is a title that can only be passed down through inheritance and is reserved for sovereign princes and independent lords.

In times of peace, a soldier serving in the cavalry has nothing to do but take care of his horse and escort the Imam or the *Dola* <term>governor</term> to the mosque, depending on whether he is stationed in Sana'a or in one of the provinces. The Arabs are extremely attentive to the breeding and management of their horses. Each horse is

### CHAPTER VIII.

->*Of the Arts and Commerce of Yemen.*<-

Despite the natural abilities of the Arabs, the arts receive no encouragement and are totally neglected in the Imam’s dominions, as well as in the neighboring countries. Books are scarce in Arabia because the Arabs have a dislike for printed characters. Their intricate alphabetical writing is best performed by hand; they can hardly read books produced by our printing presses. For this reason, *Ibrahim Effendi’s* attempt to introduce printing to Constantinople <note>Ibrahim Muteferrika (1674–1745) established the first Ottoman printing press in 1727, though it faced significant opposition from scribes and religious conservatives.</note> was unsuccessful, and the convert <note>original: "renegado," a term used for a person who has changed their religion; here referring to Ibrahim Effendi, who was of Hungarian origin.</note> was financially ruined by the project. Indeed, Hebrew characters are much easier to cast into type; therefore, the Jewish printing presses at Constantinople, Smyrna, and Thessaloniki <note>original: "Salonica"</note> may possibly maintain their position. (M.) <note>This "M." likely refers to Johann David Michaelis, the scholar who drafted the research questions for the expedition.</note>

A country that provides so few items for sale cannot have a large trade. Coffee is almost the only item exported from Yemen; it is a valuable commodity, and in exchange for it, many of the goods this country requires from abroad can be easily acquired.

I have mentioned the imports in my account of the trade of Mocha. Nearly all the commerce of Yemen passes through this port, with the exception of small quantities of coffee exported through Loheya and Al Hudaydah <note>original: "Hodeida"</note>. Therefore, what has been said regarding the trade of Mocha can be considered as applying to the trade of all Yemen.

The history of Arabia displays, throughout its entire course, nearly the same political arrangements that appeared to have prevailed in Europe for several centuries during the Middle Ages; with this difference only: that the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> have seldom been in a state of vassalage and never experienced feudal government.

The nature and local circumstances of Arabia are favorable to the spirit of independence that distinguishes its inhabitants from other nations. Their deserts and mountains have always protected them from the encroachments of conquest. Those inhabiting the plains have indeed been subdued, but their servitude has been only temporary; the only foreign powers to whose arms they have yielded have been those bordering on the two gulfs <note>original: "two gulphs"; referring to the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.</note> between which this country lies.

Independent Sheikhs are therefore found among the *Bedouins*, or wandering Arabs, who escape oppression due to the barrenness of their lands and the ease with which they can retreat into the deserts, where no armies can follow them. They are also found among the *Kobails* <note>original: "Kobails"; likely a transliteration of the Arabic "Qabail" (tribes), here referring specifically to mountain-dwelling tribes.</note>, or Arabian Highlanders, who inhabit wild and lofty mountain chains that are nevertheless fertile enough to support a frugal...

Among the latter are the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> established within the Imam’s dominions. One example that shows the ease with which the Sheikhs defend themselves is that the Imams—although they had little difficulty in expelling the Turks from the low country—have never been able, despite all their efforts, to subdue these Highlanders. I could not learn the names of all those Sheikhs or their specific territories. In terms of noble lineage and dignity of rank, these two princes are inferior to none in Arabia.

The prince of *Ofab* <note>likely Afar or a similar local district</note> is a member of the Imam’s <term>Imam: here referring to the ruler of Sana and spiritual leader of the Zaydi state</term> family and is a vassal to that prince; his principality consists of territory that has been separated from the dominions of Sana.

In no district is there a greater number of prominent Sheikhs <term>Sheikh: an Arabic title meaning a leader, elder, or chief of a tribe or village</term> than in *Kusma* <note>likely the Raymah region</note>, the westernmost range of the "coffee mountains." This district, consisting entirely of steep hills planted with coffee trees up to their very summits, is naturally populous because it produces such a profitable crop as coffee in such great abundance. For this reason, the local gentry here are very wealthy and numerous. I was told of more than thirty Sheikhs who draw large revenues from the markets within their territories, where an astonishing quantity of coffee is sold. These Sheikhs are all independent and reside in fortified castles upon the mountains.

Yet, despite these advantages, he has been reduced to a state of <term>vassalage: a status of dependency where a local ruler owes allegiance and often tribute to a superior sovereign</term>, probably because his territory was too flat and too narrow to be defended against an enemy. In this principality is *Muakeb*, a city of a unique construction; all of its houses are carved out of the natural rock.

From this detailed account, it appears that the political state of *Yemen* is not unlike that of *Germany* <note>at the time of Niebuhr's writing, Germany was a collection of many semi-independent states within the Holy Roman Empire</note>. The Arabs lack only a central head; they already have princes, a body of nobility, and an aristocratic league.

## SECTION XX.

->OF THE PROVINCE OF HADRAMAUT.<-

---

### CHAPTER I.

->*Of the General Character and the Commerce of this Province.*<-

Hadramaut is bounded on the west by Yemen, on the southeast by the ocean, on the northeast by Oman, and on the north by a great desert. It encompasses a wide extent of country, especially if, following the Arabs, we include the district of *Mahhra* <note>original: "Mahhra" — modern-day Al-Mahrah, the easternmost governorate of Yemen</note>. *Mahhra* seems to be like *Tihama* <note>original: "Tehama" — the hot, sandy coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula</note>, a sandy plain extending inland from the shores of the ocean to where the hill country begins.

These plains were likely once covered by the sea.

Given this state of the coast and the highlands, Hadramaut—like Yemen—exhibits a great diversity of soil and terrain. Some parts of it are dry and desert-like, but the hills are extremely fertile and are divided by well-watered valleys.

The inhabitants of this province are also divided, much like those of Yemen, into Arabs settled in towns, wandering Bedouins, and <term>Kobails: mountain-dwelling tribes or highlanders</term>. A native of Hadramaut, with whom I had several opportunities to speak, described his country as a center of science and religion. Other Arabs are less favorable in their accounts, and not without reason, if one may judge by the coarseness of the dialect spoken in this province. It differs so considerably from the dialect of Yemen that I required an interpreter to assist me in conversing with the man who entertained me with the <term>pompous elogium: a grand, formal speech of praise</term> <note>original: "pompous elogium"</note> of his country mentioned above. The religion of his countrymen must be a collection of bizarre superstitions, for the <term>Sunnites: Sunni Muslims</term> are the dominant sect among them. <note>Niebuhr, writing from an 18th-century European perspective, often viewed unfamiliar Islamic practices through a lens of skepticism, frequently labeling them "superstition."</note>

## CHAPTER II.
### Regarding the Principal Towns in Hadramaut.

There are many significant towns in Hadramaut that were perhaps better known to the ancients than they are today. Despite the effort I took, I could learn the names of only a few of those places. What I know of the rest, I heard from people who were not very well acquainted with the current state of Hadramaut. I shall repeat what I was told concerning some of those cities.

An Arab from *Marib* informed me that he had not found a single village in *Al-Jawf* <note>original: "Dsjof"</note> on his way from his native city; however, as he traveled through *Hadhramaut*, he had been in several significant towns. *Shibam* seems to be the *Saba* of the ancients, from which the *Sabaeans* <note>original: "Sabeans"</note> took their name. This people occupied the southern parts of Arabia before *Marib* became the capital of their empire.

*Doan* <note>modern: Wadi Doan</note>, in which a *Sheikh* <note>original: "Schiech"</note> resides, is twenty-five days' journey eastward from *Sanaa* and eleven from *Qishn* <note>original: "Keschim"</note>. An inhabitant of *Doan* whom I met in *Yemen* told me that it was a larger and more elegant city than *Sanaa*.

*Dhofar* <note>original: "Dafar"</note> is a well-known seaport town from which incense, called in Arabia *Olibanum* <note>original: "Oliban"</note> or *Liban*, is exported. This incense is not nearly as good as that of India. The Arabs are criticized for selling both their incense and their gum without purifying them. This neglect causes a decline in quality and a reduction in price. A *Sheikh* also resides in *Dhofar*.

*Qishn* <note>original: "Keschim"</note> is a seaport town and the seat of a sovereign prince. Its inhabitants are said to be highly civilized and to receive all strangers hospitably.

These observations lead me to think that a journey through this province might prove at least as interesting as our journey through Yemen. The difficulties involved in such an expedition could not be greater than those we had to struggle against. I knew a Turk <note>term: in this context, a subject of the Ottoman Empire</note> who told me how easily and safely he had visited the various sea-port towns in Southern Arabia. The inhabitants of that coast, remembering the wealth that strangers used to bring there in former times and being long accustomed to treating them well, would undoubtedly give Europeans a favorable reception today.

### Chapter III

#### *Of the Sovereign Princes in Hadhramaut <note>original: "Hadramaut"</note>.*

The Bedouins and the inhabitants of the hills have many independent sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> here, just as they do throughout the rest of Arabia; however, since I do not know the specifics, I can say nothing further about them.

The coasts and the adjacent countryside are shared among sovereigns of higher dignity. Although travellers have called them "kings," they actually take only the title of sheikh or sultan. I have already mentioned the Sheikh of Shibam <note>original: "Schibam"</note> as one of the most powerful.

Daw’an <note>original: "Doan"</note> belongs to a sheikh whom I believe to be a descendant of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> and of the family of the Imams; for the man who reigned in 1763 was called Sayyid <note>original: "Sejid"; a title denoting a descendant of the Prophet Muhammad</note> Isa el-Amudi. In a neighboring city are the tombs of all the princes of the illustrious house of Amudi.

The Sheikh of Dhofar <note>original: "Dafar"</note> is also a sovereign prince; however, I know neither his name nor the extent of his power.

The Sheikh of Qishn <note>original: "Keschim"</note>, called by some travellers the "King of Fartak," is the most powerful ruler. His dominions include a considerable number of cities, among which is the city of Fartak; and because of this—

The first Portuguese explorers who visited Arabia found the Prince of Qishn still in the undisturbed possession of this part of his family's ancient dominions.

The principality of *Einat* <note>original: "Ainad"</note> must be extensive, if the account I received from a native of the city of the same name can be credited. But I have reason to suspect that the Sovereign of Einat is one of those Sultans of *Yafe* <note>original: "Jafa"</note> who have conquered some territories in Hadhramaut <note>original: "Hadramaut"</note>.

There are probably still other sovereign states in this widely extended province. However, I did not have opportunities to acquire further knowledge of a country which, for many reasons, deserves to be better known.

## SECTION XXI.

### OF THE PROVINCE OF OMAN.

---

### CHAP. I.

->*Of Oman in general.*<-

The province of Oman is bordered on the east by the ocean; on the north by the Persian Gulf <note>original: "Gulph"</note>; and on the west and south by extensive deserts <note>original: "desarts"</note>. I did not visit any part of it except for the surroundings of Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>; therefore, I do not speak about it based on my own personal observation.

The region is ruled by a number of minor sovereigns, the most significant of whom is the Imam <note>The Imam was traditionally an elected leader in Oman who held both spiritual and temporal authority</note> of Oman or Muscat. The princes of *Dsjau, Gabria, Gafar, Rank, Gabbi, Dahhara, Makaniat,* and *Seer* hold the title of Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"; a title for a tribal leader or local ruler</note>.

The entire western side of Oman is a single sandy plain, a day’s journey in length, stretching from the village of Seeb <note>original: "Sib"</note> to the town of Sohar. The Imam’s territories are mountainous right up to the edge <note>original: "brink"</note> of the shore. The rivers continue to flow throughout the year, all except

The country produces plenty of cheese, barley, lentils, along with several different sorts of grapes. ## CHAP. II.

### *Of the Territories of the Imam of Oman, or Muscat <note>original: "Maſkat"</note>.*

The territory possessed by the Imam of Oman is quite extensive and contains many towns, most of which are very little known. I shall mention only a few details which I learned concerning the most remarkable among them.

Rostak <note>original: "Roſtak"</note>, a city at some distance from the sea, is the seat of the Sovereign. In its neighborhood
