They are permitted to live according to <note>original: "agreeably to"</note> their own laws, to bring their wives here, to set up idols in their chambers, and to burn their dead <note>referring to the practice of cremation, which was generally prohibited in other Islamic regions</note>. If a Banian has an affair <note>original: "intrigues"</note> here with a Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note> woman, the government does not treat him with the same severity that he would encounter elsewhere.

Regarding the Imam’s revenue, I could learn nothing except that the taxes <note>original: "duties"</note> levied upon merchant goods amount to about a hundred thousand rupees. At Muscat, Europeans pay five percent on imports; Muslims pay six and a half; and Jews and Banians pay seven percent. The Imam’s native subjects pay six percent in kind <note>payment made with goods rather than money</note> on exported dates, which are the primary product that the country produces.

## CHAPTER III.

### *The Revolutions of Oman.*

There are three very ancient and famous <note>original: "illustrious"</note> families in Oman: the Gafari, the Hamani, and the Arrabi. The latter family claims <note>original: "pretends"</note> to be descended from the Quraysh <note>original: "Koreisch"</note> of Mecca, who were famous even before the time of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>. Regardless of the truth of this claim, the Arrabi family reigned at Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note> for a long time, though they do not currently hold supreme power. The events that removed them from the throne are linked to the history of Nadir Shah <note>original: "Nadir Schah"</note>, the last great monarch of Persia. To explain these events clearly, it is necessary to look back at some things that happened in the last century.

Imam Malik <note>original: "Malek"</note>, of the house of Arrabi, was the ruler of all Oman. He expanded his territory through conquest, adding Kung <note>original: "Kunk"</note>, Qeshm <note>original: "Kifchme"</note>, Hormuz <note>original: "Hormus"</note>, and Bahrain <note>original: "Baharein"</note> to his dominions. His son expanded these conquests even further, taking control of Kilwa <note>original: "Kiloa"</note> and Zanzibar <note>original: "Sinsjibar"</note> in Africa. However, during the reign of his grandson, Bin Saif <note>original: "Ben Seif"</note>, the new ruler of Persia, Nadir Shah, sent an army to conquer Oman. The Persians suffered heavy losses among the hills and were driven back. Bin Saif accordingly

## CHAPTER IV.

### *Of the Reigning Imam.*

At the time of Taqi Khan’s <note>original: "Tæki Khan"; the Persian governor of Shiraz</note> expedition into Oman, there was a governor in Sohar named Ahmed bin Said <note>original: "Achmed ben Sajid"; he was the founder of the Al Said dynasty, which still rules Oman today</note>, a native of a small town within the Imam's territory. This Ahmed, being a man of talent and ambition, and realizing that—after the deaths of the two previous Imams—he would be forced to submit to such powerful enemies as the Persians, made peace with the invaders. He managed the situation so well that Taqi Khan confirmed his position as governor.

During the civil wars in Persia, a high-ranking prince of the House of Yaruba <note>original: "Arrabi"; the dynasty that ruled Oman before the Al Said</note>, the Prince of Seer <note>now known as Ras Al Khaimah</note>, and a nobleman named Bel Arab <note>original: "Bel Arrab"</note> had divided the territories of the last Imam among themselves. Bel Arab had even taken the title of Imam for himself.

Ahmed, capturing the Persian officers in Muscat by surprise, forced the garrison to surrender and made himself master of the city without any bloodshed <note>original: "effusion of blood"</note>. Winning the support of the chief Qadi <note>original: "Cadi"; a judge of Islamic law</note>, who serves as the Mufti <note>a legal expert empowered to give rulings on religious law</note> in Oman, he obtained a ruling from him stating that he, as the savior of his country, deserved to be

In 1765, Imam Ahmed <note>original: "Achmed"</note> had reigned sixteen years, to the full satisfaction of his subjects. He saw justice promptly and uprightly administered, without partiality to rank or religion. Theft was almost never heard of. At Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>, goods remained safely in the streets by night, and few people even took the trouble to bolt their doors. ## SECTION XXII.

### CHAPTER I.

->*Of Al-Ahsa <note>original: Lachsa</note> in Particular.*<-

This country is bordered to the east by the Persian Gulf, to the south by Oman, to the west by the province of Najd <note>original: Nedsjed</note>, and to the north by the territories of the nomadic <note>original: wandering</note> Arabs near Basra.

It is also called Hajar <note>original: Hadsjar</note>, and sometimes *Bahrain* <note>original: Bahhrein</note>. This latter name, strictly speaking, belongs only to the island of *Awal* <note>original: Aual</note> and the small islands that depend upon it.

Al-Ahsa <note>original: Lachsa</note> does not yield a great variety of products. Its donkeys <note>original: asses</note> and camels are considered to be of an excellent breed; several thousand of the latter are sold to Syria every year. In the interior parts of this province, the inhabitants live largely on dates. Along the coasts, pearl fishing <meta>catchword: fishing</meta>

Regarding religion, the inhabitants of Al-Ahsa <note>original: Lachsa</note> are divided. This country was once a province of the Ottoman Empire. However, the Arabs have long since shaken off the Ottoman yoke. Many Turks, descended from the former Pashas <note>original: Pachas; high-ranking Ottoman officials</note>, still remain in the province and own significant estates, but they have no role in the government.

Sovereignty over the province of Al-Ahsa currently belongs to the Sheik <note>original: Schiech</note> of the Arab tribe of Bani Khalid <note>original: Beni Khaled</note>. In 1765, the reigning Sheik was Arar. The Bani Khalid tribe is one of the most powerful in Arabia. They are spread so widely throughout the desert that they often harass the caravans traveling between Baghdad and Aleppo <note>original: Kaleb</note>. Most of Al-Ahsa is inhabited by Bedouins and other smaller tribes, but they all acknowledge the authority of the Sheik of Bani Khalid.

I could learn nothing concerning the cities in the interior parts of this province. Al-Ahsa, the seat of the reigning Sheik, is likely a large city containing significant buildings.

*Qatif* <note>original: Katif</note>, a town of considerable size, stands upon the coast at a distance of about five German miles <note>A German geographical mile was approximately 4.6 statute miles or 7.4 kilometers; thus, this distance is about 23 miles or 37 kilometers.</note> from the island of Bahrain. However, the air in this country is believed to be very unhealthy <note>original: insalutary</note> in the summer. The ruins of an old Portuguese fortress are still to be seen near this place.

*Kuwait* <note>original: Koueit</note> or *Grane* <note>original: Græn</note>, as it is called by the Persians and Europeans, is a seaport town three days' journey from *Az Zubayr* <note>original: Zobejer</note>, or Old Basra. The inhabitants live by the harvesting of pearls and fish. They are said to employ more than eight hundred boats in this branch of maritime industry. In the favorable season of the year, this town is left almost deserted, as everyone goes out either to the fishing grounds or on trading expeditions. *Grane* is governed by a specific Sheik of the *Utub* tribe <note>original: Othema; likely referring to the Bani Utbah, the tribal confederation from which the Al Sabah family of Kuwait emerged</note>, who is a vassal to the Sheik of Al-Ahsa <note>original: Lachsa</note> but sometimes aspires to independence. In such cases, when the Sheik of Al-Ahsa advances with his army, the citizens of *Grane* retreat with their belongings to the little island of *Failaka* <note>original: Feludsje</note>. Near *Grane* are the remains of another Portuguese fortress.

## Chapter II

->*Concerning the Province of Najd <note>original: Nedsjed</note>*<-

This province is of vast extent. It includes all the interior parts of Arabia lying between the provinces I have briefly described above and the Syrian Desert. The soil varies; it is fertile among the hills, producing an abundance of fruits, especially dates. However, because the province is surrounded by arid tracts of country, its rivers are merely short streams. After passing through the valleys, their waters are absorbed into the sandy plains before they can reach the ocean. For this reason, the inhabitants are obliged to dig deep wells in many places, and cultivation there is difficult or almost impossible.

The Bedouins inhabit a large portion of this province. The remainder is mountainous, filled with cities and villages, and divided among so many minor rulers <note>original: petty Sovereigns</note> that almost every small town has its own Sheik. Formerly, when the power...

At present, they pay nothing.

The inhabitants of this vast country resemble the other Arabs in their character; they are at once robbers and hospitable. Because these petty sovereigns are so numerous in Najd <note>original: Nedsjed</note>, it is impossible for any traveler to pass safely through this country. The first Sheik whose territory a traveler enters will be sure to rob him. This is done if only to prevent a neighbor, with whom the Sheik is at war, from profiting by this act of greed <note>original: rapacity</note> if he himself should abstain from it. 

The caravan does indeed travel safely between Oman and Mecca, because it consists of beggars from whom nothing can be gained. However, the Sheiks of Najd extract a payment <note>original: levy a contribution</note> from the caravan coming from Baghdad on its way to Mecca, in the same manner as the Sheiks of Hejaz extract payments from the caravans coming from Syria and Egypt. I have, however, learned that the inhabitants of Najd carry on a considerable trade among themselves and with their immediate neighbors. It is therefore not improbable that a European might travel in safety, even through this remote part of Arabia.

The people appear to be of a very warlike character and are almost constantly under arms.

It is said that none of their young men are allowed <note>original: suffered</note> to marry until after they have performed some brave deed.

Najd <note>original: Nedsjed</note> is divided into two wide districts: Al-Arid <note>original: El Arad</note>, which borders Oman; and Al-Kharj <note>original: El Kherdsje</note>, stretching to the border of Yemen. Several of the towns in Al-Arid were named to me; among others, Al-Uyayna <note>original: El Aijane</note>, the birthplace of the new prophet Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab <note>original: Abd ul Wahheb</note>, of whom I shall shortly speak. 

In the district of Al-Kharj, extending northward from Hejaz <note>original: Hedsjas</note> to the desert, is the city of Yamama <note>original: Imam</note>, famous even before the days of Muhammad <note>original: Mahomet</note> for being the native city of Musaylimah <note>original: Moseilama</note>, who claimed to be a prophet <note>Musaylimah was a contemporary rival of Muhammad known in Islamic tradition as "the Liar."</note>. This district also contains many other cities. 

North of Najd, and about ten days' journey from Baghdad, is the famous mountain of Shammar <note>original: Schamer</note>, which is of considerable size and fertility. Between this mountain and Syria is a hilly region called Jauf al-Sirhan <note>original: Dsjof al Sirhan</note>, which is populous and cultivated.

The Muslim <note>original: Musulman</note> religion, as practiced by the Sunnis, is certainly very different from how it was established by Muhammad <note>original: Mahomet</note>. This sect follows the authority of certain commentators who explain the Quran <note>original: Alcoran</note> according to their own whims and elevate their private opinions into the official doctrines of the Islamic <note>original: Mahometan</note> system. It recognizes a long succession of saints who are called upon in times of need and to whom many absurd miracles are attributed. These miracles are said to have been performed for the benefit of people who prayed to the saints instead of to God. It places faith in the power of amulets and the effectiveness of foolish vows. In short, it has gradually adopted many superstitious practices that are condemned in the Quran and justified only by the forced interpretations of the religious scholars <term>Doctors</term>. Other sects, such as the Zaydites <note>original: Zeidites; a branch of Shia Islam prevalent in Yemen</note>, have corrupted the religion of Muhammad less, although even among them it is far from remaining in its original purity.

The new religion of Abd al-Wahhab should therefore be seen as a reformation of Islam <note>original: Mahometism</note>, returning it to its original simplicity.

## SECTION XXIII.
### OF THE INDEPENDENT ARABIAN STATES UPON THE SEA COAST OF PERSIA.

## CHAPTER I.
### *Of the Arabs living around the Persian Gulf.*

Our geographers are wrong, as I have noted elsewhere, in representing a part of Arabia as being subject to the monarchs of Persia. Far from this being the case, the Arabs actually control <note>original: possess</note> the entire sea coast of the Persian Empire, from the mouths of the Euphrates nearly to those of the Indus River.

Indeed, these settlements upon the coast of Persia do not belong to Arabia proper <note>original: Arabia properly so called</note>. However, since they are independent of Persia, use the same language, and exhibit the same customs <note>original: manners</note> as the native inhabitants of Arabia, I shall add <note>original: subjoin</note> a brief account of them here.

It is impossible to determine <note>original: ascertain</note> the exact period in which the Arabs established <note>original: formed</note> their settlements upon—

There is a striking similarity <note>original: analogy</note> between the customs <note>original: manners</note> ascribed to the ancient *Fish-eaters* <note>original: *Ichthyophagi*; a Greek term used by ancient geographers to describe coastal peoples who lived primarily on fish</note> and those of these Arabs.

They all live in nearly the same way, leading a seafaring life and occupying themselves with fishing and gathering pearls. They eat little else besides fish and dates, and they even feed their cattle on fish.

They value freedom as highly as their relatives <note>original: brethren</note> in the desert. Almost every town has its own Sheikh <note>original: Schiech</note>, who receives hardly any income <note>original: revenue</note> from his subjects. If he has no private fortune, he must, like his subjects, support himself through his own labor <note>original: industry</note>, either by transporting goods or by fishing. If the leading inhabitants happen to be dissatisfied with the reigning Sheikh, they remove <note>original: depose</note> him and choose another from the same family.

Their weapons are a matchlock musket <note>original: match-firelock; an early firearm where the powder was ignited by a burning cord</note>, a saber, and a small shield <note>original: buckler</note>. All their fishing boats serve occasionally as warships. But a fleet like this—which must frequently stop to catch fish for food when they should be pursuing the enemy—can never perform any very great achievements <note>original: exploits</note>. The *Dutch* continued to conduct small-scale trade here for a time, but since they established a settlement on the island of *Kharg* <note>original: "Karek"</note>, they have completely abandoned Gambron.

The island of *Hormuz* <note>original: "Ormus"</note>, once so famous in history, now retains none of its former glory. It currently belongs to *Mulla Ali Shah*, a *Persian* who seized control of it immediately after the death of *Nadir Shah*, under whom he had served as an admiral. This Prince of *Hormuz* also owns part of the island of *Qishm* <note>original: "Kishme"</note>, while the other part is ruled by the Prince of *Seer*.

### CHAPTER III.

### *Concerning the Territories of the Huwala Tribe.* <note>original: "Houle"; the Huwala are a group of Arab tribes who migrated to the Persian coast.</note>

This numerous tribe controls the entire coast from Bandar Abbas to Cape Bardistan <note>original: "Berdistan"</note> and possesses all the ports along this stretch of coastline. One part of the region is parched and barren, but a range of hills, such as *Dahr Asban*, extends nearly to the sea and provides timber, which is harvested and exported by the inhabitants.

Despite these natural advantages, the Huwala Arabs do not cultivate their lands, but instead live by hunting and fishing. They are Sunnis <note>Followers of the Sunni branch of Islam.</note>;

### CHAPTER 5

### *Concerning the Tribe of Ka'b and their Sheikh Salman*

The Arabian tribe of Ka'b <note>original: "Kiab"; a powerful tribe that controlled the borderlands between modern-day Iraq and Iran</note>, or as the Persians pronounce it, Chab <note>original: "Tsjab"</note>, inhabit the farthest point on the side of the Persian Gulf. They were of little importance before the reign of their current Sheikh Salman <note>original: "Soliman"</note>, whose fame has even reached Europe as a result of a conflict he had with the English, during which he captured some of their ships.

This Sheikh took advantage of the unrest in Persia and the weaknesses in the government of Basra. He began by subduing his small, independent neighbors; after this, he made himself master of several large districts in Persia and promised to pay tribute to the Khans <note>rulers or military commanders</note> who were then fighting for the throne of that troubled empire. None of them ever attempted to demand <note>original: "exact"</note> tribute except for Karim Khan <note>original: "Kerim"; the founder of the Zand Dynasty of Persia</note>, and he was satisfied with only a small sum. ## CHAP. VI.

->*Of some other independent States.*<-

**Hendijan** <note>original: "Hindian"; a district in the Khuzestan province of modern-day Iran</note>, north of Bandar Rig <note>original: "Bender Rigk"</note> and bordering the possessions of the Ka'b <note>original: "Kiab"</note> tribe, is a small district subject to its own sovereign. The Arabs who inhabit it live upon the produce of their lands and their cattle.

**Hoveyzeh** <note>original: "Havisa"; a city in the Khuzestan province of Iran</note>, a city and district in the interior of the country bordering the Persian Gulf, belongs to a descendant of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>. This prince is titled **Mawla** <note>original: "Maula"; a title often used for religious or sovereign leaders</note> and enjoys the privilege of minting his own money.

Upon the eastern coast of the Persian Gulf are many islands, most of which are inhabited. Except for **Hormuz** <note>original: "Ormus"</note>, none of them constitute an independent state. The different princes on the mainland possess the islands adjoining their respective dominions.

On the western side of the Gulf is an island, or rather a cluster of islands, known to Europeans by the name of **Bahrain** <note>original: "Bahhrein"</note>. The Arabs call the largest of these islands **Awal**; and each of the smaller ones has its own particular name. As this island is famous for the pearl fishery and has under- <note>The text continues on the next page: "...gone many revolutions."</note>

Sea travel <note>original: "navigation"</note> is continually disturbed and interrupted by these intense <note>original: "strong"</note> quarrels. On board any Arab vessel, passengers are always in danger of falling into the hands of one enemy or another. It is only on board a European ship, which the small Arab boats <note>original: "Arabian small craft"</note> dare not attack, that one can perform this voyage in safety.

### CHAP. VII.

#### *Of the Island of Karek.*

This island <note>original: "ifle"; modern-day Kharg Island</note>, which lies on the east coast of the Persian Gulf, between Abu Shahr <note>original: "Abu Schæhhr"; modern-day Bushehr</note> and Bandar Rig <note>original: "Bender Rigk"</note>, contains only a single village. However, the aqueducts cut into the rocks, which still remain, show it to have been once more populous in proportion to its size, which is about five leagues <note>a league is roughly 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers</note> in circumference.

Karek has become famous because of the settlement recently formed upon it by the Dutch, which they have since abandoned. As this event has caused some stir in the world, I shall give a brief account of it.

The Dutch carried on a great trade at Basra <note>original: "Bafra"</note> and had a Baron Kniphausen as the principal director of their factory <note>original: "factory"; a merchant's trading post or warehouse</note> there, who was much respected in that city. This German, having embroiled himself with the Governor as a result of a romantic entanglement <note>original: "affair of gallantry"</note>, was thrown into prison and might have lost his head had he not paid a large sum of money for his liberty. Before he sailed for Batavia <note>the capital of the Dutch East Indies, modern-day Jakarta</note>, he obtained from the factory at Basra a written testimony of the innocence of his conduct, and the Dutch East India Company approved of all he had done.

As a result of his dispute with the Governor of Basra, Mr. Kniphausen had made an agreement with Mir Nasir <note>original: "Mir Naſer"</note>, Prince of Bandar Rig <note>original: "Bender Rigk"</note>, who owned Kharg Island <note>original: "Karek"</note>. After governing Kharg with sovereign authority for five years, Baron Kniphausen was succeeded by Mr. Vanderhulst. Because Vanderhulst had previously worked at Basra and was familiar with the Arabs, he felt it was his duty to continue the war against Mir Mahenna—the new Prince of Bandar Rig—which had been started against his father. # SECTION XXII.

### OF THE BEDOUINS, OR WANDERING ARABS.

---

### CHAPTER I.

->*Distinctive Customs of the Bedouins.*<-

The Arabs settled in cities, and especially those in the seaport towns, have lost some of their distinctive national customs <note>original: "manners"</note> through their interaction <note>original: "intercourse"</note> with foreigners. However, the Bedouins, who live in tents and in separate tribes, have still retained the customs and behaviors of their earliest ancestors. They are the genuine Arabs and show, as a whole <note>original: "in the aggregate"</note>, all those characteristics which are found individually <note>original: "distributed respectively"</note> among the other branches of their nation.

I have frequently mentioned <note>original: "repeatedly noticed"</note> the different meanings <note>original: "acceptations"</note> in which the word *Sheikh* <note>original: "Schech" or "Schiech"</note> is used. Among the Bedouins, it is a title belonging to every nobleman, whether of the highest or the lowest rank. Their nobles are very numerous and make up almost the entire nation; the commoners <note>original: "plebeians"</note>

<summary>Niebuhr introduces the Bedouins as the "genuine Arabs" who have preserved their ancestral customs, unlike city-dwelling Arabs. He also explains that the title "Sheikh" is used broadly among Bedouin nobility.</summary>

<keywords>Bedouins, wandering Arabs, Sheikh, Arab customs, tribal structure, social hierarchy, ethnographic study</keywords>

<header>IN ARABIA, &c.</header>

commoners <note>original: "plebeians"</note> are invariably motivated <note>original: "actuated"</note> and guided by the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note>, who oversee and direct every transaction.

The Sheikhs and their subjects are born to the life of shepherds and soldiers. The larger tribes raise many camels, which they either sell to their neighbors, or use for transporting goods or in military expeditions. The smaller <note>original: "petty"</note> tribes keep flocks of sheep. Among those tribes that engage in agriculture, the Sheikhs at least always live in tents and leave the farming <note>original: "culture"</note> of their grounds to their subjects, whose dwellings are miserable huts.

It is the difference in their lifestyles that creates the major distinctions characterizing the various tribes. The genuine Arabs despise farming <note>original: "husbandry"</note> as a profession that would degrade them. They keep no domestic animals except sheep and camels, and perhaps horses. Those tribes that are of a pure Arab race <note>This refers to the author's categorization of lineages</note> live on the meat of their buffaloes, cows, and horses, and on the produce of a little farming. The former tribes, distinguished as noble by their possession of camels, are called *Abu el Abaar* <note>original: "Abu el Abaar"; likely referring to 'Abu al-Ibil' or 'father of camels'</note>; and the second group is called *Moædan*. The latter are considered a middle class between genuine Arabs and peasants. I have heard some tribes mentioned with contempt because they kept buffaloes and cows. The

The *Moadan* <note>original: "Moadan"; refers to the cattle-rearing tribes mentioned on the previous page as being of a lower social rank than camel-rearing Arabs</note> transport their dwellings from one country to another, according as pasturage fails them; so that a village often arises suddenly in a situation where, on the day before, not a hut was to be seen.

The genuine Bedouins, living always in the open air, have a very acute sense of smell. They dislike cities on account of the fetid <note>original: "fœtid"; foul-smelling</note> exhalations produced about them. They cannot conceive how people, who regard cleanliness, can bear to breathe such impure air. I have been assured, by persons of undoubted truthfulness <note>original: "veracity"</note>, that some Bedouins, if carried to the spot from which a camel has wandered astray, will follow the animal by smelling its track, and distinguish the marks of its footsteps, by the same means, from those of any other beasts that may have traveled the same way. Those Arabs, who wander in the desert <note>original: "desart"</note>, will live five days without drinking, and discover a pit of water by examining the soil and plants in its environs. They are said to be addicted to robbery; and the accusation is not entirely unfounded; but it may be laid equally to the charge of all nations that lead a nomadic <note>original: "erratic"</note> life. The Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> ride continually about on their horses or dromedaries <note>one-humped camels</note>, inspecting the conduct of their subjects, visiting their friends, or hunting. Traversing the desert, where the horizon is as wide as on the ocean, they perceive travelers at a distance.

<summary>Niebuhr describes the mobile lifestyle of the Moadan and the remarkable sensory adaptations of the Bedouins, including their ability to track animals by scent and survive long periods without water.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the Bedouin people, shifting from their physical senses and survival skills to their social interactions with travelers and their specific code of conduct regarding robbery and hospitality.</meta>

<page-num>161</page-num>
<header>IN ARABIA, ETC.</header>

As travelers are rarely encountered in those wild regions, the locals naturally approach anyone they spot. They are often tempted to rob these strangers when they find their own party is the stronger of the two. Furthermore, travelers crossing these deserts <note>original: "desarts"</note> usually move in caravans; therefore, a lone individual or a small group appears unusual and suspicious, which serves as a temptation to the Bedouins.

In Arabia, as in all other sparsely populated countries, robbery is practiced. However, Arabian robbers are not cruel and do not murder those they rob, unless the travelers defend themselves and happen to kill a Bedouin—whose death the others are then determined to avenge. In all other circumstances, they act in a way that is consistent with their natural hospitality. On this subject, I have heard several anecdotes that are worth sharing here.

A Mufti <note>an Islamic legal expert and religious leader</note> of Baghdad, returning from Mecca, was robbed in Najd <note>original: "Nedsjed"; the central highland region of the Arabian Peninsula</note>. He entered into a written agreement with the robbers, who undertook to escort him safely to Baghdad for a specific amount, payable once he reached his own house. They handed him over to the neighboring tribe, who then passed him to a third; in this way, he was escorted from tribe to tribe until he arrived safely home.

upon his journey. The Arabs, seeing him too weak to follow his companions, took him with them, lodged him outside their camp, cared for him until he was cured, and then sent him to Basra <note>original: "Basra"; a major port city in modern-day Iraq</note>.

An Englishman, who was traveling on an express route to India and could not wait for the departure of a caravan, hired two Arabs at Baghdad to accompany him to Basra. Along the way, he was attacked by some Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; tribal leaders or elders</note>, against whom he at first defended himself with his pistols; but, being hard-pressed by their lances, he was forced to surrender. The Arabs, at whom he had fired, beat him until he could not walk. They then carried him to their camp, hosted <note>original: "entertained"; in this context, it refers to providing the obligations of hospitality</note> him for some time, and at last escorted him safely to Basra. When Mr. Forsskål <note>Peter Forsskål (1732–1763), a Swedish naturalist and explorer who was a key member of Niebuhr's expedition</note> was robbed by the Arabs in Egypt, a peasant who accompanied him was beaten by the robbers because he had pistols, even though he had made no attempt to defend himself with them.

The looting of caravans is not always due merely to a natural inclination toward robbery among the Arabians. They usually consider their raiding expeditions to be lawful acts of war <note>original: "hostilities"</note> against enemies who would defraud the nation of its rightful dues <note>referring to transit taxes or tribute traditionally paid to tribes for safe passage through their territory</note>, or against rival tribes who have undertaken to protect those illegal traders.

In one of those expeditions undertaken a few years ago against the Pasha of Damascus <note>original: "Pacha"; a high-ranking official in the Ottoman Empire</note>, who was the leader of the Syrian caravan to Mecca, the tribe of the Anizzah <note>original: "Anase"; one of the largest and most powerful Bedouin tribal confederations</note>, which gained the victory, showed instances of their ignorance and the simplicity of their manners. Those who happened to take goods of value did not know their worth but exchanged them for trifles. One of those Arabs, having obtained a bag of pearls for his share, thought they were rice—which he had heard was good food—and gave them to his wife to boil. When she found that no amount of boiling could soften them, she threw them away as useless.

## CHAP. II.

->On the political structure of the wandering Arabs.<-

In treating the government of the Arabs in general, I have already said a few words occasionally concerning that of the Bedouins. To avoid unnecessary repetition, I shall add here only a few particulars, chiefly concerning their political interests in respect to neighboring nations.

The dignity of Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"; a leader or elder of an Arabic tribe</note> is hereditary, but it is not confined to the order of <term>primogeniture</term> <note>the right of the firstborn legitimate child to inherit the entire estate or title</note>. The petty Sheikhs, who form the hereditary nobility,

choose the Grand Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note> from the reigning family, without regarding whether he is more nearly or more distantly related to his predecessor.

Little or no revenue is paid to the Grand Sheikh, and the other Sheikhs are his equals rather than his subjects. If they are dissatisfied with his government, they depose him or leave with their cattle to join another tribe. These migrations, which happen quite frequently, have reduced some tribes that were once powerful to a low and insignificant state; conversely, they have greatly increased the numbers and power of some petty tribes.

Personal slavery is established among the Bedouins, but none of them are *bound to the land* <note>original Latin: "ascripti glebae"; a legal term for serfs who were legally tied to the land they worked and could be sold with it</note>. A peasant, when dissatisfied with his master, may leave his service and move anywhere else.

The Bedouins who live in tents in the desert have never been subdued by any conqueror. However, those who have been enticed by the prospect of an easier way of life to settle near towns and in fertile provinces are now, to some degree, dependent on the sovereigns of those provinces.

Such are the Arabs in the different parts of the Ottoman Empire. Some of them pay a rent or tribute for the towns or pastures which they occupy. Others frequent the banks of the Euphrates only in one season of the year; and, in

<meta>catchword: winter,</meta>

winter, return to the desert. These latter tribes acknowledge no dependence on the Porte <note>The "Sublime Porte" was the central government of the Ottoman Empire</note>.

Neither are they, properly speaking, subjects of the Turks. On the contrary, they would be dangerous neighbors to the Turks if the Pashas <note>original: "Pachas"; provincial governors in the Ottoman Empire</note> did not find ways to sow discord among the tribes and great families when there is more than one claimant to the title of Sheikh of Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiech of Schiechs"; a paramount chief over multiple tribes</note>.

Turkish policy causes frequent wars among the Bedouins, but these conflicts are neither long nor bloody.

Whenever the Turks interfere in their quarrels, all the tribes unite to repel the common enemy of the entire nation.

Every Grand Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note> rightly considers himself the absolute lord of his territories. Accordingly, he imposes the same taxes on goods carried through his dominions as are levied by other princes. Europeans are mistaken in assuming that the sums paid by travelers to the Grand Sheikhs are merely a ransom to prevent them from being plundered <note>original: "pillage"</note>.

The Turks, who send caravans through the desert to Mecca, have agreed to pay these duties. They pay a specific annual sum to the tribes who live near the road to Mecca; in return, the Arabs keep the wells open, allow the passage of merchandise, and escort the caravans.

If the Bedouins sometimes plunder those caravans, the arrogant and treacherous <note>original: "perfidious"</note> conduct of the Turkish officers is always the primary cause of such hostilities. Those insolent Turks look upon all the Arabs as rebels—that is, in the modern sense of the word, as a people who, although weak, have the audacity to resist the oppression of their stronger neighbors. As a result of this selfish reasoning, they violate their agreements, and the Arabs take their revenge by plundering the caravans.

The famous *Ali Bey* <note>Ali Bey al-Kabir (1728–1773) was a Mamluk leader in Egypt who sought independence from the Ottoman Empire.</note>, when he led the Egyptian caravan to Mecca, refused to pay all the required taxes <note>original: "duties"</note> on his way there. He promised to pay the remainder upon his return but forgot his promise. The following year, the Arabs assembled in greater numbers and forced the leader <note>original: "Captain"</note> of the caravan to pay for both himself and *Ali Bey*. The Turks denounced this as an act of robbery, yet the Arabs had only secured the justice they were owed.

The conduct of *Abdalla*, Pasha <note>original: "Pacha"; a high-ranking official or provincial governor in the Ottoman Empire.</note> of Damascus, who commanded the Syrian caravan in 1756, was even more detestable. When the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"; tribal leaders.</note> of the Harb tribe came to meet him to receive the agreed-upon toll, he gave them a friendly invitation to visit him. However, instead of paying the toll, he cut off their heads and sent them to Constantinople as proof of his "victory" over the "rebel" Arabs. The blow which those tribes suffered by the death of their...

Consequently, the caravans traveled in triumph to Mecca, and the Turks boasted of the courage <note>original: "valour"</note> and wisdom <note>original: "prudence"</note> of Abdalla Pasha <note>original: "Pacha"</note>. But, in the third year, the Arabs avenged the murdered Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note>. With an army of eighty thousand men raised from all the different tribes, they routed the Turks and plundered the caravan. The tribe of *Anase* <note>The Anizah (or 'Anazzah) tribe, one of the largest and most significant Bedouin confederations in the Middle East.</note>, under the command of their Sheikh, distinguished themselves particularly in this expedition.

There is a clear hierarchy <note>original: "subordination"</note> among the tribes. The smaller tribes, being unable to defend themselves, place themselves under the protection of the larger ones and are governed by their laws. In this way, powerful tribes are formed by the union of several small tribes.

The Arabian nation is much more numerous and more widely spread than people generally suppose. They occupy countries that were once cultivated and populous, but whose ancient inhabitants have disappeared. The period in which these Arabian settlements were formed cannot now be determined; nor is it known whether they might have existed before <note>original: "anterior to"</note> the reign of the Caliphs <note>The political and religious successors to the Prophet Muhammad who led the Islamic Empire.</note>. The ancient historians did not distinguish accurately between different nations. For example, the Kings of Palmyra <note>An ancient city in modern-day Syria; its most famous ruler was Queen Zenobia.</note>, who have been thought to be Jews, were more probably Arabs.

### CHAP. III.

#### *On the Bedouins on the borders <note>original: "confines"</note> of the Desert.*

The most ancient and powerful tribes of these people are those who can easily retreat into the desert when attacked by a foreign enemy. These groups have preserved their national character in its greatest purity and have maintained their liberty unimpaired. Among this number are the following tribes, of whom I shall mention such details as have come to my knowledge.

The *Bani Khalid* <note>original: "Beni Khaled"</note> are one of the most powerful tribes in all Arabia, due to their conquests, their wealth, and the number of other tribes subject to them. From the desert of *Najd* <note>original: "Nedsjed"; the central highland region of the Arabian Peninsula</note>, they have advanced to the sea and have conquered the country of *Al-Hasa* <note>original: "Lachsa"; an oasis region in eastern Saudi Arabia</note>, as I mentioned in the appropriate section. The Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note> of this tribe does not always live in the city of Al-Hasa, but sometimes lives in tents in the desert.

The tribe of *Ka'b* <note>original: "Kiab"</note>, who live north of the *Persian Gulf* <note>original: "Persian Gulph"</note> and whom I have already mentioned, rarely set up camps; they have possessions in the province of *Khuzestan* <note>original: "Susistan"</note> in *Persia*.

However, the successors of the Sheikhs <note>original: "Schiechs"</note> who have been beheaded are always just as great enemies to the Turks and just as eager to maintain their liberty as their predecessors were.

The *Muntafiq* <note>original: "Montefidsi, or Montefik"</note> are the most powerful tribe north of the desert, both in respect to the size of their territories and the great number of subordinate <note>original: "subaltern"</note> tribes who acknowledge their authority. They control all the land on both sides of the Euphrates, from Qurna to *Arje* <note>original: "Ardje"</note>.

I was told the names of more than twenty <note>original: "a score"</note> inferior tribes who all live in subjection to the Muntafiq <note>original: "Montefik"</note>, which, by itself, is not extremely numerous. All these tribes upon the borders of the desert, whose names I have mentioned, are genuine Arabs who breed sheep and camels and live in tents. ## Chapter 4.

->*Concerning the Bedouins of Mesopotamia.*<-

The rich plains of Mesopotamia and Assyria, which were once cultivated by a populous nation and watered by impressive <note>original: "surprising"</note> efforts of human industry, are now inhabited—or rather ravaged—by wandering Arabs. As long as these fertile provinces remain under the government, or rather the anarchy, of the Turks, they must continue to be deserts in which nature fails <note>original: "dies"</note> for lack of the fostering care of man. Only a hereditary sovereign <note>A ruler whose title is passed down through their family, rather than a temporary appointed governor</note> stationed at Baghdad, and no one else, might restore this country to its once flourishing state.

The Pashas <note>original: "Pachas"; Turkish provincial governors</note>, not knowing how to improve the value of these depopulated districts and being unable to drive away the Arabs, permit them to cultivate those lands or feed their flocks upon them in exchange for an annual rent. But these people are passionately fond of liberty and show <note>original: "shew"</note> by their conduct that they do not consider themselves subject to the Turkish yoke. The frequent wars in which several of the tribes are engaged with the Pasha of Baghdad—although viewed as rebellion by the Ottoman <note>The Turkish empire that ruled much of the Middle East at the time</note> officers—are proofs of the independence of the Arabs.

*Khafail* <note>original: "Khafaal"</note>, a powerful tribe of farmers, also located on the east side of the Euphrates. They have a great many small Arab tribes who live in villages and are subject to them. One of these smaller groups includes twenty-five lower-ranking tribes, and two others consist of forty each. The tribes that practice farming seem, therefore, to be less numerous than the Bedouins, who often unite into very large groups. The tribe of *Khafail* can assemble two thousand cavalry and a corresponding number of infantry soldiers. The Pasha <note>original: "Pacha"; the Ottoman governor</note> of Baghdad has recently waged war against these people with mixed success. These Arabs are Shiites <note>One of the two main branches of Islam. The Ottoman Turks were Sunnis, and this religious difference often fueled political conflict</note>, which is another reason for their conflict with the Turks. The reigning Sheikh is named *Hammoud*, and he collects customs duties from vessels traveling up the Euphrates.

### CHAP. V.

->*Of the Bedouins of Syria.*<-

The Pashas <note>original: "Pachas"; the title for high-ranking Ottoman officials or governors</note> of this province deal with the wandering Arabs as much as the Turkish governors do on the Persian frontier. It is of great importance to the cities of Aleppo and Damascus that their caravans, traveling to Baghdad <note>original: "Bagdad"</note> or Basra <note>original: "Basra"</note>, be allowed to pass safely through the desert. Without escorting them with an army, the Pashas could not protect them from insult and robbery <note>original: "pillage"</note>, unless they artfully plotted to employ one tribe of Arabs against the rest.

With this goal in mind, the Pasha gives the title of Emir <term>Emir: a title of high rank, often translated as "commander" or "prince"</term> to the most powerful Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note> in the neighborhood. This emir is required to guide the caravans, to keep the other Arabs in check <note>original: "in awe"</note>, and to collect the taxes <note>original: "dues"</note> from those who graze their cattle on the Pasha’s lands. As payment for his trouble and to reimburse his expenses, he receives a set sum of money every year. However, since the Arabs have little trust in Turkish promises, the Pasha assigns the Emir a number of villages, the taxes <note>original: "revenues"</note> of which provide the agreed-upon sum. These villages were miserable enough before, but have been absolutely ruined... <meta>catchword: ruined</meta>

A few years since, an Emir, foreseeing that he was to be deposed, plundered a caravan, carried away 30,000 head of cattle from the pastures around Aleppo, and conveyed his booty to a place of safety near the Euphrates.

These exaggerated accounts of the pilgrims' sufferings at the hands of those "inhuman" Bedouins will therefore continue as long as they serve the purpose for which they are intended.

It must be admitted, however, that this tribe of *Jarhamie* forms, in one instance, a remarkable exception to the ordinary national character of the Arabs, who generally never mistreat a stranger unless they have first been provoked. However, these Arabs in the neighborhood of Jerusalem have a deep-seated hatred for the monks; in other respects, they are honest enough people.

## SECTION XXV.

### ON THE RELIGION AND CHARACTER OF THE

### CHAPTER I.

### *Concerning the different Sects of Muslims in Arabia.*

One might expect that the Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> religion would be preserved in its highest purity in Arabia, which was its cradle, and that no conflicting opinions or diversity of sects would have arisen there. An old tradition records a saying of Muhammad’s <note>original: "Mahomet’s"</note>, from which he appears to have foreseen that it was impossible for his followers to remain in perpetual harmony regarding doctrine and worship. He is said to have predicted that his new religion would be divided into seventy different sects, just as the Christians of his time were.

This prediction is partially fulfilled; for there are currently several Muslim sects in Arabia.

The doctrines and rites of the Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note> religion are generally well known. I <meta>The text continues on the next page with: "I shall..."</meta>

<summary>Niebuhr introduces the religious climate of Arabia, noting that despite being the birthplace of Islam, the region is home to various sects, a development he links to a prophecy attributed to Muhammad.</summary>

I shall satisfy myself by mentioning some remarkable peculiarities that distinguish the sects established in Arabia, which influence the moral character or political state of the nation.

The most significant <note>original: "considerable"</note> sects among the Arabian Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> are:

1. That of the *Sunni*, to which the Turks also belong. This is the most numerous sect in Arabia; its opinions are held by the inhabitants of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, and by the Sharifs <note>original: "Sherriffes"; refers to the descendants of the Prophet who governed Mecca</note> of those cities, who are considered the successors of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>.

2. The sect of the *Shia* <note>original: "Schya"</note>, which the whole Persian nation professes. In the eastern parts of Arabia, there are some followers of this sect, and it prevails all along the borders of the Persian Gulf. The *Metaueli*, or *Mut-Ali*, in Syria, are likewise Shiites.

3. The sect of the *Zaidis* <note>original: "Zeidi"</note>, which prevails in Yemen, and of which the Imam of Sana’a is a follower.

4. The sect of the *Ibadi* <note>original: "Beiasi, Beiadi, or Abadi"</note> is the principal sect in Oman. It is said to owe its origin to the enemies of the Caliph Ali, two of whom went into Oman after a defeat that only nine of them survived. <note>This refers to the Kharijite movement, an early branch of Islam distinct from both Sunnism and Shiism.</note>

7. The sect of *Dajjal* <note>original: "Djedsjal"</note>, which is followed by the inhabitants of Makran <note>original: "Mecran"</note>, a coastal province of Persia.

8. Finally, the sects of *Shahriari* <note>original: "Schabreari"</note> and *Merdinar*, which include the Baloch <note>original: "Belludsje"</note> people—Arabian tribes living on the borders of the Makran province, as I mentioned previously.

All these various sects acknowledge Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> as their prophet and regard the Quran <note>original: "Koran"</note> as their code of civil and religious <note>original: "ecclesiastical"</note> laws. However, they all view one another as *Kharijites* <note>original: "Chauaredsji"</note> or *Rafida* <note>original: "Rafidi"</note>—that is to say, heretics.

The Sunnis <note>original: "Sunnites"</note> allow only the four sects they consider orthodox—the Shafi'i, Hanafi, Maliki, and Hanbali <note>original: "Schafei, Hanefi, Maleki, and Hanbali"</note>—to have houses of prayer around the Kaaba <note>original: "Kaba"</note>. To compensate for being excluded, the Zaidis <note>original: "Zeidites"</note> have envisioned for themselves an invisible house of prayer in the air, directly above the Kaaba. In their own view, this gives them possession of these sacred sites. Despite these high-minded <note>original: "lofty"</note> claims, every pilgrim from this sect is still required to pay a high

## Chapter II.

### *On the Other Religions Tolerated in Arabia.*

Throughout all Arabia there are Jews, who are held in much greater contempt than Christians. I have already mentioned the Jewish tribes settled in the neighborhood of Kheibar, where they are not merely tolerated, but hold sovereign authority in their own hands.

The Jews dispersed through different cities have synagogues and enjoy a great deal of freedom. They are fond of living together and commonly form a village near every principal town. In Oman they are treated even better and are permitted to wear the dress of Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>.

Christians were once numerous in Arabia. I know of no Christian church remaining at present in all this country. In the province of Lachsa <note>modern-day Al-Ahsa</note> there are many Sabaeans, or Christians of Saint John. However, the Christianity of this sect seems to be a confused medley of the opinions and ceremonies of several different religions.

Banians <term>Hindu merchants or traders from India</term> from India are settled in great numbers in the commercial cities. At Mokha <note>also spelled Mocha</note> they suffer many hardships <note>original: "mortifications"</note>. However, at Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>, among the tolerant sect of the Beiasi <note>referring to the Ibadi branch of Islam</note>, they

### CHAPTER III.

->*On the Character of the Arabs.*<-

Climate, government, and education are undoubtedly the primary factors that form and shape the characters of nations. To the first of these (climate), the Arabs owe their liveliness and their tendency toward laziness <note>original: "indolence"</note>. The second (government) increases their laziness and gives them a spirit of deceit <note>original: "duplicity"</note>. The third (education) is the cause of that formal seriousness <note>original: "gravity"</note> which influences their mental faculties as well as their posture <note>original: "carriage"</note> and outward appearance.

Nothing could be more different than the education of the Arabs compared to that of Europeans. The former strive as much to hasten the age of maturity as the latter do to delay it. The Arabs are never children, while many Europeans remain children all their lives.

In Arabia, boys remain in the <term>harem</term> <note>original: "Haram"; here referring to the private women's quarters of a household.</note> among the women until the age of five or six. During this time, they engage in the childish amusements suitable for their years. However, as soon as they are removed from that environment of playfulness <note>original: "frivolity"</note>, they are accustomed

<summary>Niebuhr identifies climate, government, and education as the three main influences on the Arab character, contrasting their rapid transition to adult maturity with the prolonged childhood of Europeans.</summary>

accustomed to think and speak with seriousness <note>original: "gravity"</note>, and to pass whole days together in their father’s company—at least if he is not in a financial position to hire a tutor <note>original: "preceptor"</note> who might educate them. Since music and dancing are considered indecent among the Arabs, women are also excluded from all social gatherings <note>original: "assemblies"</note>, and the use of alcohol <note>original: "strong drink"</note> is forbidden. The Arabian youth are strangers to the so-called pleasures that are so eagerly pursued by the youth of Europe. Consequently, because they are always under the supervision of adults, young Arabs become thoughtful <note>original: "pensive"</note> and serious even in childhood.

Yet, beneath this appearance of seriousness and composure <note>original: "recollection"</note>, the nation actually possesses a high degree of liveliness <note>original: "vivacity"</note> in their hearts, which varies across the different provinces. The inhabitants of Yemen, living in a mild climate and a pleasant atmosphere, have more animation in their character than those of Hejaz <note>original: "Hedſjas"</note> and Stony Arabia <note>original: "Arabia Petræa"</note>, whose imagination takes on a more gloomy tone <note>original: "cast"</note> from the constant sight of barren deserts and bare rocks. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *Of the Vengeance of the Arabs.*

A lively, animated people, possessed of quick and violent passions, are naturally led to carry the desire for vengeance for injuries to its highest excess. The vindictive spirit of the Arabs—which they share with other inhabitants of hot climates—varies, however, according to the different modifications of their national character.

The Arabs are not naturally quarrelsome; but, when any dispute happens to arise among them, they make a great deal of noise. I have seen some of them, however, who, although armed with daggers <note>original: "poignards"</note> and ready to stab one another, were easily calmed. A reconciliation was instantly achieved if any neutral <note>original: "indifferent"</note> person simply said to them, "Think of God and his Prophet." When the contest could not be settled at once, arbiters <note>original: "umpires"</note> were chosen, to whose decision they submitted.

The inhabitants of the East in general strive to master their anger. A boatman from Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>...

Now obsessed with <note>original: "breathing nothing but"</note> vengeance, he sought him everywhere. Not finding him, he killed several of his relatives in the meantime.

However, the vengeful Arab would rather face death than give up his revenge. Then the governor, to save a man of such high honor, persuaded him to reach an agreement. By this deal, the original offender gave his daughter, along with a handsome dowry <note>original: "portion"</note>, in marriage to the man he had offended. But the father-in-law never dared to appear before his son-in-law again.

The thirst for vengeance also reveals itself in the peculiar way in which murder <note>original: "murther"</note> is prosecuted here. In the highlands of Yemen, the supreme court of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana"</note> usually prosecutes murders in the same way as other countries. However, in several districts of Arabia, the relatives of the deceased are permitted either to accept a financial settlement <term>composition: a legal payment made to settle a debt or crime, often known as "blood money" or *diya* in Islamic law</term>, to require the murderer to surrender himself to justice, or even to take their revenge upon his entire family. In many places, it is considered unlawful to accept money for the shedding of blood which, according to the laws of Arabian honor, can only be atoned for <note>original: "expiated"</note> by blood. They care little about having an assassin punished, or even put to death, by the hand of justice; for doing so would actually deliver the murderer's family from an unworthy member, who deserved no such favor at their hands.

For these reasons, the Arabs instead take revenge, as their custom allows, upon the family of the murderer. They seek an opportunity to kill the head of the family, or its most prominent member, whom they regard as the person truly guilty of the crime. They believe the crime must have been committed because of his negligence in supervising the conduct of those under his authority. In the meantime, the judges seize the murderer and detain him until he has paid a fine of two hundred crowns <note>original: "crowns"; Niebuhr uses this European currency term to approximate the value of local fines</note>. Had it not been for the profit from this fine, such an absurd law would likely have been repealed long ago.

From this point on, the two families live in continual fear until someone from the murderer's family is killed. No reconciliation can take place between them, and the quarrel is periodically renewed. There have been instances of such family feuds lasting forty years. If, during the conflict, a member of the victim's family happens to be killed, there can be no peace until two others from the murderer's family have been slain.

### CHAPTER I.

->*On Marriage Among the Arabs.*<-

Europeans are mistaken in thinking that the state of marriage among Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note> is significantly different from what it is among Christian nations. I could not discern any such difference in Arabia. The women of that country seem to be as free and happy as those of Europe can possibly be.

Polygamy is indeed permitted among Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, and the sensibilities of our European ladies are shocked by this idea. By law, a husband is required to treat his wives according to their social standing and to share his attention <note>original: "favours"</note> among them with complete equality. Arab women enjoy a great deal of liberty and often hold significant power within their families. They remain in control of <note>original: "mistresses of"</note> their dowries and the annual income those dowries provide throughout the marriage; in the case of a divorce, all of their own property is kept by them. Because of this, when a man of limited means <note>original: "narrow circumstances"</note> marries a wealthy woman, he is entirely dependent on his wife and does not dare to divorce her.

It is ridiculous <note>original: "absurd"</note> to claim, as some travelers have, that Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> wives are all slaves and so entirely the property of their husbands that they are even inherited by his heirs. In this

The opinion that women are slaves in Arabia seems to have arisen from the mistaken notion that fathers there sell their daughters to the highest bidder. It certainly happens many times that a poor man who has a beautiful daughter is pleased to marry her to a rich man from whom he may receive occasional gifts. Additionally, wealthy men who live for pleasure <note>original: "voluptuaries"</note> and choose to marry more than one wife are forced to take young women from lower social classes. These women are either compelled by self-serving <note>original: "interested"</note> parents or seduced by splendor to accept a husband who places them alongside other wives and eventually divorces them.

Instead of selling his daughter, every man in reasonably comfortable circumstances strives to give her a dowry, which remains her own property. The marriage contract is drawn up by the <term>Cadi</term> <note>a judge who presides over matters of Islamic law</note> and signed in his presence. In this document, not only is her dowry secured to the wife, but also a separate allowance for her support <note>original: "maintenance"</note> in the event of a divorce. The rich often prefer to give their daughters to poor men, believing their children are more likely to be happy when settled this way than if they were married to rich men. Many ridiculous stories have been told regarding the physical signs of virginity that an Arab expects when he marries a young woman. However, most of these stories greatly exaggerate the truth. The Bedouins <term>nomadic Arab tribes</term> and the mountain dwellers of Yemen—who are a rugged and almost primitive <note>original: "rude and almost savage"</note> people—do indeed regard the absence of those signs as proof of dishonor. They consider themselves obligated to send a woman back to her relatives if her chastity cannot be demonstrated in this way. But the townspeople, being more refined, never concern themselves with such a triviality. In such instances, a son-in-law simply forces an increase to the dowry from his father-in-law by threatening to send his daughter home, though he almost never actually carries out the threat. In Basra, I heard of only a single instance of divorce for this reason, and the man belonged to the lowest social class.

Many superstitious practices regarding marriage still persist in Arabia. They are brought from Upper Egypt but are mostly natives of the interior and little-known provinces of Africa. The Arabs loathe the cruel surgery required to make a man a "fit" guardian for a harem's chastity.

Eunuchs born in climates that tend to "inflame the blood" <note>An 18th-century medical theory suggesting hot climates increased sexual desire</note> are not entirely without passion for women. While at sea between Suez and Jeddah, I met a eunuch traveling with his own harem, and in Basra, I heard of another wealthy eunuch who kept female slaves for his own private amusement.

Much has been said in Europe concerning the origin of the practice of polygamy, which is so generally prevalent throughout the East. Assuming that having multiple wives is not merely allowed by law, but actually occurs in practice, some of our philosophers have imagined that in hot countries, more women than men are born. However, I have already stated that some nations do not take advantage of the permission given by Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note> law for one man to marry several wives. It would be unfair to judge the manners of an entire people by the extravagant luxury of the elite. It is vanity that fills seraglios <term>secluded living quarters for women in a palace or large house</term>, and they are filled chiefly with slaves, most of whom are only servants to a few favorite women. The number of female servants in Europe—who are, in the same manner, largely condemned to celibacy—is equal to or even greater than the number of those who are confined in the harems <note>original: "harams"</note> of the East.

It is true that European clergymen and physicians settled in the East have assumed that more girls than boys are born here. I obtained some lists of Christian baptisms in the East; however, some of those were filled with inconsistencies, and in others, the amount by which the female births exceeded the males was indeed very small. I have reason, therefore, to conclude that the proportion between male and female births is the same here as it is elsewhere.

<summary>Niebuhr challenges the European theory that polygamy in the East is caused by a biological surplus of women, arguing instead that the practice is a result of the vanity of the wealthy and that birth ratios are the same as in Europe.</summary>

## Chapter II.

### *On the Domestic Life of the Arabs.*

Arabia offers no elegant or magnificent <note>original: "splendid"</note> apartments for the traveler to admire. The houses are built of stone and always have flat, terraced roofs. Those occupied by the common people are small huts with rounded roofs covered with a specific type of grass <note>original: "herb"</note>. The huts of the Arabs on the banks of the Euphrates are made from the branches of the date palm and have rounded roofs covered with mats made of rushes. The tents of the Bedouins are similar to those of the Kurds <note>original: "Kurdes"</note> and Turcomans <term>nomadic Turkic people of Central Asia and the Middle East</term>. They have the appearance of a tattered hut. I have previously mentioned that they are made from coarse fabrics <note>original: "stuffs"</note> prepared by the women.

The palaces and houses of high-ranking Arabs <note>original: "Arabians of rank"</note> display no outward magnificence. Ornaments

The men of every family always occupy the front <note>original: "fore"</note> part of the house, and the women occupy the back part. The floor was to be furnished with sofas and spread with carpets.

I have seen some people of rank use a spittoon <note>original: "spitting-box"</note>, while others spit at the base of the wall behind the cushions on which they sat.

Since the floors are covered with carpets and cushions are placed against the walls, one cannot sit down on the ground without some discomfort if not used to it, and the use of chairs is unknown in the East. The Arabs practice several different ways of sitting. When they wish to be completely relaxed, they cross their legs under their bodies. I found, indeed, by experience, that this way of sitting is the most comfortable <note>original: "commodious"</note> for people who wear long clothes and wide trousers <note>original: "breeches"</note> without any tight bindings <note>original: "confining ligatures"</note>. It seems to provide better rest after exhaustion than our habit of sitting on chairs. In the presence of superiors, an Arab sits with his two knees touching each other, with the weight of the body resting upon the heels. Because a person occupies less room in this position than in the other, this is the posture in which they usually place themselves at the table. I often tried it, but found it extremely uncomfortable, and could never accustom myself to it. In many parts of Arabia, there are long, low benches <note>original: "chairs"</note> made of straw mats, but they sit cross-legged on them just as they do on the carpets.

The life which the Arabs lead in their houses is so empty and repetitive that they cannot help but find it tedious <note>original: "irksome"</note>. Their natural energy <note>original: "vivacity"</note> drives them to seek entertainment out of doors. They frequent coffee houses and markets and are fond of gathering in public meet-

## CHAP. III.

### Of the Food of the Arabians, and their Manner of Eating.

Just as the people of the East sit cross-legged <note>original: "squat themselves"</note> on the ground, their way of eating meals matches this sitting posture. They spread a large cloth in the middle of the room, place a small table only one foot high on top of it, and set a large round plate of tinned copper on the table. On this plate, they place various copper dishes that are neatly coated with tin both inside and out. Instead of napkins, high-ranking Arabians use a long linen cloth, which those at the table lay across <note>original: "put under"</note> their knees. When this linen cloth is unavailable <note>original: "wanting"</note>, everyone uses their own small handkerchief. They use neither knives nor forks. The Turks sometimes use spoons made of wood or horn; but the Arabians use their fingers with great skill <note>original: "dexterity"</note> and eat every dish with their hands.

If we were to judge them by the standards of our own etiquette <note>original: "manners"</note>, the people of the East might seem to behave very poorly <note>original: "indecently"</note> at a European table. I was quite struck by the behavior of the first Turk I saw eating; he was the comptroller of customs for the Dardanelles <note>The Dardanelles is a narrow natural strait in northwestern Turkey that connects the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara.</note>, dining in the company of

The only difference between their method of preparation and ours is that they pound their coffee beans in a mortar instead of grinding them. We brought a coffee mill with us to Arabia, but we soon found that the taste of pounded coffee was much better than ground coffee, and we stopped using our mill. The pounding seems to better extract the oily parts of the bean, which give the coffee its distinctive flavor. The people of the East always drink their coffee black, without either milk or sugar.

It is quite strange that in Yemen—the very country where the coffee plant is native—so little actual coffee is consumed. In Yemen, the bean is called *Bunn* <note>original: *Bunn*; refers to the coffee berry or bean</note>, and it is believed to have "heating" effects on the blood. The favorite drink of the Arabs in this province is prepared from the husks of coffee beans, which are lightly roasted and pounded. It is called *Kahwe*, or more commonly *Kischer* <note>original: *Kischer*; modern: *Qishr*, a traditional Yemeni beverage made from coffee husks, ginger, and sometimes cinnamon</note>. It tastes more like tea and is considered refreshing. People of high social standing drink it from porcelain cups, while the lower classes use cups made of coarse earthenware.

Although Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note> are forbidden from using any intoxicating liquors, many of them are passionately fond of these drinks and consume them privately at night in their own houses.

The Arabians are, in general, a sober and frugal nation, which is probably the cause of their leanness and seemingly small stature. Their usual articles of food are rice, legumes <note>original: "pulse"</note>, milk, butter, and *keimak* <note>original: "Keimak"; whipped cream</note>. They are not without animal food, but they seldom eat it, for it is thought very unwholesome in these hot countries. Mutton is the most common species of animal food used here, and it is what the Arabians of the desert chiefly live upon. As the castration of animals—though not forbidden by Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note> law—is little practiced here, meat from castrated rams <note>original: "wedder-mutton"</note> is never used by the Arabians.

The common people in Arabia have little other food but bad bread made of *durra* <note>original: "Durra"; a type of coarse millet or sorghum</note>, produced by kneading it with camel's milk, oil, butter, or grease. I could not eat this bread at first and would have preferred the worst bread I had ever eaten in Europe; but the people of the country, being accustomed to it, prefer it to barley bread, which they think is too light.

The modes of baking bread are different in various places in Arabia. In the ship in which we sailed from Jeddah <note>original: "Jidda"</note> to Al Luheyah <note>original: "Loheya"</note>, there was a sailor whose task every afternoon was to prepare *durra* for the next day's bread. ### CHAP. IV.

### *Of the Dress and Fashions of the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note>.*

When speaking of the dress of the inhabitants of the East in general, I shared some idea of the clothing used by the Arabs. I described the attire of people of rank <note>original: "distinction"</note> in Yemen when I had the opportunity to mention the ceremonial dress with which I was honored <note>original: "favoured"</note> by the Imam of Sana. However, there is a great variety in the national clothing of the Arabs, and various fashions prevail among them which I must not leave unnoticed.

Nothing can be more inconvenient or expensive than the head-dress worn by fashionable Arabs. They wear fifteen caps, one over another; some of these are indeed made of linen, but the rest are of thick cloth or cotton. The cap that covers all the others is usually richly embroidered with gold and always has some verse from the Quran <note>original: "Koran"</note> embroidered upon it. Over all these

### CHAP. V.

### *Arabian Politeness.*

In Yemen, Oman, and Persia, a European is treated with as much politeness <note>original: "civility"</note> as a Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> would find in Europe. In Turkey, Europeans are treated less kindly. A comparison of the manners of the Turks with those of the Arabians clearly demonstrates the superior politeness of the latter nation.

The Turks generally dislike Europeans, likely due to a vague memory of the bloody wars they have fought at various times against the people of the West <note>This likely refers to the Crusades and the ongoing conflicts between the Ottoman Empire and European powers</note>. Europeans are particularly hated in Damietta, Damascus, and Cairo <note>original: "Kahira"</note>. The Arabians, having never had any conflicts with the people of Europe, do not have the same reasons for viewing them with such dislike.

The behavior of the Turks toward Christians matches the insulting language they use to address them. Throughout the Turkish Empire, Christians are forced to wear a badge that signifies their subordinate status and are required to pay a poll tax <note>a tax levied on every individual, regardless of income</note>. In Constantinople <note>modern-day Istanbul</note>, Christians walking through the streets are required to either sweep the roads and remove waste or pay a fee to be exempt from this labor. Although the government does not officially authorize these annoying demands, the Christians' social position is so low that they do not dare to complain about mistreatment by a Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note>. They risk being insulted if they appear in public during days of festival and celebration.

I will mention one example among many that I witnessed of Turkish arrogance. In Anatolia <note>original: "Natolia"</note>, we met a Turk on the highway who, as he was about to mount his horse, forced a respectable Greek merchant to get off his mule and hold his stirrup for him. An Arab would be ashamed of such rudeness. In contrast, a Sheikh <note>original: "Schiech"</note> from whom we had hired camels often offered his own back as a step so that I could mount my dromedary <note>a one-humped camel</note>.

### CHAPTER VI.

#### *Some Peculiar Customs*

In hot countries, cleanliness is indispensably necessary for health. Common people, who reflect little on such things, might forget or neglect a care so necessary to their welfare. For this reason, it seems, the founders of various religious sects have commanded purifications and ablutions <note>ritual washings of the body</note> as a religious duty.

The Arabs are required to be extremely clean by the laws of both their climate and their religion, and they observe these precepts with the most scrupulous exactness. They not only wash, bathe, and trim <note>original: "pair"</note> their nails very often, but they also remove all hair from the body. They even pluck them from those parts where a razor cannot be used, so that not the slightest impurity remains upon them. Those who work in uncleanly trades are held in contempt, such as the ser- <note>The text continues on the next page with "vants" (servants)</note>

#### IN ARABIA, ETC.

Much has been said concerning the origin of the custom of circumcising infants, which seems, at first glance, so absurd. Some have attributed it to a human inclination to offer to the Deity a part of what they hold dearest and value as most precious. But this seems to be an awkward attempt at a joke, and besides, it is not true; otherwise, circumcision would be practiced among all nations, in all climates, and would be regarded as a religious ceremony. Instead, it exists only in hot countries, and even there not as a religious institution, but as an ancient custom.

It is true that several nations in hot climates do not practice it, such as the Persians, the Indians, and many of the inhabitants of Africa; but there are others who observe it, although it is not commanded by the precepts of their religion. Such are the Christians of Abyssinia <note>modern-day Ethiopia and Eritrea</note>, and many of the polytheistic <note>original: "idolatrous"</note> people of Africa. Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> do not consider circumcision to be a religious duty, but merely as a praiseworthy custom of their ancestors, worthy of being maintained. None but the Jews—whom the author views as superstitious—appear to attach ideas of religious sanctity to a practice that is purely civil <note>original: "civil"; here meaning a social or hygienic regulation rather than a spiritual one</note>.

The custom of circumcising infants certainly owes its origin to the physical nature of these climates. There are some physical <note>original: "corporeal"</note> defects and ailments <note>original: "infirmities"</note> more common in some countries than in others, which this practice has a tendency to remedy; and, where these prevail, circumcision is used. Nothing is more effective <note>original: "effectual"</note> in preventing those diseases which, in hot countries, are liable to attack certain parts, than keeping those parts very clean by frequent washing <note>original: "ablution"</note>. Circumcision renders this washing necessary and reminds those who might otherwise neglect it of its utility. Lawmakers <note>original: "Legislators"</note> have accordingly thought it their duty to make people take suitable precautions for the preservation of health by giving this useful custom the authority <note>original: "sanction"</note> of civil and religious laws.

This theory <note>original: "conjecture"</note> will appear more likely <note>original: "probable"</note> when it is considered that the practice of circumcising girls is general in the same countries in which boys are circumcised.
