In Egypt, we expressed our curiosity about how girls were circumcised to a nobleman who had invited us to his country estate. He immediately called in a young Arabian girl, who had been circumcised and was then eighteen years old. In the presence of his servants, he allowed us to examine the physical changes produced by the operation and even let us make a drawing of them. I was convinced that the practice of circumcising women was originally adopted for cleanliness and to make ritual washing <note>original: "ablution"</note> easier. No law has formally established it, any more than for boys; it is a custom <note>original: "usage"</note>, rather than a religious obligation <note>original: "duty"</note>.

The decomposition <note>original: "corruption"</note> of dead bodies has a highly destructive effect on health in hot countries, much more so than in temperate climates. It was therefore necessary to protect the inhabitants from its harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note> influence by using religious motives to increase their natural aversion to dead bodies <note>original: "carcases"</note>. For this reason, Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> and other founders of religious sects have associated the act of touching a corpse with spiritual impurity. Some Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note> require significant purification rituals to cleanse a man who has been "defiled" in this way, separating him from society for a period of time.

The Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> are less rigid; when a person of this nation has had the misfortune to touch a corpse <note>original: "carcase"</note>, he washes himself carefully, and when no mark of external impurity remains, he then returns to the ordinary interactions of life.

A frugal nation, who regard even sobriety as a virtue, must naturally attach ideas of shame to everything that indicates any degree of intemperance. The Arabs are greatly shocked when that accident happens to a man which is the natural consequence of the fullness of the intestines after too large a meal, or the indigestion of gas-producing <note>original: "windy"</note> foods. The *Chevalier D’Arvieux* <note>Laurent d'Arvieux (1635–1702), a French diplomat and traveler known for his detailed accounts of Bedouin life.</note> has been accused of exaggeration in what he says concerning the sensitivity <note>original: "delicacy"</note> of the Arabs on this point; but I have found all that he says of the manners and customs of this nation to be strictly true. I am, therefore, inclined to believe equally what he relates concerning things which I could not observe or verify myself. It appears that not all Arabs are equally shocked by such an involuntary accident. Yet, a Bedouin guilty of such a piece of indecency would be despised by his countrymen. I was told of an instance involving an Arab of the *Belludje* <note>original: "Belludſje"</note> tribe who, for a reason of this sort, was obliged to leave his country and never dared return.

The ignorance of the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> subjects them to all the illusions of superstition. Because the Arab nation extended their conquests and established colonies throughout much of Asia and nearly all the coasts of Africa, the various peoples they conquered were forced to speak the language of their new masters and neighbors. However, these people also retained terms and phrases from their original languages. This has corrupted <note>original: "debased"</note> the purity of Arabic and created a wide variety of dialects.

These different dialects within Arabia strongly resemble the regional variations found in Italy. Outside the borders of Arabia, the relationships between these dialects are similar to the relationships between the languages of Provence <note>referring to Occitan</note>, Spain, and Portugal—all of which are derived from Latin. Even within the small territory ruled by the Imam of Sana'a <note>original: "Sana’s"</note>, the diversity of dialects is quite significant. Not only does the language of the Tihama <note>original: "Tehama," the coastal plain of Yemen</note> differ from the language spoken in the highlands, but even within the same regions, the upper classes <note>original: "people of rank"</note> use words and phrases that are completely unknown to the rest of the population. Furthermore, the dialects of Yemen differ even more from those used by the Bedouins in the desert than they do from one another.

The invention of the modern script <note>original: "characters"</note>, which is very different from the *Kufic* <note>the oldest calligraphic form of the various Arabic scripts</note>, is attributed to a *vizier* <note>a high-ranking political advisor or minister</note>. The handwriting used by Arabs in the common business of life is difficult to read <note>original: "not legible"</note>. When their letters are folded, they are an inch in width, and the pages are pasted together at one end. They cannot use wax seals, for wax becomes so soft in hot countries that it cannot hold an impression.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Concerning the Education and Schools of the Arabs.*<-

The monarchs of the East do not take the same care, or spend the same money <note>original: "expence"</note>, for the encouragement of science as the sovereigns of Europe. In Arabia, therefore, there are neither numerous academies nor men of profound learning.

Yet the Arab youth are not entirely neglected. In the cities, many of the poorest <note>original: "lowest"</note> people are taught both to read and write; these same skills are also common among the Sheikhs <note>original: "Shiechs"</note> of the desert and in Egypt. People of high rank <note>original: "distinction"</note> keep private tutors <note>original: "preceptors"</note> in their families to instruct their children and young slaves; for they raise those young slaves who appear to possess natural talent just like the children of the family.

In almost every mosque is a school, called a *Madrasa* <note>original: "Maddrasse"; an Islamic educational institution</note>, which has an endowment <note>original: "foundation"</note> for the support of teachers and the housing <note>original: "entertainment," meaning the provision of food and lodging</note> and instruction of poor students. In large towns, there are also other schools where people of middle rank send their children to receive religious instruction and to learn reading, writing, and arithmetic. ### CHAP. III.

## *Of Arabian Poetry and Eloquence.*

THE Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> have always been considered admirers of poetry. Their early history records many instances of the high esteem <note>original: "estimation"</note> in which they held this art, even before the days of Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note>, and of the glory that any family acquired which produced a poet.

The Arabs have no great poets among them today, although they still cultivate poetry and sometimes reward those who excel at it. The best poets are found among the Bedouins <note>nomadic Arab tribes of the desert, often credited with preserving the purest form of the language and poetic tradition</note>

### CHAP. IV.

#### *Regarding the Astronomy of the Arabians.*

The methods of dividing time in use among the Arabians demonstrate how little progress this nation has made in astronomy. They know, indeed, a little of its basic elements; but this, it seems, is derived more from tradition than from any observations of their own.

The Arabian day consists of twenty-four hours and lasts from sunset to sunset. Their hours are, therefore, of uncertain duration and vary with the length of the natural day, or the time during which the sun is above the horizon. As they are unfamiliar with the use of watches, none of them has any precise idea of the exact length of their hours. Instead, like the peasants of Europe, they distinguish the different parts of the day by vague, imprecise names <note>original: "denominations"</note>, which only approach the truth.

Their year consists of twelve lunar months. They begin the month with the new moon; and,

When the sky is so cloudy that they cannot see the moon rise, they have no problem with beginning the month a day or two later. Consequently, all their months rotate through the seasons, and this division of the year marks out no fixed period for the work of farming <note>original: "husbandry"</note> or any of the other duties of civil life. To address <note>original: "obviate"</note> this inconvenience, the learned men calculate using other months that correspond to the course of the solar year, which consist of the same number of days as our own.

In Arabia, as in other Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> countries, two great festivals are celebrated annually: that of offerings, called *Arafa* or *Corban* <note>Known today as Eid al-Adha</note>, and that of *Beiram* <note>Known today as Eid al-Fitr</note>, which takes place immediately after *Ramadan*. Because they use lunar months, these festivals also circulate through the entire year. When the fast of *Ramadan* falls in summer, it is extremely distressing; for the people, no matter how hard they must work, dare not taste anything—even during the longest days of the year—until the sun has set.

In Constantinople <note>modern-day Istanbul</note>, the Sultan's astronomer creates a portable almanac every year, of which at least several copies are made. However, in Egypt and Arabia, this method of informing the people about the return of festivals and the progression of the seasons has not been introduced. ### CHAPTER 5.

#### *Regarding the Diseases and Medicine of the Arabians.*

A regular and temperate lifestyle protects the body from the attacks of disease. Consequently, the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> are rarely sick and almost never turn to physicians or medicine. When forced by severe illness to call for a doctor, they pay him poorly and barely cover the cost of his medicine. If the patient dies, the doctor can hope for no payment; if the patient recovers, he soon forgets the services he received. The ingratitude of their patients has taught doctors to use tricks—often dishonest and shameful—to secure payment from the patient in advance.

Therefore, one cannot expect to find great physicians in Arabia. Those who practice medicine there know little more than technical terms found in the books of Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), a Persian polymath whose medical encyclopedia, *The Canon of Medicine*, was a standard textbook in both the Islamic world and Europe for centuries</note> and some basic knowledge regarding the use of medicinal herbs <note>original: "simples"</note>. All the physicians I knew in Yemen also acted as chemists, pharmacists <note>original: "apothecaries"</note>, surgeons, and veterinarians <note>original: "horse-doctors"</note>; yet, despite practicing all these arts combined, they could hardly earn a living.

Leprosy seems to have always been an endemic <note>native to a specific region or people</note> disease in Arabia; indeed, there is one species of leprosy which authors distinguish as "Arabian." Mothers perform this operation on their children, pricking the skin of the arm with the point of a thorn. An Arab from the island of Lam <note>likely Lamu Island, off the coast of modern-day Kenya</note>, situated on the southeast coast of Africa, informed me in Bombay that inoculation had been known and practiced in his country for several centuries.

A description of these sciences would be too humiliating to human pride if it did not also offer us comfort by showing the endless absurdities from which we are saved by the study of sound philosophy, especially the physical sciences <note>original: "physics," which in the 18th century referred to the general study of the natural world and laws of nature</note>.

These so-called occult sciences <note>mystical or supernatural arts such as magic, alchemy, and divination</note> are highly esteemed among the Arabs. No one dares to practice them unless they have been previously authorized by a master of the art after serving a kind of apprenticeship; or, as the Arabs say, without having "spread the prayer carpet before the feet of a famous master" for some time. Definite proof of their respect for these sciences is that one of the most prominent men in Mecca, belonging to the highest nobility in Arabia—*Sheikh Mohammed el-Janadjeni*—is currently the most celebrated master of the science of *Ism Allah* <note>Arabic for "The Name of God"</note>.

This science of *Ism Allah*, or "The Name of God," is considered the most sublime of all. In this belief, God is the lock and Muhammad <note>original: "Mahomet"</note> is the key; consequently, no one but Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note> can acquire this knowledge. It supposedly enables its possessor to discover what is happening in the most distant countries, to become familiar with spirits <note>original: "genii"; in Arabic folklore, these are supernatural beings (jinn) who can be good or evil</note> and compel them to obey his wishes, to control the winds and seasons as he chooses, and to cure snake bites and many other diseases or ailments. The science of *Kurra* <note>likely referring to the art of reciting the Qur'an or, in this context, the practice of creating charms based on it</note> teaches how to create small slips of paper <note>original: "billets"</note> that protect the wearer from the power of magic <note>original: "enchantment"</note> and from accidents of all kinds. The science of *Ramle* <note>original: *Ramle*; an Arabic term for geomancy, or divination using sand or markings on the ground</note> is properly the art of fortune-telling. Jews, as well as Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note>, deal in it. When a man falls sick, his friends, in order to learn whether he will recover, send to consult a Mullah <note>a Muslim scholar or religious official</note>, who returns an answer after examining his book and receives a rooster or a sheep for his trouble.

The Sunni <note>original: "Sunnite"</note> clergy condemn the practice of these last two sciences; yet they are tolerated because they afford a livelihood to a great number of poor scribes. As the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> are in general seen as being fond of money <note>original: "covetous"</note>, men of wealth and distinction too often practice these low arts for financial gain.

A science truly occult, and which every person of worth <note>original: "Arabian of worth"</note> must hold in abhorrence, is what they call *Sihhr* <note>original: *Sihhr*; Arabic for magic or sorcery</note>, or pure, open sorcery. The end goal of this science is more to do mischief to another person than to do good to the person who practices it. It is sometimes employed, however, to seduce a wife from the arms of her husband into those of a stranger. All that is requisite for this is to fix a certain slip of paper <note>original: "billet"</note> on her door. # IN ARABIA, &c.

They know nothing of the art of riding through the air on a broomstick, or of nocturnal assemblies presided over by the devil.

I found in Arabia more followers than I expected of a different kind of occult science: the pursuit of the **philosopher’s stone** <note>a legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and providing the "elixir of life"</note>. The Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> are so passionately devoted to this science—which is the object of their highest wishes and most eager research—that they often ruin their fortunes by it, just as the alchemists of Europe have traditionally done. They assume the secret of making gold is known in Europe, especially among the Venetians. They have books in their own language which deal with that science and inspire them with wild hopes. It appears that the idea of the philosopher’s stone is originally Eastern <note>original: "oriental"</note> and was brought westward like many other foolish fables.

At Beit el Fakih <note>a town in the Tihamah region of Yemen, a major center for the coffee trade in the 18th century</note>, we became acquainted with two alchemists who each worked according to the instructions <note>original: "precepts"</note> of a specific book. One of them, who was a friendly and otherwise sensible man, was sure of success if he could find a certain herb which he believed grew on the hills of Yemen. Since he assumed that we were also alchemists and had come specifically to seek that wonderful herb, he cultivated a friendship with Mr. Forskal <note>Peter Forsskål (1732–1763), the Swedish naturalist and botanist on Niebuhr's expedition</note> and was of great use to him during his botanical excursions.

### CHAP. I.
#### *Fertility of the Soil.*

A traveler, who is forced to spend most of his time in towns and sees only a passing <note>original: "transient"</note> view of the countryside, cannot easily gain accurate <note>original: "just"</note> ideas about the fertility of the land or the methods of cultivation. I did not miss any opportunity to gather information about the state of agriculture in the East from people I believed were most qualified to provide it. Here, I will record what I learned regarding the fertility of Arabia Proper <note>Arabia Proper refers to the Arabian Peninsula itself, as opposed to territories where Arabs had settled elsewhere</note> and other countries where the Arabians have settled.

These particulars may afford some general idea of the productive powers of land in the East. The ancients, and some modern travelers—with the intention, it would seem, to decorate their works with wonders—have related things absolutely incredible regarding the fertility of these regions. Their calculations have either been intentionally exaggerated beyond the truth, or the natives have deceived them.

Yet it is not impossible to bring their accounts within the bounds of probability. It is a vague way of estimating the fertility of any soil to say that the produce is in such a proportion to the seed. Skillful modes of tilling and sowing may result in a great saving of seed, as I shall soon have occasion to remark when speaking of the agriculture of the peasants of *Yemen*. If, then, a piece of ground where one-half of the seed has been lost through the lack of skill of the sower still produces a tenfold crop, another piece of ground of the same degree of fertility—but sown with only half the quantity of seed—will yield twenty-to-one. Consequently, it will seem, upon a hasty consideration, to be twice as fertile. This circumstance does not appear to have been properly considered by either the ancients or

We have seen that there is a great difference between the yield of wheat and that of *darra* <note>original: "darra" — sorghum, a drought-tolerant grain often called "great millet"</note>. This latter grain, a sort of coarse millet known in Denmark by the name of *Sargo* <note>original: "Sargo" — Sorghum</note>, has been found in Europe to be beneficial to the fertility of the soil on which it is sown. However, being of little value in comparison with our other grains, it is now very seldom planted. In the East, it appears to have been in use since time immemorial. The Arabians use it as their primary food source. It is sown in Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Assyria. The peasants of Syria and Palestine sell their wheat and live on *durra*. Therefore, it seems that what some authors have reported concerning the astonishing fertility of certain countries in the East should be understood as referring to this *durra*.

# CHAPTER II.

## *Of the Methods of Plowing and Sowing.*

Because the soil is not equally good everywhere, and the climate varies greatly across the countries of the East, the methods of cultivation practiced here are also considerably varied. In Egypt, Assyria, Mesopotamia, and Syria, agriculture is very much neglected; these provinces are so sparsely populated that much valuable land is left to go to waste.

In Arabia, where the government is less unfavorable to agricultural effort <note>original: "industry"</note>, farming <note>original: "husbandry"</note> is in a more prosperous state. However, the farming tools are, even here, crude and poorly made. The plow used is of a very simple design; it is drawn by oxen and dragged over the ground in every direction until the soil appears sufficiently broken and loosened to receive the seeds. In the neighborhood of Baghdad, I saw donkeys <note>original: "asses"</note> yoked to the plow with oxen, and near Mosul, I saw two mules used. To cultivate their gardens and areas of their fields inaccessible to the plow, the Arabs use a type of hoe; for very deep digging, they use a large crowbar <note>original: "crow"</note> operated by two men.

<meta>catchword: one</meta>

<summary>Niebuhr describes the regional differences in agricultural productivity, noting that while farming is neglected in sparsely populated areas like Syria and Egypt, it thrives more in Arabia despite the use of very simple, crude tools.</summary>

## CHAP. III.

->*Of the Harvest.*<-

The beginning of the harvest varies greatly throughout Arabia. This is due not only to the differences in latitude between locations, but chiefly as a result of the diverse geography—specifically the difference between high and low elevations—and the different times during the season when it becomes practical to irrigate the land. Even within the small territory of the Imam of Sana <note>The ruler of Yemen, based in the capital city of Sana'a</note>, there are great differences in this respect. At Sana, the barley was harvested <note>original: "cut down"</note> on the 15th of July, while at *Chamis*, closer to the mountains, the lentils <note>original: "lentiles"</note> were only just being sown at that time. In the plain of *Beit el Fakih*, the sorghum <note>original: "durra"; a cereal grain widely cultivated in arid regions</note> was seven feet high during the first days of August; at the same time, the fields were being plowed and watered for a second planting in the valley of *Zebid*, which is only a very short day's journey from *Beit el Fakih*.

In *Muscat* <note>original: "Maskat"; the capital of modern-day Oman</note>, wheat and barley are sown in December and harvested around the end of March. However, sorghum is sown in August and harvested at the end of November. The date trees are pollinated <note>original: "fecundated"</note> in the month of December; and,

### Chapter 4

#### *Regarding Domestic Animals*

Arabia has an abundance of all the domestic animals common in hot climates. The Arabs breed horses, mules, donkeys <note>original: "asses"</note>, camels, dromedaries, cows, buffaloes, sheep, and goats. In the fertile provinces, wild birds <note>original: "fowls"</note> are so plentiful that they are sold at a very low <note>original: "trifling"</note> price.

Of all their domestic animals, it is well known that the Arabs place the highest value on their horses. There are two main lineages <note>original: "branches"</note> of horses: the *Kadischi*, whose ancestry is unknown, and the *Kochlani* <note>the *Kuhaylan* breed, considered the oldest and purest line of Arabian horses</note>, for whom a written genealogy has been kept for two thousand years. The *Kadischi* are held in no higher regard than our European horses,

The ***Kochlani*** <note>the *Kuhaylan* breed, considered the oldest and purest line of Arabian horses</note> are reserved solely for riding. They are highly esteemed and, consequently, are very expensive. They are said to descend from King Solomon's stables <note>original: "studs"</note>. However this may be, they are fit to endure the greatest exhaustion <note>original: "fatigues"</note> and can go for whole days without food. They are also said to show uncommon courage against an enemy. It is even claimed that when a horse of this race finds himself wounded and unable to carry his rider much longer, he retires from the fight <note>original: "fray"</note> and conveys him to a place of security. If the rider falls to the ground, his horse remains beside him and neighs until assistance is brought. The *Kochlani* are neither large nor handsome, but they are amazingly swift. It is not for their appearance <note>original: "figure"</note>, but for their speed <note>original: "velocity"</note> and other good qualities, that the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> value them.

These *Kochlani* are bred chiefly by the Bedouins settled between Basra, Mardin <note>original: "Merdin"</note>, and Syria, in which countries the nobility never choose to ride horses of any other breed <note>original: "race"</note>. The entire breed is divided into several families, each of which has its own name; the family of ***Dsjulfa*** <note>likely the *Jilfan* strain of Arabian horses</note> seems to be the most numerous. Some of these families have a higher reputation than others on account of their more ancient and pure <note>original: "uncontaminated"</note> lineage.

# IN ARABIA, etc.

[A na]turalist finds few objects to observe; the natural history of such a country can never be extensive. In Arabia, the heat of the sun is so intense that flowers wither almost as soon as they bloom <note>original: "blow"</note>. If a botanist, tracking many plants at once, misses the exact moment a new flower blossoms, they will have no other opportunity to examine it until the following season.

This difficulty could be avoided by studying plants in gardens, but there is perhaps no country in the world where gardening is as neglected as it is in Arabia. There is hardly a single small garden in the vicinity of even the largest towns. At Beit el Fakih <note>A major trading city in the Tihama region of Yemen</note>, there is only one, which was established by a former Dola <note>original: "Dola"; a title for a local governor or magistrate in Yemen</note>. The Arabs, a simple and frugal people, are content with the plainest food and do not take the trouble to provide themselves with a variety of dishes. What seems to discourage them from gardening are the long droughts, which sometimes last for more than a year and destroy every sprout of vegetation, along with the ravages of locusts <note>original: "grasshoppers"</note> which complete the devastation of the fields. The Banians <note>original: "Banians"; Indian merchants, typically Hindu, living and trading in Arabian ports</note>, who are restricted to a vegetarian diet by their religion, plant large quantities of <term>pulse</term> <note>edible seeds of leguminous plants such as beans, lentils, or peas</note>; however, these are mostly species native to

In addition to these physical obstacles to investigating the natural history of the East, there is another challenge arising from the social character of the people who inhabit these regions. The Arabs—whom the author characterizes as an uneducated, greedy, and suspicious people—cannot understand why Europeans would be motivated by mere curiosity to expose themselves to such danger and exhaustion. They attribute to them self-interested motives, believing they have a great skill for discovering hidden treasures. This widespread belief in the wealth of travelers puts any inquisitive person at great risk of being robbed by wandering bandits.

## CHAPTER II.

### *Climate and Soil of Arabia*

A country such as Arabia, extending from 30° to 13° north latitude and consequently situated partly within the tropics, would naturally be expected to have a very hot climate. In some provinces of Arabia, the heat is excessive. However, in this country, as in most others, varying degrees of elevation, the relative location of places, and the nature of the soil cause considerable variations in temperature.

Before one can understand these variations, it is necessary to have an accurate idea of the physical geography <note>original: "circumstances"</note> of Arabia. This country may be considered as a mass of mountains encircled by a belt of flat, dry, and sandy ground. Towards the north and the mainland, this belt is formed by the deserts of Syria,

ria, and Arabia Petræa <note>Arabia Petræa: A Roman name for the province that included the Sinai Peninsula and parts of modern-day Jordan.</note>. The plains called *Tehama* <note>The Tihama is the coastal plain along the Red Sea.</note> by the Arabians, and extending from the seashore to the hills, bound Arabia on those sides on which it is washed by the waters of the Red Sea, of the Indian Ocean <note>original: "Eastern Ocean"</note>, and of the Persian Gulf.

In these deserts, broken here and there only by bare rocks, and in these flat plains, there is nothing to soften the force of the sun’s rays; all plants <note>original: "vegetables"</note> are scorched, and the soil is everywhere reduced to sand. The drought is so extreme that entire years will pass without rain, and the torrents which fall from the hills are lost among the sands long before they can reach the sea. Were it not for these river waters—which swell during the rainy season and are diverted to fertilize the lands—the farmer <note>original: "husbandman"</note> would be unable to raise even those meager crops which his harvests currently afford. By observations made with accurate thermometers, we found that in these plains—as, for instance, at Al Luheyah <note>original: "Loheya"</note>, Mocha <note>original: "Mokha"</note>, and Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>—the heat was as intense as in any other hot country in the world.

In the interior of the country, the temperature of the atmosphere is very different. The great ranges of lofty mountains attract clouds <note>original: "vapours"</note>; and these falling down in plentiful rains cool the air and stimulate plant growth <note>original: "quicken vegetation"</note>. [Occasion]ed by the height of the country, produces falls of snow; but this never lies long upon the ground. The position of these mountains in the middle of a peninsula also occasions another phenomenon that is equally observable in the peninsula formed by the Ganges <note>A reference to the Indian subcontinent</note>, which is intersected by mountains in the same manner. The rainy seasons, which are regular in the countries between the tropics, are diversified here by this peculiarity of situation. Westward, in Yemen, the rainy season is of great service to the country; for it arrives in the month of June and ends in the middle of September. During these months, the heat is most intense, and the earth and its inhabitants are in the greatest need of such refreshment. In the eastern part of these mountains, near Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>, those rains fall between the middle of November and the middle of February. In Hadhramaut <note>original: "Hadramaut"</note> and Oman, to the south, the rainy season lasts from the middle of February to the middle of April. It would seem, therefore, that the rains make a circuit <note>original: "the tour"</note> of the peninsula.

every season, as driven <note>original: "impelled"</note> by the prevailing winds. In the Tihama <note>original: "Tehama"; the hot, narrow coastal plain of Arabia along the Red Sea</note> of Yemen, we also heard of a rain in spring, the timing of which is uncertain, but on which the success of the harvests depends.

These regular rains make the valleys nestled among the mountains fertile and delightful. The highlanders, who breathe a fine, fresh air, are handsome, healthy, and brave. Another advantage which the Arabians owe to the geographic situation of their country is that it provides them, at the same time, with the products of different climates. In the plains, several vegetables transplanted from India thrive well enough, and many animals from hot countries multiply there. The mountains produce the plants and animals of temperate climates. Arabia may thus be regarded as a collection <note>original: "assemblage"</note> of different climates, the respective advantages of which are all to be found in the region lying between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf <note>original: "Gulph"</note>.

The nature of the winds in Arabia differs according to the point of the compass from which they blow and the terrain over which they respectively pass. The same wind is dry or moist in different places, depending on whether it blows over the ocean or over deserts. On the shores of the Persian Gulf, the southeast wind is accompanied by a degree of moisture which, when the heat is

This wind heats metal objects in the shade as if they were sitting in direct sunlight; its heat, combined suddenly with the temperature of the atmosphere, often suffocates people and animals. When the Arabs travel, they carry garlic and raisins <note>original: "dried grapes"</note> with them to revive anyone who might collapse from the effects of these hot blasts.

Despite its scorching nature, this northwest wind helps the Arabs cool their drinks in the middle of summer. To do this, they put their water into *bardaks* <term>unglazed earthenware pots made of porous clay</term>. By placing these pots where they are exposed to the current of this hot wind, the water becomes very cool. This phenomenon is well known in hot climates and is currently attributed by scientists <note>original: "naturalists"</note> to the effects of rapid evaporation.

Another more dangerous wind is the famous *Sam*, *Smum*, or *Samiel* <note>original: "Sam, Smum, or Samiel"; now commonly known as the Simoom, from the Arabic *samum*, meaning "poisonous"</note>, which rarely blows deep within Arabia but frequently occurs on its borders. This wind prevails only on the edges of the Great Desert, where the movement of the air creates a current for the vapors raised by the sun's heat from that parched land. The effects of the Simoom <note>original: "Smum"</note> are instant suffocation to every living creature that happens to be within the range of its activity, and the immediate putrefaction <term>the process of decay or rotting in a body</term> of the carcasses of the dead. Because a similar rapid rate of decomposition has been observed in bodies killed by lightning <note>original: "thunder"</note> or by electric shock, it has been speculated that electricity—which is very generally spread through nature—might be the cause of the uniquely harmful qualities of this wind. 

The Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> recognize the approach of the Simoom by an unusual redness in the air, and they say that they notice a smell of sulfur as it passes. However this may be, the only way any person can survive these harmful blasts is by throwing himself down with his face against the earth until this whirlwind of poisonous vapors has blown over; the wind always moves at a certain height in the atmosphere. Instinct even teaches the animals <note>original: "brutes"</note> to lower their heads to the ground on these occasions.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Arabian weather phenomena, shifting from the deadly Simoom wind to more common atmospheric occurrences like lightning, dew, and the region's year-round greenery.</meta>

<page-num>319</page-num>

<header>IN ARABIA, etc.</header>

The other atmospheric phenomena <term>original: "meteors"; in the 18th century, this term referred to any weather-related or atmospheric occurrences, such as rain, rainbows, or lightning</term> of Arabia are similar to those in all other hot countries. A clear sky, which is rarely hidden by clouds, makes storms very infrequent in the plains. The air discharges its electrical energy in the form of fireballs and by the phenomena called shooting stars, which are not infrequent and are quite large in size. In the driest regions near the sea, the dew is remarkably heavy <note>original: "copious"</note>. Despite this humidity, the air is so pure that the inhabitants sleep outdoors. I never slept more soundly than when I found my bed completely soaked with dew in the morning. There are, however, places where one does not dare to sleep in the open air for fear of being struck with paralysis <term>original: "palsy"; a condition involving muscle weakness or loss of movement, often attributed in historical accounts to the effects of damp or cold night air</term>. Through long experience, the inhabitants of those parts have learned what precautions to take, and these are always particularly necessary for a European unaccustomed to the climate.

Arabia enjoys the sight of almost constant greenery <note>original: "verdure"</note>. This is not to say that most of the trees do not shed their leaves, or that annual plants do not wither and regrow. However, the interval between the shedding of leaves in one year and the growth of new leaves for the next is so short that the change is hardly noticeable. Year-round greenery is common in those countries that have no frost, but instead experience a rainy season in place of our winter.

Because of the unique geographical location of Arabia, one can infer the variations in its landscape even without further information. These variations are indeed very remarkable. On one side are frightening deserts, and on the other, fertile and delightful valleys. The sandy belt that encircles this peninsula is almost entirely barren and presents a consistent picture of desolation.

This belt, called the *Tehama* <term>the low-lying, hot, and arid coastal plain of the Arabian Peninsula</term>, as has been mentioned several times, begins at Suez and extends around the whole peninsula to the mouth of the Euphrates. Its width varies; however, it is mostly about a two days' journey from the seashore to the rise of the hills—at least, this is the width of the plain adjacent to the Red Sea. It bears every mark of having been part of the seabed in ancient times. Its bottom soil is a grayish clay with a large proportion of sand, containing marine remains <note>original: "exuviæ"; Latin for the discarded remains or shells of animals, such as fossils</note> scattered at a great distance from the seashore. It contains large layers <note>original: "strata"</note> of salt, which in some places even rise up into hills. Its steady slope toward the sea indicates that it has risen out of the water gradually. The small heights on the borders of this plain are composed of limestone <note>original: "calcareous stones"</note> with a blackish appearance, looking as if they were burnt by the sun. The adjoining hills contain schist <note>original: "schistus"</note> and basalt <note>original: "basaltes"</note>;

The barrenness <note>original: "sterility"</note> of the former [Hejaz] was due to the lack of water. However, he was certainly mistaken, for the soil of Egypt is formed from the sediment of the Nile, whereas that of Hejaz <note>original: "Hedsjas"</note> consists of the remains of the seabed. The limestone <term>calcareous stone</term> of the hills in this latter province eventually decomposes into a blackish earth, which over time becomes capable of growing some hardy <note>original: "coarse"</note> vegetables.

In the Highlands of Arabia, there are as many varieties of soil as in most other cultivated countries. The most common characteristic of the soil on these slate-like <term>schistous</term> hills is clay mixed with sand. However, the shape of the hills is unfavorable to their fertility. They are usually so craggy and steep <note>original: "precipitous"</note> that they provide neither enough space nor soil for growing plants, as the fertile earth is constantly washed away by the rains. These conditions also make the cultivation of such places extremely difficult and expensive.

Terraces must be constructed; indeed, their building is sometimes made easier by piles of basalt <note>original: "basaltes"</note> that are naturally formed into regular five-sided <term>pentagonal</term> shapes. These pieces break off from the rocks from time to time and serve as materials for the terrace walls.

Arabia is a country that is interesting in many respects, but it is, in general, neither wealthy nor fertile.

## CHAPTER III.

### *Arabian Quadrupeds.*

When discussing Arabian agriculture, I had the opportunity to mention their domestic animals. Some of these seem to be native to the country, as they are not common in other parts of the East. In Arabia, they retain their natural instincts more perfectly and are more clearly distinguished by their strength and beauty than anywhere else. These include the horse, the donkey <note>original: "ass"</note>, the camel, and perhaps the ox as well. The camel, with its ability to endure thirst and its internal reservoir for water <note>A common 18th-century belief; while camels are remarkably adapted for water storage, they do not have a literal "reservoir" or tank in their stomachs.</note>, seems naturally suited to live in the desert. Its hoof is shaped for walking on burning sands, and the tough <term>cartilaginous</term> texture of its mouth allows it to eat the hard, prickly plants found on those scorched plains.

# CHAPTER IV.

## *Regarding the Birds of Arabia.*

If we had limited opportunities to examine four-legged animals <note>original: "quadrupeds"</note>, we were no more fortunate when it came to birds. It is not that Arabia lacks a variety of species; on the contrary, its natural resources are enough to sustain a vast <note>original: "prodigious"</note> number of them. However, a traveler rushing through a country has even less opportunity to become acquainted with the creatures of the air than with those of the earth. 

One cannot see many birds, or observe them at leisure, unless one is among people who are fond of bird-hunting <term>original: "fowling"</term>. Such people, as they seek out and sell game, bring specimens they have caught or killed to curious observers, and they are able to provide some account of their respective names and behaviors <note>original: "instincts"</note>.

In Arabia, we had no such advantage. The Arabs look down on the use of wild birds <note>original: "wild fowl"</note> for food, and they care for neither the amusement nor the exercise of bird-hunting. I believe I can identify two causes for their dislike of a pastime which

A people who are naturally temperate and frugal, and who live in a climate where eating meat <note>original: "animal food"</note> is harmful to health, cannot be fond of game. The principles of the Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note> religion must also discourage the Arabs from hunting wild animals, especially birds. A hunter wastes his effort, and his prey becomes ritually unclean <note>original: "impure"</note>, if he neglects to say even one short prayer when he kills the animal. It is also unclean if the animal has not lost the exact amount of blood required by religious law, if the bird was still struggling with life after being shot, or if it fell on a place that was inhabited or otherwise defiled. Consequently, we saw no birds other than those we killed ourselves or those we could observe in the wild <note>original: "at liberty"</note>.

In the fertile regions of Arabia, domesticated birds are very plentiful, and all types of poultry are bred in great abundance. The Guinea fowl <note>original: "pintado"</note> is not domesticated, but these birds live in the woods in such numbers that children kill them with stones and collect them to sell in the towns. The pheasant is also a native of Arabia and is found in great numbers in the forests of Yemen, as are the wood-pigeon and several other varieties of the pigeon species. The services done by this bird in countries exposed to the ravages of those insects have given rise to several absurd and superstitious practices in Syria. It is thought to be attracted from Khorasan by water which is, for this purpose, brought from a distance with great ceremony and preserved in a stone reservoir on the top of the minaret of a mosque <note>original: "tower of a mosque"</note>. We heard much talk of two species of birds which are highly valued by the Arabs and are called *Salva* and *Sumana*. As for quails, we received no evidence that they are migratory birds; nor is it probable that this bird would cross deserts where no food <note>original: "subsistence"</note> is to be found.

The Arabs also named several other birds to Mr. Forsskål <note>Peter Forsskål, the expedition’s naturalist</note> which he was never able to see, and consequently could not determine their scientific genus. One such bird is the *Achjal*, famous for two beautiful feathers with which the mountain people <note>original: "Highlanders"</note> decorate their caps; to keep these feathers from being damaged, the bird apparently leaves a hole in its nest. Another, the *Thaer el Hind* <note>Arabic: "Bird of India"</note>, is rare and remarkable for its golden <note>original: "gilded"</note> plumage and is sold at a very high price in Arabia. Its name seems to indicate that it is a migratory bird which is supposed to come from India.

## CHAPTER V.

### *Regarding Amphibious Animals and Fish.*

In the Arabian seas, we never encountered the sea turtle <note>original: "sea-tortoise"</note>; the land tortoise is much more common. The peasants bring the latter by the cartload to the markets of several towns in the East. The Eastern Christians eat these animals during Lent and drink their blood with great enjoyment <note>original: "relish"</note>.

We saw several kinds of lizards, of which the only dangerous one was the species called *Gecko* by the Egyptians. It is said that the saliva of this creature, if it falls upon food <note>original: "victuals"</note>, infects the people who eat it with leprosy <note>This was a common folk belief in the region during the 18th century, though not scientifically accurate</note>.

There are several kinds of snakes <note>original: "serpents"</note> in Arabia, the bite of which is often fatal. However, harmless snakes are as numerous as the dangerous ones. The bite of some causes only a disagreeable itching, which the Arabs cure by applying the leaves of the caper tree <note>The *Capparis spinosa*, a common shrub in the Middle East</note> to the wound. In general, life is endangered only by the bite of snakes that have a distinct row of teeth larger than the rest of the teeth. The Arabs in Egypt are acquainted with this rule regarding the anatomy <note>original: "structure"</note> of reptiles and play safely with snakes after pulling out the long teeth, which

The Arabs living along the shores of the Red Sea survive almost entirely on fish, as I have already mentioned, and they even feed their cattle with the same food. Although fish are so plentiful, a living fish is rarely seen among them. For fear of violating some precept of Islamic law <note>original: "Mussulman law"</note>, the fishermen kill all their fish before they bring them ashore.

### CHAPTER VI

->*Insects and Shells*<-

Locusts have a great influence on the living conditions of the inhabitants of Arabia and several other countries in the East; therefore, I shall describe this insect at a length that others do not deserve. However, we did not find their numbers to be as large as people in Europe commonly suppose them to be.

In Egypt, I saw a swarm <note>original: "cloud"</note> of locusts only once; it was brought by a south wind from the deserts of Libya. The locusts fell in huge quantities on the roofs of the houses and in the streets of Cairo <note>original: "Kahira"</note>. I saw no more of them until November 1762 at Jeddah <note>original: "Jidda"</note>, when a large swarm was driven over the city by a west wind. This swarm came from the other side of the Arabian Gulf <note>original: "Arabic Gulph"</note>; therefore, many of the insects must have drowned during the crossing. In the following July, we found a small number near Mount Sumara, which seemed to have stayed in Arabia for the season. These swarms often cross the Red Sea a second time to return to Egypt. The region of Upper Egypt, which borders the deserts of Libya, seems to be the breeding ground <note>original: "cradle"</note> for these insects. I also saw swarms of them in Persia and Syria. Near Mosul, I found the insects' nesting sites, which a diligent local administration <note>original: "careful police"; referring to public management or regulation</note> could largely destroy. Young locusts, the size of a fly, grow with amazing speed and reach their full size within a few days.

The swarms of these insects darken the air and appear at a distance like clouds of smoke. The noise they make while flying is terrifying and deafening <note>original: "stunning"</note>, like that of a waterfall. When such a swarm falls upon a field, it is laid waste and stripped of its greenery <note>original: "verdure"</note>. ### CHAP. VII.

#### *The Common and Rare Plants.*

As has already been noted, Arabia’s location allows it to benefit from both hot and temperate climates. Therefore, in the highland regions of the country, one finds plants common to northern Europe and Asia. On the other hand, the plains produce plants <note>original: "vegetables"</note> similar to those found in India and Africa. It is likely, however, that many of these latter plants were introduced to Arabia by the Banians <note>Indian merchants, specifically those from the Hindu trading caste</note> from their native land.

Of the 800 plants described by my late friend, I shall content myself with speaking of a small number remarkable for their novelty or usefulness. The first place is, no doubt, due to those which are used for food. I have already had occasion to name some of them in my account of Arabian agriculture. This latter grain, *sorgo*, or great millet, seems to be native to Arabia, for several wild species of it are found here, which the birds eat. When cultivated, it requires considerable warmth to reach full maturity, and in good soil, it grows to a great height.

The Arabs cultivate several culinary herbs <note>original: "pot-herbs"; plants grown for the cooking pot, such as greens or root vegetables</note> of the same nature as ours, such as lettuce (of which there is also a wild variety that is not used), spinach, and the carrot <note>original: "*Daucus, Linn.*"</note>.

Meadows are rare and not very lush in hot countries; in Arabia, therefore, there are not many plants suitable for forage <note>term: "forage" (food for livestock)</note>. Horned cattle are not common here and are poorly fed; consequently, their meat tastes bad. Animals naturally suited to the climate, such as camels and donkeys, are—as I have already mentioned—satisfied with the driest and toughest food. We have seen camels eat a species of spurge <note>original: "Euphorbia"; a genus of plants that typically produce a milky, irritating sap</note> after it had undergone some slight preparation in a hole dug in the ground. This animal also browses on the dry and prickly herbs and shrubs of the desert, such as bean-capers <note>original: "Zygophyllum"</note>, sweet-vetch <note>original: "Hedyrarum"; likely *Hedysarum*</note>, bladder senna <note>original: "Colutea"</note>, and others. The ice plants <note>original: "Mesembryanthema"; succulent plants named for their glistening, water-storing cells</note>, which are succulent herbs, provide another resource for the animals of the sandy plains. The Bedouins also prepare a type of bread from the seeds of a species of ice plant <note>original: "Mesembryanthemum"</note>, which they eat as willingly as wheat bread. The donkey even eats a species of viper's grass <note>original: "Scorfonere"; modern: *Scorzonera*</note> that is so rough and bitter that even the camel refuses it.

All simple nations use vegetables as remedies, possessing a traditional knowledge of their healing properties. The Arabs also have medicines of this kind, which they have used from time immemorial with a degree of success that a stranger can never be absolutely certain of. I need say nothing of plants as well-known as aloes and euphorbia <note>original: "euphorbia"; a diverse genus of plants commonly known as spurge, often characterized by a milky, irritating sap</note>. In Arabia, the different species of the latter are so numerous that Arabia may certainly be regarded as its native country. In hot countries, antivenoms <note>original: "counterpoisons"</note> are highly esteemed on account of the many venomous animals with which such countries are infested. By long experience, the inhabitants of those countries have learned which plants are beneficial <note>original: "salutary"</note> to man and harmful <note>original: "noxious"</note> to venomous animals. 

The Arabs, however, appear to be ignorant of the virtues of the *Ophiorrhiza* <note>original: "Ophiorrhiza"; literally "snake-root," a genus of plants in the coffee family used in various cultures to treat snakebites</note>, which is very common on their hills. In their opinion, a man who drinks the decoction <note>term: "decoction" (a concentrated liquor made by boiling medicinal herbs in water)</note> of this herb for forty days is in no future danger of being bitten by those venomous animals. ### CHAPTER VIII.

->*Of Trees and Shrubs.*<-

The sandy plains of Arabia are almost completely devoid of trees; only a few palms are scattered here and there. Forests are found only in the highland provinces where the hills retain enough soil for vegetation, but even in the highlands, they are rare. The trees in those forests are either completely unknown to us or are at least different from European trees of the same genus <note>original: "genera"</note> or species. The most important of them are the following, which I will discuss in more detail: *Sceura* <note>now known as *Avicennia marina*, a type of mangrove</note>, *Tomex*, *Catha* <note>the Khat plant, *Catha edulis*</note>, *Cynanchum*, *Maru*, *Baka*, *Haledi*, and

The Arabians cultivate several of our fruit trees. They have pomegranates, almonds, apricots, pears, and apples. There is a species of pear tree and a cornel tree <note>original: "corneil-tree"; likely a variety of Dogwood</note> which are unique to *Arabia*. The Arabians also eat the fruit of several of our shrubs, such as the *Asclepias* <note>the milkweed family</note> and the *Rhamnus* <note>the buckthorn family</note>.

Although the Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> drink no wine, the Arabians nevertheless plant the vine and have a great variety of grapes. They dry a small sort of grape called *Kishmish* <note>original: "Kischmisch"; a small, seedless variety of grape known today as Kishmish or Sultanas</note>, which has no stone but only soft, nearly imperceptible seeds; they sell a large quantity of these grapes to their neighbors. They also make a syrup from mint called *Dibs* <note>original: "Dub"; typically refers to a thick fruit molasses or syrup</note>, which they find to be a fairly lucrative article of trade.

Several sorts of lemons and oranges are found in *Arabia*. If we can infer anything from the names the Arabians have given them, one would suppose they received one type of orange tree from *Portugal* and two types of lemon trees from *Italy*. From common oranges—cut through the middle while they are green, dried in the open air, and steeped for forty days in oil—an essence is prepared that is famous among older women for restoring a fresh black color to gray hair.

The Banians <note>Indian merchants, often from the Hindu trading caste, who were influential in Middle Eastern ports</note> have brought various fruit trees from India that are now naturalized in Arabia. These include the banana tree (*Musa* <note>as classified by Linnaeus</note>), the mangosteen (*Mangifera* <note>original: "Mangoustan"</note>), the papaya (*Carica Papaya*), and the *Cissus* <note>a genus of woody vines in the grape family</note>. Arabia produces the date tree, but their other palms—especially the coconut <note>original: "Cocos"</note>—seem to have been introduced from India.

The Indian fig tree (*Ficus vasta* <note>original: "Ticus varta"; likely a typographical error in the original text for Ficus vasta</note>), although now very common in Arabia, is perhaps not native to this country. The unique property this tree possesses of spreading itself—by means of aerial roots <note>original: "filaments"</note> growing from its branches which, when they reach the ground, take root and form new trunks—is well known. Mr. Forsskål <note>Pehr Forsskål, the Swedish naturalist on the expedition</note> saw twelve species of native fig trees in Arabia that are not mentioned by Linnaeus. Their fruit is far from delicious and is rarely edible. The bark of one species is used for tanning leather. Of another, the leaves are so rough that they are used for cleaning and polishing iron. The rest are merely some of the many useless trees of the forest.

The tamarind is just as useful and pleasant in Arabia as it is in India. It has a pulp with a tart, wine-like taste <note>original: "vineous"</note>, from which a healthy, refreshing drink is prepared. Its shade protects houses from the scorching <note>original: "torrid"</note> heat of the sun, and its beautiful appearance <note>original: "fine figure"</note> greatly enhances the landscape of the country.

Arabia appears to be very rich in indigenous <note>native to a specific region</note> trees, the number of which is more than proportionate to its unique herbaceous plants. However, large trees are not easily moved from one place to another, and those of the forests in the remote back-country are seen by travelers less often than other vegetables. Therefore, it is no wonder that we have remained so ignorant of the trees of Arabia until now. More than half of the new genera <note>the plural of genus, a category in biological classification</note> classified by Mr. Forsskål <note>Pehr Forsskål, the expedition’s naturalist who died during the journey</note> consist entirely of trees. *Catha* <note>now known as *Catha edulis*, or Khat</note> is one of those new genera unique to Arabia. This tree, which can be improved through cultivation, is commonly planted among the coffee shrubs on the hills where they grow. The Arabs are in the habit of constantly chewing the buds of this tree, which they call *Kaad* <note>modern spelling: Qat</note>. They are as addicted to this practice as the Indians are to the habit of chewing betel <note>a stimulant made from areca nut and betel leaf</note>. They believe *kaad* has the virtues of assisting digestion and of strengthening the body <note>original: "fortifying the constitution"</note> against infectious diseases <note>original: "distempers"</note>. *Elcaya* <note>likely *Trichilia emetica*, the Natal mahogany</note> and *Keura* <note>likely *Pandanus odorifer*, the screw-pine</note>, two trees famous for their perfume, are unknown to European science but constitute two new genera <note>the plural of genus, a category in biological classification</note>. Children eat the fruit of a large tree called *Oncoba* <note>likely *Oncoba spinosa*, the snuff-box tree</note> and a tall shrub named *Maerua* <note>original: *Mærua*</note>, though the taste is quite bland <note>original: "insipid enough"</note>. Other discoveries include the *Chadara*, a large tree, and the *Antura*, a smaller tree; neither has any remarkable features except for the quality of their wood and the fact that they were previously unknown. The *Culhamia*, a large tree also unknown to botanists, is notable only for its practical uses. *Cadaba* and *Maesa* <note>original: *Mæsa*</note> are shrubs with no particularly distinctive qualities, and they might have been overlooked entirely had Mr. Forsskål not documented them.

The tree does not have a beautiful appearance, and surprisingly, its special qualities are not known to the inhabitants of Yemen where we found it. They only burn its wood as a perfume. The sensitive plant, of the genus *Mimosa*, is well known. In Arabia, there are several species of this genus, all of which are either trees or shrubs that serve the inhabitants for both use and pleasure. One of these trees droops its branches whenever a person approaches it, appearing as if it is saluting those who retire under its shade. This mute hospitality has so endeared this tree to the Arabs <note>original: "Arabians"</note> that injuring or cutting it down is strictly prohibited. Another of these (*Mimosa Selam*) produces splendid flowers of a beautiful red color, with which the Arabs crown their heads on their days of festivity. The flowers of another (*Mimosa Lebbex*) are no less remarkable for a fine silky tuft formed by their pistils. The leaves of another (*Mimosa Orfata*) preserve camel’s milk from becoming sour, so that it retains all its sweetness for several days. The smoke of the timber of this same tree expels a worm <note>Possibly referring to a parasite like the Guinea worm, though the text associates it with epilepsy.</note> which fixes itself in the flesh of the human neck and produces epileptic fits. This species of the *Mimosa* is dispersed through Asia, Africa, and America; it is well known that the sensitive plant was brought into Europe from the latter of these continents.

Arabia does not produce many poisonous plants <note>original: "vegetables"</note>; yet a very dangerous shrub of a new genus is found here, called <term>*Adenia*</term> by Mr. Forsskål <note>Peter Forsskål (1732–1763), the naturalist on the expedition.</note>. The buds of this shrub are one of the most potent poisons if dried and administered as a powder in a drink; they have the sudden effect of causing the body to swell in an extraordinary manner. A type of caper tree (<term>*Capparis spinosa*</term> <note>Named by Linnaeus; commonly known as the caper bush.</note>) is the only remedy against the effects of this poison. This latter shrub is so common in Arabia that the antidote is always to be found growing right beside the poison.

We neglected to inform ourselves, while in Arabia, concerning the production of manna; and what we learned from a monk, in a convent near Suez, was a monastic legend not worth repeating. As Stony Arabia <note>original: "Arabia-Petræa"; a historical name for the northwestern region of the Arabian Peninsula, including the Sinai Peninsula and parts of modern Jordan.</note> abounds in prickly shrubs, this manna may possibly be found there as well, although in those desert places it cannot be very plentiful. Both these types of manna are used as sugar in several meat dishes, especially in pastry. They are nourishing and, when newly gathered, have no purgative <term>purgative: a substance used to stimulate or increase bowel movements; a laxative</term> qualities.

The cedar does not grow in Arabia, but seems to be a tree unique to Mount Lebanon <note>original: "Mount Libanus."</note>. The Arabs have little wood suitable for building; their trees are mostly of a light, porous texture. *Sceura* <note>A genus of mangrove, now usually classified as *Avicennia*.</note>, a new genus described by Mr. Forsskål, is a tree that grows on the seashore; its wood is so soft that it cannot be put to any use.

### CHAPTER IX.

->*The Minerals of Arabia.*<-

In the account of my journey, and in speaking of the soil of Arabia, I have already had some occasion to mention the nature of those stones of which the hills here are composed. Arabia does not appear to be rich in metals. Ancient Greek and Latin authors even went so far as to claim that it is completely lacking in iron. This is not true, as grains of iron can be seen in the sand washed down by the rains. Magnets <note>original: "Magnets"; likely referring to lodestones, naturally magnetized pieces of the mineral magnetite.</note> are commonly found in the province of Kusma, and there are iron mines at Sa'dah <note>original: "Saade"; a city in northern Yemen long known for its ironwork and leather industry.</note> that are currently being worked. However, it must be admitted that Yemeni iron is coarse and brittle—flaws that cannot be fixed. Furthermore, the scarcity of wood <note>Wood was required as fuel for the smelting process, making local production difficult and expensive.</note> makes this iron more expensive than that imported from distant countries. For this reason, iron is a commodity that foreign traders can always sell profitably in the ports of the Red Sea.

In Oman, there are many very rich lead mines. Because this metal is more easily melted <note>original: "fusible"</note>, the inhabitants of this province export it in large quantities. This trade is conducted through the harbor of Muscat <note>original: "Maskat"</note>.

Since the ancients honored one part of Arabia with the title of "Happy" <note>original: "Happy"; a reference to *Arabia Felix*, the Latin name for the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula.</note>, they seem to have attributed every possible advantage to it. Consequently, Greek and Latin writers frequently mention the immense quantities of gold produced by this country. In ancient times, perhaps, when the Arabs acted as middlemen <term>factors: agents or merchants who manage trade for others</term> for the trade with India, much of this precious metal may have passed through Arabia into Europe; but

## VOYAGE FROM MOCHA TO BOMBAY.

### CHAPTER I.

->*Departure from Mocha.*<-

The ship belonging to Mr. Scott, with whom we were to take our passage to Bombay, had been delayed for a long time at Mocha <note>original: "Mokha"; a major port city on the Red Sea coast of Yemen, legendary for its coffee trade.</note>. Because of this, we could not leave the city until August 23, 1763. Although Messrs. Cramer <note>Christian Charles Cramer, the expedition’s physician.</note> and Baurenfeind <note>Georg Wilhelm Baurenfeind, the expedition’s artist. Both men would unfortunately pass away during this voyage.</note> were very ill at that time, they nevertheless determined not to miss the opportunity of leaving Arabia. As for myself, my health had recovered so far that I could safely venture upon the voyage to India.

The famous Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb <note>original: "Babel-Mandel"; the narrow passage between Yemen and the Horn of Africa. The name translates from Arabic as the "Gate of Tears" due to the dangers of navigating it.</note>, where the Red Sea <note>original: "Arabian Gulph."</note> joins the ocean, and where we arrived on the second day of our voyage, is about ten German miles <note>A German geographical mile was historically equal to approximately 7.5 kilometers or 4.6 miles.</note> wide. In the sea between Arabia and India, there is generally a rapid current driving to the east with so much violence that it is impossible to calculate the rate at which a ship travels while passing through here. In this sea, we also encountered north winds so cold that we were forced to put on warmer clothes.

In this first part of our voyage, Mr. Cramer’s <note>Christian Charles Cramer, the expedition’s physician.</note> health seemed to improve daily; but Mr. Baurenfeind <note>Georg Wilhelm Baurenfeind, the expedition’s artist.</note> grew worse and worse. The day after Mr. Baurenfeind died, our servant *Berggreen* also passed away. He was a Swede who had served in several campaigns under a Colonel of Hussars <note>Light cavalry soldiers in European armies, known for their speed and endurance.</note>. This man, who was naturally robust and had been accustomed to fatigue, had at first laughed at the idea of the hardships of a voyage to Arabia; but he finally succumbed to them, as did Mr. Cramer, as I shall relate later.

The voyage between Arabia and India was previously considered very dangerous. Ships were swept along by such a rapid current that they could neither maintain their navigation records <note>original: "keep their reckoning"</note> nor identify the coastline during the rainy season. As a result, several ships were lost on the low-lying shores of the Malabar Coast <note>The southwestern coast of the Indian subcontinent.</note>. These accidents have stopped occurring since a particular observation was made. Although this discovery was thought to be new, Arrian <note>A 2nd-century Greek historian who documented early voyages in the Indian Ocean.</note> mentions it as being known to the ancients: in the Indian Ocean, at a certain distance from land, many sea snakes <note>original: "water serpents"</note>, about twelve to thirteen inches long, can be seen rising above the surface of the water. When these snakes are seen, they are an indication that the coast is exactly two degrees away <note>Approximately 120 nautical miles.</note>.

We saw some of these snakes for the first time on the evening of September 9th; on the 11th, we landed in the harbor of Bombay <note>Modern-day Mumbai, India.</note>; and on the 13th, we entered the city.

## CHAP. II.

->*Concerning the Island and the City of Bombay.*<-

The island of Bombay is about nine miles <note>original: "two German miles"; a German mile at this time was roughly 4.6 English miles or 7.4 kilometers.</note> in length, and a little more than two miles in breadth. A narrow channel separates it from another small island of little value, which the English call *Old Woman’s Island* <note>One of the original seven islands of Mumbai, now part of the Colaba area.</note>. Bombay produces nothing but coconuts <note>original: "cocoa's"</note> and rice, and a considerable amount of salt is collected along the shore. The inhabitants are required to bring their provisions from the mainland or from Salsette <note>original: "Salset"</note>, a large and fertile island near Bombay that belongs to the Marathas <note>original: "Marattas," a powerful Hindu confederacy that controlled much of western and central India.</note>. Since I left India, the English have made an attempt to take Salsette, which is indeed very much within their power, and the public newspapers say they have been successful. I do not know whether they will be able to maintain their position there against the Marathas, whose armies are very numerous.

The sea breezes and frequent rains cool the atmosphere and make the climate of this island temperate. Its air was formerly unhealthy and dangerous, but it has become pure since the English drained the marshes in the city and its surrounding areas. Still, however, many Europeans die suddenly

This is because they keep the body comfortable in wide, flowing robes, abstain from animal food and strong liquors, and eat their principal meal in the evening after sunset.

The city of Bombay, situated in the northern part of the island, is a quarter of a German mile <note>Approximately 1.15 miles or 1.85 kilometers.</note> in length, though it is narrow. It is defended by a mediocre <note>original: "indifferent"</note> citadel facing the sea and located at the middle of the city. On the landward side, its fortifications are very good. During the war, the East India Company expended no less than 900,000 French livres <note>The *livre tournois* was the currency of France until 1794; this represents a massive financial investment in colonial infrastructure.</note> a year in the construction of new works for its defense. There are some small forts on the island sufficient to protect it from any raids <note>original: "irruption"</note> by the local Indians. In this city are several handsome buildings, among which are the Director’s palace and a large, elegant church nearby. Unlike the rest of the East, the houses here do not have flat roofs but are covered with tiles in the European style. The English have glass windows. The other inhabitants of the island have windows made of small pieces of transparent shells framed in wood, which makes the rooms very dark. Throughout the East, it is the fashion during the dry season to live in rooms that are open on one side. In general, the houses of Bombay are neither particularly splendid nor very comfortable <note>original: "commodious"</note>.

The harbor is spacious and sheltered from all winds. A valuable project, constructed at the East India Company’s expense, consists of two basins <note>dry docks used for ship maintenance</note> carved out of the rock, where two ships may be careened <note>To "careen" a ship is to tilt it on its side to clean, caulk, or repair the hull.</note> at the same time. A third is currently being prepared. This project, while very expensive to build, also brings in a significant annual profit. Foreigners pay a high price for the privilege of repairing their ships in these basins. While I was there, I saw a warship belonging to the Imam of Sana <note>The ruler of Yemen, based in the capital city of Sana'a.</note>, which he had sent to Bombay specifically to be refitted.

## CHAPTER III.

->The Inhabitants of Bombay<-

The religious tolerance granted by the English has made this island very densely populated. During the hundred years it has been held by the East India Company, the number of inhabitants has grown significantly. They are now estimated at 140,000 people, even though just twenty years ago they did not even reach 70,000.

Of these, the Europeans are naturally the smallest group. This is largely because they do not marry <note>The author likely refers to the fact that many European employees of the Company were men who did not bring families or marry locally.</note>, and so their numbers do not increase through birth. The other inhabitants include the Portuguese, or Indian Catholics; **Hindus**, the original owners of the land; **Persians** from **Kerman** <note>A city and province in southeastern Iran, likely referring here to the Parsi community who fled Persia to escape religious persecution.</note>; **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahometans"</note> of various sects; and finally, some Middle Eastern <note>original: "Oriental"</note> Christians. My journey to **Surat** <note>A major port city in the Indian state of Gujarat.</note> will provide an opportunity to speak in more detail about the Hindus and Persians, who mostly live in the outskirts <note>original: "invirons"</note> of that city. I will also include the observations I made about these people while in Surat.

The English, as I have mentioned, have a beautiful church in Bombay, but only one English

### CHAPTER IV.

->*Of the Government and Power of the English on the Coast of Malabar.*<-

The English East India Company governs its settlements using a system of administration different from that of the Portuguese and the Dutch. These latter nations entrust the management <note>original: "disposal"</note> of all locations to the authority of a single governor: the Portuguese to the viceroy of Goa and the Dutch to the governor-general of Batavia <note>modern Jakarta</note>. The English territories <note>original: "conquests"</note> are, on the contrary, divided into four independent governments, each of which receives its orders directly from the Court of Directors in London. The seats of these four governments are: *Bombay* for the *Malabar* coast, *Madras* for the *Coromandel* coast, *Calcutta* for *Bengal*, and *Bencoolen* for the island of *Sumatra*.

Although independent of one another, the various English governors are nonetheless required to provide mutual aid to each other in extraordinary emergencies <note>original: "exigencies"</note>. On a recent <note>original: "late"</note> occasion, when news was received at Bombay of an uprising <note>original: "insurrection"</note>, the council of Bombay—without waiting for orders from the Court of Directors in London—sent troops

The council or governing body <note>original: "regency"</note> of Bombay consists of a governor, who holds the title of president, and twelve counsellors. These counsellors were originally all merchants, with the exception of the commander of the troops, who until recently held the rank of major. The Company has recently made some changes to this arrangement. The president must now be a military man; the commander of the troops is a brigadier and has a vote <note>original: "voice"</note> in the council; and the director of naval affairs now holds a seat among the twelve counsellors, who were formerly all merchants. 

The other employees <note>original: "servants"</note> of the Company are factors <note>mercantile agents who managed trading posts and conducted business</note> and writers <note>junior clerks or administrators responsible for bookkeeping and records</note> of various ranks. These individuals rise from lower to higher positions based on seniority—advancing even to the highest offices, with the sole exception of the president, who is appointed by the Court of Directors in London. 

The employees of the Company are sometimes transferred from one department to another. Mr. Spencer, a very intelligent man who was a counsellor at Bombay during my visit, was shortly afterward transferred to the position of first president at Calcutta.

The soldiers are mostly Europeans, except for some Topasses <term>Luso-Indians or Indian Christians who wore European clothes and served as soldiers</term>, who are Catholic Indians dressed in the European style. In Bombay, there is also a force of 3,000 Sepoys <term>Indian soldiers serving in the British military</term> (both Hindus <note>original: "Pagan"</note> and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometan"</note>), who wear their own traditional dress and are led by their own officers. Each company of this corps has a lower-ranking European officer to train the Sepoys in their military drills; for, when led by Europeans, they become excellent troops. At Surat, the Company employs a small corps of Arabs from the Persian Gulf. They have such a high reputation for courage in India that every Rajah <term>an Indian prince or king</term> desires to have some of them in his service.

### Chapter 5

->*Regarding the Trade of Bombay.*<-

The permission granted to the East India Company’s employees <note>original: "servants"</note> to trade for their own personal profit <note>original: "on their own account"</note> seems to many people to be harmful <note>original: "injurious"</note> to the Company's interests. It must be admitted <note>original: "confessed"</note> that this private trade is subject to abuse and can, at times, be damaging to the Company's business. However, looking at the situation as a whole, I am inclined to believe it is beneficial for both the employers and the employees. The freedom to trade for themselves motivates agents <term>factors</term> <note>original: "factors" – agents who buy or sell goods on commission for a principal merchant or company</note> with energy and initiative <note>original: "spirit and activity"</note>. It also provides them with the means to gather more complete information about various sectors of commerce. In this way, trade in general is improved and business is expanded.

A recent example will demonstrate both the positive and negative aspects of this arrangement. In the first part of my work, I mentioned the privilege the English enjoy at Jeddah <note>original: "Jidda"</note>, where they pay lower customs duties <note>original: "duties"</note>
