### CHAPTER VI.

#### *Antiquities of the Isle of Elephanta.*

This small island, situated near Bombay, belongs to the Marathas <note>original: "Mahrattas," a powerful confederacy that controlled large parts of India in the 18th century</note>, and is inhabited by a hundred poor Indian families. Its proper name is *Gali Pouri* <note>Now commonly known as Gharapuri</note>. Europeans call it *Elephanta* because of a statue of an elephant, carved from black stone, which stands on this island in the open plain near the shore. Since this island is of little importance, the Marathas take no care of it; the English are at liberty to visit it without passports, which are required when they go to the island of *Salsette* <note>original: "Salset," the island north of Bombay</note>.

Several travelers mention the island of *Elephanta* and the Indian temple within it, but they do so only in passing <note>original: "in a transient manner"</note> and without appearing to have recognized the full importance of these remains of remote antiquity. To me, the temple appeared so remarkable that I visited the island three different times in order to draw and describe its curiosities.

It is one hundred and twenty feet long and the same in width, not including the measurements of the chapels and the adjacent chambers. Its interior height is nearly fifteen feet, although the floor has been raised significantly by the accumulation of dust and the sediment from water that flows into it during the rainy season. This entire massive structure, situated within a hill of considerable height, is carved out of the solid rock. The pillars supporting the roof are also parts of the original rock that were left standing by the architect. They belong to an unusual architectural style, but they create a pleasant enough effect.

The walls of this temple are decorated with figures in *bas-relief* <term>bas-relief: a style of sculpture where the carvings project from a flat background</term>, which are so prominent that they are attached to the rock only at the back. Many of these figures are of a colossal size, standing 10, 12, or even 14 feet high. Admittedly, these *bas-reliefs* cannot be compared with the works of Greek <note>original: "Grecian"</note> sculptors in either design or execution. However, they are far superior in elegance to the remains of ancient Egyptian sculpture. They are also finer than the *bas-reliefs* from the ruins of Persepolis <note>Persepolis: the ancient ceremonial capital of the Persian Empire in modern-day Iran, known for its extensive stone carvings</note>. There is no doubt, then, that the arts were practiced by the ancient Indians with much greater success than is commonly supposed.

One perfectly like this is to be found in the vicinity of the town of Tiruchirappalli <note>original: "Teridschanapalli"</note>.

These monuments of the ancient splendor of the Indians deserve the attention of our scholars for several reasons. We travel to see pyramids that are in no way <note>original: "nowise"</note> worthy of comparison with these temples <note>original: "pagodas"</note>. It would require more labor...

<meta>This page continues Niebuhr's comparison of ancient architectural feats, specifically contrasting the rock-cut temples of India with the pyramids of Egypt, and discusses the value of Indian antiquities in understanding world history.</meta>

<page-num>398</page-num>

...and skill to carve such spacious chambers <note>original: "apartments"</note> into the rocks and to decorate them with such large and beautiful sculptures than to build those huge piles of soft limestone <note>original: "calcareous stones"</note> which the builder found ready at hand. The pyramids appear to have been built through the labor of brutal slavery; the temples of India are the works of a grand and enlightened people.

Furthermore, the Indians are the most ancient of the nations with a known history and have best preserved their ancient customs and beliefs. We know that the inhabitants of other countries in the East, the Greeks, and perhaps the Egyptians as well, derived the foundations of their knowledge from India. It may further be assumed that an examination of Indian antiquities would shed new light on those beliefs and forms of worship which were gradually spread through other parts of the East and eventually reached Europe. These discoveries, in turn, would shed new light on the antiquities of other nations.

These hopes are all the more reasonable since the Indians still possess books which were written in the most ancient times and whose language is still understood today. These books could explain the monuments, and the monuments in turn could serve as a commentary on those books and the history of the nation.

It is to be hoped that some enlightened scholars will undertake a voyage to India for the purpose of investigating its antiquities. However, such an undertaking is more than can be expected from any private individual and would be worthy of the patronage of a prince or a nation. The Portuguese, who were masters of Salsette <note>original: "Salset"; an island near Mumbai, famous for its rock-cut caves</note> for two centuries, must have been well acquainted with these temples, for they converted the temple of *Kanari* <note>original: "Kanari"; modern: the Kanheri Caves, a group of caves and monuments cut into a massive basalt outcrop</note> into a church. But instead of trying to make those monuments known to other nations, they sought to hide them and covered the finest of the *bas-reliefs* <note>sculptures that project slightly from a flat background</note> with plaster. The English, although they have been settled at Bombay <note>modern: Mumbai</note> for a hundred years now, have still neglected these investigations. It is to be hoped that they will finally consider earning the public's gratitude by bringing to light those hidden curiosities that lie within the extensive continental territories now possessed by that nation.

# SECTION XXXI.

## VOYAGE TO SURAT.

---

### CHAP. I.

#### ->*Occasion of this Voyage, and Departure from Bombay.*<-

The reader will recollect that Mr. Cramer and I were both sick when we arrived at Bombay <note>modern: Mumbai</note> in September 1763. Our intention was to return to Europe through Turkey and to take our passage on board a ship belonging to the East India Company <note>original: "the Company’s"</note> which was to sail for Basra at the beginning of the next year; however, the state of our health would not allow us to take that opportunity. Mr. Cramer, finally succumbing to his ailments <note>original: "complaints"; a common 18th-century term for physical illnesses or medical conditions</note>, died at Bombay on February 10, 1764, despite the care of a skillful English physician.

As I was now the sole survivor of our entire party, I felt it my duty to attend to my own preservation and to ensure the safe delivery of our papers to Europe, for I feared that these would be lost if I also died during the journey.

We sailed from Bombay <note>modern: Mumbai</note> on March 24, 1764, and were obliged to stop at Mahim, a small town in the northern part of the island where a member of the Council of Bombay constantly resides. Proud of their ancient conquests, they scorn to make peace with any of the *Indian* nations, all of whom they regard as rebels. Being thus in terms of continual hostility with their neighbors, they dare not sail these seas without an escort. A small fleet of merchant ships bound from *Goa* to *Diu*, under the protection of two frigates, was seen one evening off Bombay. ### CHAPTER II.

## *Of the City of Surat and its Environs.*

This city stands in a large and fertile plain on the banks of a considerable river named the *Tapi* <note>original: "Tappi"</note>. On the land side, it is encompassed by two brick walls, which divide it into the inner and the outer town. The citadel stands within the inner town on the shore of the *Tapi* and is separated from the town by trenches. One can walk around the outer wall in two and a half hours; the space it encloses is primarily occupied by gardens, containing only a few houses.

The larger houses here are flat-roofed, as throughout the rest of the East, with courtyards in front of them. The houses of the common people have high roofs. Although Surat has been long under the dominion of the Muslim Mughals <note>original: "Mahometan Moguls"</note>, there is no handsome mosque with towers <note>minarets</note> here, such as those found among the Turks and Arabs. The squares of this city are large and the streets are spacious, but they are not paved; consequently, the dust is insufferable. Each street has its own gates, with which it

is shut up during times of unrest; and these occur as frequently here as in Cairo.

In Surat, food supplies are plentiful and inexpensive; the air is also healthy, despite the warmth of the climate. While here, I recorded a temperature of 98° on Fahrenheit's thermometer in the month of March, even while a north wind was blowing. In May, the thermometer reached 93° in Bombay, which is located two degrees further south.

One disadvantage for Surat is that ships cannot enter the harbor because the *Tapi* <note>original: "Tappi"</note> river is full of sandbanks. This river is too shallow during the dry season; however, during the rainy season, it swells so suddenly and to such a height that it floods the entire surrounding neighborhood. If the river were contained by dikes, the current—which often rises twenty-eight feet above its normal level during the rains—would wash away all the sand. By clearing the channel in this way, it would allow ships access right up to the city walls. However, the despotic governments of Asia neglect everything that might contribute to the general welfare of their subjects.

General religious tolerance and complete liberty are enjoyed in this city by all faiths; consequently, its population is very large. The Europeans living here estimate the city's population at one million people <note>original: "souls"</note>.

One singular thing in Surat is that there is no hospital for human beings, but there is an extensive establishment of this nature for sick or injured animals. The surroundings of Surat are not without gardens, which are owned by either Europeans or the local people. The finest of those belonging to Europeans is the property of the Dutch East India Company. Its appearance is rich and charming.

To get an idea of the character of an Indian garden, I went to see one that was created by a late Nabob <note>term: a governor or person of high status during the Mughal Empire; the word is the origin of the English term 'nabob' used for the wealthy.</note> at a cost of 500,000 rupees. The English governor of Surat, for instance, would not allow a Frenchman to live in a high-story apartment from which he might have a view of the citadel. ### CHAPTER III

#### *Of the Inhabitants of Surat and Some Peculiar Customs*

A great commercial city is necessarily populated by people of different nations. The principal inhabitants of Surat are Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>, and mostly foreigners, though many are employed in the service of the government. They are just as zealous in observing their religious laws as the Turks and Arabs. Although they belong to the Sunni <note>original: "Sunnites"</note> sect, they tolerate the Shias <note>original: "Shiites"</note> and even allow them to celebrate the festival of Hussein <note>original: "Hassein"; referring to the mourning of Muharram</note>. They have no hesitation about drinking wine in public or lending money at interest <note>Niebuhr notes this because both practices are traditionally forbidden in Islamic law</note>.

All people of high standing in Surat, and throughout the rest of India, speak and write the Persian language. Because of this, Persian has been adopted at the courts, and a knowledge of it is very useful for conducting business. In trade, a broken form of Portuguese <note>original: "corrupt Portuguese"</note> is the language used; in India, this serves the same purpose as the *Lingua Franca* <note>original: "Lingua Franca"; literally "Frankish language," a bridge language used for trade between people who do not share a native tongue</note> does in the Levant <note>The region of the eastern Mediterranean</note>.

<summary>Niebuhr describes the religious tolerance and social customs of the Muslims in Surat, noting their use of Persian for official business and a Portuguese-based pidgin for trade.</summary>

<keywords>Surat, Batavia, Muslims, Sunnis, Shias, Hussein, Persian language, Portuguese, trade languages, religious tolerance</keywords>

The Muslims <note>original: "Mussulmans"</note> of Surat attract a great many *Fakirs* <note>original: "Fakirs"; religious ascetics or mendicants who live on alms</note> of their own religion, who are the most persistent and demanding beggars in the world. These *Fakirs* will often sit down in front of a house and remain there until the owner pays the sum they demand or reaches a settlement <note>original: "composition"</note> with them. As the police do not interfere to restrain these insolent beggars, people must be content with getting rid of them at any price.

At Surat, I had the opportunity to witness the Muslim procession during the festival of *Bairam* <note>original: "Bairam"; a Turkish term for the Islamic festivals of Eid al-Fitr or Eid al-Adha</note>. The counselor from Bombay, who resides in the citadel of Surat and represents a *Nawab* <note>original: "Nabob"; a title for a local ruler or provincial governor</note>, is required to announce this ceremony with a discharge of cannons and to attend it in person. It is a strange sight to see an English merchant in European dress, attended by a party of British soldiers and with the entourage of an Indian prince, conducting and regulating a religious festival of the Muslims. The English director made the Indians aware of his importance on this occasion by refusing to fire his cannons during the night—a favor requested of him by the *Nawab* of the city to give the people timely warning of the approach of the festival.

In this procession there was nothing remarkable except the large numbers of *hackeries* <note>original: "kakkris"; light bullock-drawn carts or carriages</note>, *palanquins* <note>covered litters or chairs carried on the shoulders of bearers</note>, and horses, along with a few cannons, a great deal of military music, and the *Nawab*’s soldiers. The governor rode on an elephant, on the back of which he sat in a kind of throne supported by four pillars. This elephant was—like most of the horses and oxen that drew the hackeries <note>original: "kakkris"; light, two-wheeled carriages drawn by oxen</note>—painted red.

Hackeries, the carriages most common throughout India, are of a very simple construction; they run on two wheels and are drawn by oxen. The driver sits on a large pole made of several bamboo canes. It is not in the ornamentation of these vehicles, but in the cattle that draw them, that the Indian finds an object of pride and expense; a pair of white oxen for one of these carriages can cost 600 <term>rupees</term> <note>the standard currency of India</note>. These oxen have the tips of their horns decorated with silver; their pace is quick, though less so than that of horses.

The citizens of Surat also display their magnificence through their palanquins. A palanquin is known to be a kind of couch suspended from a bamboo pole and carried by four men. The traveler reclines in this vehicle and is shaded from the sun by a curtain. A palanquin completely decorated with silver, covered with rich fabrics, and suspended from a handsome, properly curved bamboo pole, will cost over 200 pounds sterling. The bamboo pole alone for the governor of Bombay’s palanquin—excluding the other decorations—cost 125 pounds.

These men are also typically employed to keep the rooms of the houses clean. European women are initially shocked by the perceived indecency of being carried by men who are mostly naked, but they soon become accustomed to it. The <term>palanquins</term> used by Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> women are uncomfortable wooden boxes, completely enclosed and mounted on a straight pole.

The Hindus <note>original: "Hindoos"</note>, the indigenous inhabitants of the country—whom I will soon describe in more detail—make up the largest part of the population in <term>Surat</term>. They belong almost entirely to the caste of the <term>Banyans</term> <note>original: "Banians"; a Hindu caste of merchants and traders</note>. Because of this, their skill and precision in matters of calculation and finance often lead them to positions of significant trust, such as collecting taxes and customs for the Muslim authorities. These <term>Banyans</term>, being merchants by birth, have monopolized Indian commerce to such an extent that all foreign nations are forced to employ them as brokers. In this role, they provide better service than the Jewish brokers in Turkey. Europeans have never had cause to regret entrusting even their entire fortunes to the <term>Banyans</term>, who consistently provide astonishing proof of their integrity <note>original: "probity"</note> and—

In Surat, there are many **Parsis** <note>original: "Persees"</note> or **Persians**, who are skilled merchants, industrious artisans, and good servants. In the same city, there are also Armenians, Georgians, and Jews, though none of these groups are present in any considerable number. The Indian Catholics—commonly called "Portuguese" because they speak an Indian dialect of the Portuguese language—are numerous here. In Surat, the day is calculated from sunset to sunset and is divided into 60 <term>gharis</term> <note>original: "garris"; an ancient Indian unit of time</note> rather than 24 hours. There are no clocks here; the progress of the day is measured by other means. In a visible location, a man stands to place a copper cup, which is pierced with a hole in the bottom, into the water from time to time. Every time the cup sinks, one <term>ghari</term> is counted, and the man announces its passing by striking the corresponding number on a metal plate that sounds like a bell. Each <term>ghari</term> consists of 24 of our minutes. Even in the houses of the nobility, where clocks and watches are not lacking <note>original: "not wanting"</note>, this old fashion of measuring time is still maintained.

## CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning the Government of Surat and the Revolutions it has experienced.*<-

**Surat**, and the large district of which it is the capital, belonged for a long time to the **Great Mogul** <note>The emperor of the Mughal Empire in India.</note>. To keep such a distant province effectively obedient, he placed it under the governance of two **Nabobs** <note>original: "Nabobs"; provincial governors or officials in the Mughal Empire</note> who were independent of each other. One resided in the city and was properly the governor of the province. The other had command of the **citadel** <note>a fortress protecting a city</note> and held the title of **admiral**, with a small revenue set aside for the maintenance of a small fleet to defend the coast against pirates.

After **Nader Shah's** <note>original: "Shah Nadir"; the Shah of Persia who invaded India in 1738–39</note> expedition into **Hindustan** <note>original: "Indostan"; a historical name for the northern Indian subcontinent</note>, the distant Nabobs of this vast empire all aimed for independence. They left the Mogul with nothing but a shadow of authority, asking him only as a matter of formality to confirm them in their positions. **Teg Beg Khan**, the Nabob of Surat and a rich and powerful man, followed this example and arranged for his brother to be declared Nabob of the citadel. The two brothers then looked upon the entire province as their **patrimony** <term>patrimony</term> <note>an estate or inheritance from one's father or ancestors</note> and acquired immense wealth.

**Teg Beg Khan** died in 1746 without children, leaving his fortune to his relatives. This inheritance elevated several of them to a status that enabled them to aspire to the government of the city. His brother died the following year, and his widow—an extremely wealthy and ambitious woman—strove to make her son-in-law **Nabob** <note>original: "Nabob"; a provincial governor or high-ranking official</note> of both the town and the **citadel** <note>a fortress protecting a city</note> at once.

The contest between the different competitors for supreme authority produced a civil war in the city of **Surat**, similar to those that arise from time to time among the **Begs** <note>original: "Begs"; high-ranking administrative or military officers in the Ottoman Empire, here referring to those in Egypt</note> of **Cairo**, and of which we in Europe can form no concept. Each of the rivals raised as many troops as he possibly could; with these, he stationed <note>original: "cantoned"</note> and entrenched himself in his houses and gardens, and from time to time endeavored to surprise or drive away his opponents. During these hostile operations, which did not result in great slaughter, the inhabitants were content to simply shut the gates nearest to the scene of action and continued to go about their ordinary affairs without fear of being pillaged. Indeed, they were sure of receiving compensation whenever any accidental injury was done to any person because of the disturbances. Consequently, trade suffered no interruption.

In 1759, the Council of **Bombay** sent Mr. Spencer—one of their members and a capable man beloved by the Indians—to Surat with a considerable military force.

Under this title <note>Referring to the office of Admiral granted by the Mughal Emperor</note>, the Company enjoys a third of the revenue from the customs of this city, along with other even more substantial sources of income. The English are, at present, the actual sovereigns of Surat. They keep the **Nabob** <note>original: "Nabob"; a provincial governor</note> of the city in a state of absolute dependence, allowing him only enough income to live in a manner befitting his rank. The Indians are partially content with their new masters. The merchants are no longer in danger of the greedy extortions <note>original: "avaritious extortions"</note> of the former Nabobs; yet they complain of the selfish spirit of these new rulers. 

The Indians do not dare to set sail without a passport <note>A maritime permit or "dustuck" required for safe passage</note> from the Admiral. When the English wish to send goods to any specific port, the Indians are denied passports to that same port until the monsoon season is over. Meanwhile, the English are favored, ensuring they have all the time necessary to dominate the market first. I have seen instances of this myself; if such practices are frequently repeated, they will undoubtedly ruin the trade of the native inhabitants.

## CHAPTER 5.

### *Trade of Surat.*

The extensive trade conducted in Surat makes this city the warehouse for the most precious products of India <note>original: "Indostan"; a historical name for the Indian subcontinent, specifically the northern regions</note>. An immense quantity of goods is brought here from the interior parts of the empire, which merchants carry in their ships to the Arabian Gulf <note>original: "Arabic Gulph"; in this period, the term often referred specifically to the Red Sea</note>, the Persian Gulf, the Malabar Coast, the Coromandel Coast, and even to China. The provinces near this city are full of manufacturing of all sorts.

Shipbuilding is a branch of the business carried on here. In this art, the Indians are strict imitators of the Europeans, but they have a great abundance of that excellent wood called **teak** <note>original: "Tek"</note> at a low price. This wood is not liable to be attacked by worms and is so durable that there are ships to be seen at Surat that are 90 years old and are still in a condition to sail the sea.

Of the foreign nations, the Dutch have the most significant establishment at Surat after the English. They have a director, several merchants, a number of clerks <note>original: "writers"; the entry-level administrative rank for employees of the East India companies</note> and servants, and a few soldiers. Their trade has, however,

Ships belonging to nations that have no permanent establishments in the city sometimes arrive at Surat. A Danish vessel put in here while the citadel was besieged and was favored with the protection of the English, to whom the captain provided good service during that event.

## CHAPTER VI.

### *Manners of the Hindus.*

**The** Hindus <note>original: "Hindoos"</note> are the original <note>original: "primary"</note> inhabitants of the vast empire of Hindustan <note>original: "Indostan"</note>. Having lived among these people in Bombay and Surat, I shall here bring together some observations which I made regarding the Hindus in those two cities, and also regarding the *Parsees* <note>original: "Persees"</note>, a foreign <note>original: "stranger"</note> colony settled in this part of India.

These people, perhaps the earliest civilized nation in the world, are mild, hardworking <note>original: "laborious"</note>, and naturally virtuous in their dispositions. All who have opportunities to observe the lives of the Hindus admire their patience, integrity <note>original: "probity"</note>, and benevolence; but they are at the same time the most socially exclusive <note>original: "unsocial"</note> people in the world. By their customs <note>original: "manners"</note> and religious principles, the Hindus distance themselves not only from other nations, whom they consider to be impure races, but even the different castes <note>original: "casts"</note> or tribes among themselves have little mutual interaction. No Hindu will eat with a stranger, nor will any Hindu of a superior caste eat with another of a caste that is inferior. A poor servant, if he were a *Brahmin* <note>original: "Bramin"; the highest priestly caste in Hindu society</note>, would think himself dishonored <note>Note: text continues from the catchword "honoured" on the next page</note>

It is generally known that the Indians are divided into a number of tribes or castes. As far as I could learn, there are four principal castes: the *Brahmins* <note>original: "Bramins"</note>, or priests; the *Rajputs*, or men of the sword; the *Banias*, or merchants; and those of the artisans and laborers. These four general castes are subdivided into more than eighty others, each of which has its own ceremonies and patron deities, as I have been assured by several people.

Those permanent divisions have led some travelers into the mistake of thinking that a son was always obliged to follow his father's profession. While a son may not leave his native caste, he may choose among the various employments which are practiced by that caste. There are *Brahmins* who hold sovereign authority; for example, the prince of the *Marathas* <note>original: "Mahrattas"</note>. ### CHAPTER VII.

#### *Regarding the Religion of the Hindus.*

A European wishing to acquire a knowledge of the religion of these people cannot gain much information from the Brahmins <note>original: "Bramins" — the priestly caste of India</note>, who never study any European languages. I was acquainted with some Banians <note>original: "Banians" — a caste of merchants and traders who often acted as middlemen for Europeans</note> who spoke English, and from them I received some knowledge on this subject <note>original: "on this head"</note>.

They all unanimously assured me that the most sensible and enlightened Hindus <note>original: "Hindoos"</note> acknowledged and worshipped only one Supreme Being. However, the Brahmins have introduced inferior deities suited to the weak understanding of the common people, who could not comprehend abstract ideas if they were not represented by images. They also agreed that the Brahmins had, for their own purposes, gradually cluttered the original simplicity of their religion with absurd fables and ridiculous superstitions. I mentioned their passionate veneration for the cow and their various depictions of her. To this, they replied that in those images they revered only the divine goodness, which had

I could learn nothing certain concerning their inferior deities, whom they seem to revere more as saints and patrons. A Banian <note>original: "Banian" — a member of the Hindu merchant caste</note> compared their three principal deities, *Brahma, Vishnu,* and *Mahadeva* <note>original: "Medeo" — Shiva is often referred to as Mahadeva, meaning "Great God"</note>, to the Christian Trinity.

The Hindus <note>original: "Hindoos"</note> all believe in the doctrine of <term>metempsychosis</term> <note>the transmigration of souls; reincarnation</note>, and of the purification of souls by their passage through several different bodies. This doctrine is not, however, the only cause of their abstinence from eating anything that has life in it. In hot countries, the meat of animals in general, and of the ox in particular, is thought to be very unhealthy food. The Rajputs <note>original: "Rajaputs"</note> eat meat, and the Marathas <note>original: "Mahrattas"</note> provide the Europeans whom they take as prisoners in war with animal food without any hesitation <note>original: "without scruple"</note>. It might be supposed that the remarkable kindness the Indians show toward animals takes its origin from this opinion.

The religious requirement <note>original: "precept"</note> of purification with water is rigidly observed throughout all India. At Surat, I saw every morning crowds of women and young girls going out to bathe in the *Tapti* <note>original: "Tappi" — the Tapti River in Gujarat</note>. They gave their clothes to some Brahmins who sat on the banks, and, after washing, changed their wet clothes for dry dresses with such skill <note>original: "dexterity"</note> that not the smallest part of the body could be seen. The Brahmins then made a red mark <note>likely a tilak, a mark worn on the forehead for religious reasons</note>

### CHAPTER VIII.

### *Of the Parsis.* <note>original: "Persees"</note>

At Bombay, at Surat, and in the vicinity of these cities, there is a colony of ancient Persians who took refuge in India when their country was conquered by the Muslim <note>original: "Mahometan"</note> Arabs eleven centuries ago <note>original: "since"</note>. They are called <term>Parsis</term> <note>original: "Persees"; followers of the Zoroastrian faith who fled Persia to avoid religious persecution</note>. Being well-regarded <note>original: "beloved"</note> by the Hindus, they have increased in number <note>original: "multiply exceedingly"</note>; whereas their countrymen in the province of Kerman <note>original: "Keman"</note> are visibly diminishing under the yoke of the Muslim Persians.

They are a gentle, quiet, and industrious people <note>original: "race"</note>. They live in great harmony among themselves, make collective contributions for the aid of their poor, and allow <note>original: "suffer"</note> none of their number to ask for charity <note>original: "alms"</note> from people of a different religion. They are equally ready to employ their money

When a Parsi <note>original: "Persee"</note> behaves badly, he is expelled from their communion. They dedicate themselves to trade and practice all kinds of professions.

The Parsis have as little knowledge of circumcision as the Hindus <note>original: "Hindoos"</note>. Among them, a man marries only one wife and never takes a second, unless the first happens to be barren. They arrange the marriage of their children <note>original: "give their children in marriage"</note> at six years of age; however, the young couple continues to live apart in the houses of their parents until they reach the age of puberty. Their dress is the same as that of the Hindus, except that they wear a tuft of hair under each ear, like the modern Persians. They are very fond of <note>original: "addicted to"</note> astrology, although they are not very skilled in astronomy.

They retain the unique <note>original: "singular"</note> custom of exposing their dead to be eaten by birds of prey, instead of burying or cremating <note>original: "interring or burning"</note> them. On a hill in Bombay, I saw a round tower covered with wooden planks where the Parsis lay out their dead. <note>This refers to a Dakhma, or Tower of Silence.</note> When the flesh has been eaten <note>original: "devoured"</note>, they move the bones into two chambers at the base of the tower.

The Parsis, followers of the religion of *Zerdust* <note>original: "Zer-dust"; the Persian name for Zoroaster</note> or *Zoroaster*, worship only one God, who is Eternal and Almighty. They do, however, pay a certain respect <note>original: "worship"</note> to the sun, the moon, the stars, and to

Their respect for the element of fire leads them to keep a sacred fire constantly burning, which they feed with fragrant <note>original: "odoriferous"</note> wood, both in their temples and in the homes of wealthy private individuals <note>original: "private persons, who are in easy circumstances"</note>. In one of their temples in Bombay <note>modern Mumbai</note>, I saw a fire which had burned unextinguished for two centuries. They never blow out a light, so that their breath does not pollute <note>original: "foil"</note> the purity of the fire.

The religion of the Parsis <note>original: "Persees"</note> requires ritual purifications as strictly as that of the Hindus. The followers of Zoroaster <note>original: "Zerdust"</note> are not, however, required to abstain from eating meat. They have accustomed themselves to refrain from the flesh of the ox <note>beef</note> because their ancestors promised the Indian prince who received them into his dominions <note>This refers to the legendary King Jadi Rana who granted the Parsis refuge in Gujarat</note> that they would never kill horned cattle. They continue to observe this promise even under the rule of Christians and Muslims <note>original: "Mahometans"</note>. Curiously, they consider the horse to be the most impure of all animals and regard it with extreme dislike <note>original: "aversion"</note>.

Their festivals, called *Gahambars* <note>original: "Ghumbars"; these are six seasonal festivals in the Zoroastrian calendar</note>, which occur frequently and last for five days on each occasion, are all commemorations of different parts of the work of Creation. They do not celebrate them with grandeur <note>original: "splendour"</note> or with any particular ceremonies, but simply dress in better clothing during those five days.

An European who has none but natives of the country in his service would find it no easy matter to obtain these dishes if he should wish to eat a hare and bacon. The Hindu <note>original: "Hindoo"</note> would not bring them to him, for he dares not touch a dead body <note>referring to ritual impurity associated with handling meat or carcasses in many Hindu traditions</note>; nor would the Parsi, because the hare is an unclean animal <note>In Zoroastrianism, the hare was traditionally classified as a "khrafstra"—a harmful or spiritually unclean animal</note>; nor yet the Muslim <note>original: "Mussulman"</note>, for he dares not touch such dishes <note>referring to the Islamic prohibition of pork and bacon</note>.
